At least one other cast member previously complained to Ofcom about their treatment on the show, but the watchdog dismissed their complaint as it found the broadcaster had no case to answer.

An Ofcom spokesperson said such complaints are considered "on a case-by-case basis through a detailed and careful assessment process".

News.title: Lamine Yamal celebrates World Cup win with little brother who charmed fans
News.content:
Spanish footballer Lamine Yamal may have lifted the World Cup but it is his little brother Kenye who appears to have stolen the spotlight.

The three-year-old quickly become an internet sensation after footage of his exuberant celebrations following Spain's 1-0 victory over Argentina spread across social media on Sunday.

While the footballer, just 19 himself, continued his rise by helping Spain achieve football's biggest prize, attention swiftly turned to his younger brother's joyful reactions from the sidelines.

From sticking out his tongue on the big screen to wildly cheering on his older brother, Kenye has been hailed by fans as one of the unexpected breakout stars of the 2026 tournament.

News.title: Prisons minister Lord Timpson quits government
News.content:
The prisons minister has resigned from the government, the BBC has been told.

Lord James Timpson was appointed to the role in July 2024 after leaving his job as CEO of the Timpson group, a business which provides key cutting and shoe repair services and employs hundreds of former prisoners.

His arrival in government was greeted with much fanfare by some in the Labour Party and described as "radical" and "innovative".

But in a departing statement on Monday, seen exclusively by the BBC, Lord Timpson said he was stepping down and it was an "honour" to serve in the post.

His statement did not give a specific reason for resigning, but it is understood he feels he has done as much as he can in the role.

Prisons in England and Wales were at crisis point, reaching almost full capacity, when he first entered Sir Keir Starmer's government.

He oversaw the controversial early release scheme which saw tens of thousands of inmates let out to create more space in jails.

His critics will argue prisons continue to be violent, drug infused and overcrowded, while probation officers still report being overworked and unable to cope.

But figures do show assaults against staff and self-harm in prisons are falling.

Lord Timpson said in his resignation statement that he had left "our prisons and probation service in a much healthier and happier state than two years ago".

He added: "I'm proud to have become the longest-serving minister in this role for 15 years. I'm also proud that 75% of prisons and 90% of probation teams are now performing better than when I started.

"Self-harm, violence and assaults on staff are all down, and fewer people are leaving prison without a home to go to, a measure of dignity I care about deeply."

He also pointed to the Women's Justice Board he established, saying he "believe[s] most women should not be in prison at all" and "diverting them away from custody, helping them with often chaotic, damaged, and addicted lives, is one of the changes I'm proud to have achieved".

His critics may question why he is leaving before the Sentencing Act 2026 is enacted in September, when more people are expected to be released early and further criminals will serve their sentences in the community.

A source in the Ministry of Justice told the BBC: "We're gutted he's going but the new person is going to have their work cut out to get their head round what's round the corner."

News.title: South East Water hosepipe ban to affect 2.4 million people
News.content:
A hosepipe ban has been expanded to cover 2.4 million people across the south of England after record-breaking temperatures.

South East Water's ban now includes parts of Sussex, Surrey, Hampshire and Berkshire - an extra 1.5m customers. A ban in parts of Kent has been in force since 3 July.

Douglas Whitfield, SEW's water supply director, said it was "deeply sorry" and "incredibly grateful to everyone helping us protect water supplies" after exceptionally hot and dry weather.

Eastbourne MP Josh Babarinde said he was "appalled", calling it "the direct result of years of underinvestment in upgrading infrastructure and building resilience".

Under the restrictions, households in the affected area will be banned from using a hosepipe in their homes for tasks including cleaning, filling ponds, or watering plants.

The ban will officially come in from 00:01 BST on Saturday, but SEW has asked its customers to abide by the restrictions immediately.

The UK record for the hottest day in June was broken for a third day in a row last month, with temperatures reaching 37.3C, the Met Office said.

News.title: Sara Sharif killer wants inquest with jury
News.content:
The woman who murdered her stepdaughter Sara Sharif has asked for the inquest into her death to be held in front of a jury.

Beinash Batool and Sara's father Urfan Sharif were jailed for life in 2024 after the 10-year-old was found dead at the family home in Woking.

She had been violently abused in a "campaign of torture" lasting two years.

Bite marks, an iron burn and scalding from hot water were among dozens of injuries found on her body in a post-mortem examination.

On Monday, Batool's lawyer Dr Anton van Dellen said jurors would help determine if Sara was failed by people who were scared of being accused of racism.

"This is just the type of judgement where a diverse local jury would provide a helpful perspective," he added.

A review into the 10-year-old's death found that services in Surrey failed to properly investigate why Sara started wearing a hijab - that covered her bruising - for "fear of causing offence".

Neighbours also said they were worried about "being branded as being racist" if they reported concerns.

News.title: Ryanair profits drop as Iran war puts off passengers and lifts fuel costs
News.content:
Ryanair's profits have fallen sharply as war in the Middle East sent jet fuel prices soaring and customers reluctant to book flights.

The Irish airline's pre-tax profits dropped 34% to â¬593m (Â£503m) between April and June while sales were flat as the company was forced to cut fares to stimulate demand.

Ryanair also said it expects summer fares to be slightly lower than last year due to "consumer hesitancy" around air travel.

The price of fuelling a plane has jumped since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February and while Ryanair said it had "hedged" or struck deals for the most future fuel costs, those not included in these arrangements had more than doubled.

Crude oil prices hit $90 (Â£67) a barrel for the first time in a month on Monday, before falling back slightly, after a weekend of intense exchanges of fire between the US and Iran.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz â an essential route for global oil and gas supplies â has ground to a halt.

An interim peace deal last month brought some respite to oil and energy prices, but they spiked again as negotiations broke down and fighting resumed.

The airline warned that its results for the year will be "highly sensitive" to external factors such as conflict escalation in the Middle East and Ukraine as well as the price of unhedged jet fuel.

Fares for for the key summer period between July and September are on track to be "modestly" lower than last year, with many passengers booking closer to departure than normal.

The firm's finance chief, Neil Sorahan, said flights on its popular Mediterranean routes were still full. "People [are] as keen to get away as ever, albeit booking just a little bit later," he said.

Between April and June, Ryanair's revenue ticked up 1% to â¬4.4bn.

While passenger numbers rose 6% to 6.1 million- helped by the Easter holiday in April - fares fell by 6% as the airline reduced fares to entice flyers concerned about the Iran war.

Ryanair's share price fell 5% on Monday.

Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, said Ryanair was in a better position than many of its rivals, but nonetheless "visibility is worse than San Francisco airport when the fog sets in".

"The renewed escalation in hostilities in the Middle East is unhelpful and without a lasting resolution, challenging times for the airline and travel space look set to continue."

News.title: Ofcom unable to take further legal action against suicide forum
News.content:
Ofcom said it is unable to take further legal action against a pro-suicide forum which campaigners say has been linked to over 130 UK deaths.

The regulator said, external the site had blocked access for the "vast majority" of UK users, and it had "no further legal routes available" under the Online Safety Act.

But it accepted people would still be able to access the forum by using a VPN, which hides your location online.

Andy Burrows, chief executive of the Molly Rose Foundation, said the decision to take no further legal action would "result in more lost lives" and that announcing it on the day a new prime minister was named showed "an utter lack of moral courage".

In response, an Ofcom spokesperson said it had made the decision a "matter of days ago" following "months of work to exhaust all possible legal routes".

They said bereaved families were informed of the decision this morning after being contacted last week.

"In that context, we do not consider it appropriate to delay the announcement further to accommodate today's political developments," they said.

Meanwhile, Ofcom enforcement director Suzanne Cater said the regulator had used its powers "to the fullest extent possible".

"We'll continue to monitor the forum closely to check the geoblock remains in place," she said.

The geoblock means people based in the UK are unable to access the site, unless they mask their location through a VPN or similar means.

Ofcom said it was working with the government to explore whether its enforcement powers should be strengthened.

In particular, this concerns its ability to get a website blocking order through the courts, which would legally mandate internet service providers in the UK to block the website.

The regulator says it has reached the limit of what it can legally do under the Online Safety Act because the forum has implemented the geoblock.

The BBC has approached the government for comment.

News.title: 'Scrutiny' needed over baby's death, court hears
News.content:
Preston had been taken to Blackpool Victoria Hospital three times before his death and seen by a "battery of professionals" including medical staff, social workers and welfare officers from various bodies.

Wilson told the hearing an inquest had initially been opened shortly after Preston's death but was then suspended while police investigated, culminating in the trial and conviction of his adoptive parents.

Wilson said he had to consider whether an inquest should continue, given "relevant issues" had already been heard during the eight-week criminal trial.

However, while he said he would not make a final decision on Monday, subject to submissions from lawyers for other public bodies, it was "highly likely" one would take place, probably in the autumn of next year.

He said: "I feel there's sufficient reason to resume. There are acts and omissions of public authorities that need to be scrutinised in a public hearing in which Preston's family can participate.

"It's clearly going to be a wide-ranging inquiry."

The coroner said he was aware there had been calls for a public inquiry, but his role meant that was not a matter for himself to consider, but to proceed on the basis of whether or not to hold an inquest.

The court heard Oldham Safeguarding Children's Partnership, had resumed a review into Preston's death, following its suspension for the criminal trial to take place.

This review was likely only to be completed by January 2027, and the inquest cannot be held before then, the court heard.

Much of the hearing dealt with which people or public bodies should be legally represented at any inquest.

They included Preston's biological mother and grandmother, Sara and Debbie Davey, neither of whom were present for the hearing but were represented by lawyers in court.

Preston was born while his mother was in custody and a place in a mother and baby unit in prison was refused, the court heard.

Instead, he was taken from her by a court order from Oldham Council and placed with temporary adoptive parents before being adopted by Varley and McGowan.

News.title: Fire crews to remain at Arthur's Seat for days after blaze
News.content:
Firefighters are expected to remain at Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh "for a couple of days" following a large blaze on Sunday evening.

Small plumes of smoke could still be seen on Monday morning along Salisbury Crags and large swathes of vegetation below the cliff face had been burned black.

Six fire engines were sent to tackle the the grassfire on the slope between the Scottish Parliament and St Leonard's with crews working overnight to douse the flames and dampen hotspots.

The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) said there were "no reported casualties" but Police Scotland said Queen's Drive, the road that encircles the Holyrood Park hills, remained closed to all vehicles.

It is the second fire in the last three months at the landmark, an ancient extinct volcano that offers panoramic views of the Scottish capital.

Edinburgh University student Mahek Jayantilial, who lives near Arthur's Seat, said she could see the fire from her window.

"I was a bit worried because I thought the fire would come this way, but thankfully there's enough concrete here to stop it," the 24-year-old said.

News.title: Pupil not guilty of trying to murder history teacher after stabbing her in the head
News.content:
A pupil has been found not guilty of attempted murder after stabbing his teacher in the head with a kitchen knife.

The boy, 16, followed Vicki Williams into her empty classroom at Milford Haven Comprehensive School in Pembrokeshire, after asking for help with his history work on 5 February.

He pulled a knife from his bag and lunged at her. Williams told a jury at Swansea Crown Court she feared she would die.

On Monday, he was found not guilty of attempted murder but guilty of wounding with intent, and unlawful wounding. He will be sentenced on 3 September.

The boy had previously pleaded guilty to possessing a kitchen knife on the school grounds.

Judge Paul Thomas KC accepted a majority verdict on the charge of wounding with intent, which meant at least 10 jurors agreed following four hours deliberation.

During the attack, Williams grabbed the knife, pushed the boy back with her legs, and screamed.

She received injuries to her head, back and hands after the attack.

She said the look on the teenager's face was one of "pure hatred".

During a police interview, Williams said how the boy, who was 15 at the time and who cannot be named due to his age, came to her classroom "cool and collected" at the end of the school day to ask if his "work was correct".

She said that "got [her] confused" because he had "never seemed bothered before".

It was when he shut the door to the classroom, saying it was cold, that "alarm bells" began to ring in her head.

Williams said he was trying to "keep her talking" while he was "trying to find something in his bag".

"I ask him again, 'are you sure you're alright?' And then he pulls [the knife] out of the bag and lunges at me," she said.

The boy told the court Williams had seen him with the knife and "tried to grab it" from him. He said he "accidentally assaulted her" during the struggle.

She told the court she believed she was about to die, thinking: "I'm fearful that I am dying, I've seen the knife, I know I've been stabbed, all I'm thinking at that point is, 'I need help'."

Williams said the attack "came out of nowhere".

Rachel Reeves and David Lammy are among a number of senior ministers set to leave government as the new prime minister prepares to appoint his new cabinet.

These ministers will make up the top team in his new government, helping to deliver the policy agenda that he sets out.

Ahead of the major reshuffle, business secretary Peter Kyle, and housing secretary Steve Reed, have both also resigned.

Mr Burnham has been tight-lipped on his choice of appointments in the run-up to his inauguration, with speculation reaching fever pitch over the weekend.

Allies of Ms Reeves have said that she was offered a “big job” in government but decided to decline it. In her resignation statement, she wished “the very best of luck” to her successor, Mr Burnham and his cabinet.

She wrote: “It has been the privilege of my life to serve as the Chancellor of the Exchequer.

“The economy today is stronger, fairer and more resilient because of the choices we have taken as a Labour Government over the past two years.”

Home secretary Shabana Mahmood is understood to be Mr Burnham’s favourite to be the next chancellor, in a move that some have warned could divide Labour MPs.

Meanwhile, the veteran politician’s long-time ally Ed Miliband is also tipped for a promotion from his current energy brief. Insiders have hinted that he may be bound for the role of foreign secretary after initially being linked to the Treasury job himself.

For the latest political updates on Andy Burnham’s first day as prime minister, follow The Independent’s live blog

An MP from 2001 to 2017, Mr Burnham has many allies in the halls of Westminster whom he may want to keep close as he forges a new path as prime minister.

The former mayor was a frontbencher during Gordon Brown’s administration – lasting from 2007 to 2010 – in a cabinet which at points also included current ministers Ed Miliband, Yvette Cooper, Pat McFadden and John Healey.

The former Manchester mayor had been tight-lipped on his choice of appointments in the run-up to his inauguration ( Lauren Hurley/No 10 Downing St )

Delivering his inaugural speech on the steps of Number 10, Mr Burnham urged people to “pull me with me” to “build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose and positivity”.

“Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again, the moment we bring back hope,” he said.

During his six-minute address, he said he would set out a ten-year plan for Britain later this year, and measure to tackle the cost of living on Tuesday to give people “breathing space now”.

He added: “I am acutely conscious that I am the sixth person in the last 10 years to walk up this street, the seventh prime minister since 2016, making this a moment for reflection and new resolution.

“It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge.”

In the crowd for Mr Burnham’s speech was his long-term friend and ally, Liverpool mayor Steve Rotheram, former footballer Peter Reid, who played for Mr Burnham’s favourite team Everton, and Josh Simons, the former MP who stood in Makerfield to enable his return to Westminster.

This page will regularly be updated as the latest appointments are announced. Refresh or bookmark this page for updates.

Andy Burnham has made the surprise appointment of John Healey as his chancellor, as he ruthlessly purged the cabinet after entering Downing Street promising a “circuit-breaker” moment for Britain.

It follows weeks of speculation that Mr Burnham was planning to give the job to Ed Miliband or Shabana Mahmood, but there were fears either choice would be divisive within the Labour Party.

Mr Healey, who resigned from Sir Keir Starmer's government in a row over defence spending, gained respect in the party after a strong run as defence secretary – and his appointment shows Mr Burnham's commitment to bolstering Britain's military capabilities.

Mr Burnham used his first speech as prime minister to vow to end decades of failure by eradicating rough sleeping and overhauling social care, promising his arrival in Downing Street will be a “circuit-breaker” moment for Britain.

After meeting King Charles at Buckingham Palace, the new PM admitted politicians “needed to raise their game” and be better, insisting he would “make Britain believe and hope again” by winning over fed-up voters.

open image in gallery John Healey has been appointed chancellor ( Getty )

He reiterated his promise to move power outside of Westminster and said he would set out a 10-year plan later this year, adding: “Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again.”

In a sign of change he purged Starmer loyalists including former chancellor Rachel Reeves and deputy PM David Lammy.

In a short speech delivered without a lectern, Mr Burnham said: “I am acutely conscious that I am the sixth person in the last 10 years to walk up this street, the seventh prime minister since 2016, making this a moment for reflection and new resolution.

“It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge.”

In his first promise as prime minister, he said he would “end rough sleeping in our country”, having visited the homelessness charity The Passage in London’s Victoria earlier on Monday.

He also declared he would reduce Britain’s welfare bill by helping more young people into work, building more council homes and creating what he described as a “preventative state”, investing in people’s success rather than paying for failure.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham enters Downing Street after becoming prime minister ( AFP/Getty )

This, he said, “is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules, and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

He made it clear that his first priority would be to tackle the cost-of-living crisis, teasing an announcement in the next 24 hours to address issues such as bus fare or rent freezes, or a reduction in energy bills.

Earlier, Sir Keir gave his goodbye speech in Downing Street before visiting Buckingham Palace.

He said he had offered Mr Burnham his “full support” and he was leaving “with good grace and a smile”.

However, some of the other cabinet ministers to lose their jobs were less generous.

open image in gallery Deputy prime minister David Lammy and chancellor Rachel Reeves have lost their jobs ( PA Wire )

In a barbed remark, Mr Reed, who was ousted as communities secretary, wrote: “Keir Starmer showed me loyalty by appointing me to his cabinet. I make no apology for returning that loyalty. It’s what is expected of functioning teams, and I hope those who did not show loyalty to Keir will now show it to you.

“I’m proud I acted with integrity at every step over the turbulent last few months.”

Mr Lammy noted: “I would have been proud to continue serving in cabinet. But a new prime minister is entitled to build his own team.”

Speaking to journalists in the Downing Street rose garden, Mr Burnham made it clear that as well as ending rough sleeping, he wanted to ensure that he dealt with the social care crisis before his time in Downing Street came to an end.

The issue is unfinished business for Mr Burnham, who failed to get cross party consensus in 2009 when he was health secretary when his proposal for a levy was attacked by the Tories as “a death tax.”

Mr Burnham has made it clear that it is more personal to him now with his father suffering from Alzheimer’s making him unaware that his son is now PM.

He said: “I think the country needs to step back here and say, 'How have we let a situation kind of just roll on, where we know it's a major issue, and yet no one's got the courage to fix it?'

“I just think that's quite damning, really, of my generation of politicians. Has no one got the ability anymore to say: 'Right, it is a difficult thing, but we're going to do it'?

“If I look at the National Health Service right now, what I hear from people is that corridor care is becoming the norm all year round, not just in winter time, and the standards in relation to A&E are just not achievable in terms of the 90-plus percent of people coming through in four hours.”

open image in gallery Starmer says goodbye to Downing Street as he hugs his wife Victoria ( Getty )

He will also look at the way people are being made to pay more income tax through thresholds being frozen, an issue he said was the biggest complaint over voters in Makerfield during the recent by-election campaign which brought him back into parliament.

Mr Burnham though insisted he is “prudent”, and will stick to the former chancellor’s ’ fiscal rules on borrowing which she set as chancellor before being sacked.

After his speech, Mr Burnham received hugs, applause and a kiss from his wife Marie-France van Heel, before the pair entered the black door of No 10 to be greeted by cabinet secretary Dame Antonia Romeo and clapped in by staff.

News.title: Spain v Argentina LIVE: Latest updates from trophy parade as World Cup champions bask in glory
News.content:
Argentina spark shocking brawl with Spain at full time in World Cup final

Spain’s triumphant World Cup champions have arrived back in Madrid ahead of an extravagant trophy parade through the streets of the capital, while Argentina were left to return home in disgrace following the ugly scenes at the end of their final defeat in New Jersey.

Spain have plenty to celebrate after Ferran Torres’ goal secured their second men’s World Cup triumph, and it was victory for football too after Argentina offered little throughout the match and then reacted badly after the final whistle. Fifa are set to investigate the post-match scenes before deciding whether to take additional disciplinary action.

A bizarre and, at times, deeply weird final was a dire spectacle for 90 minutes. But Spain then finally made the breakthrough when Torres calmly hammered home at the start of the second half of extra time. It meant Lionel Messi was denied on surely his final World Cup appearance, with the aftermath further souring the occasion for the 39-year-old football icon.

Donald Trump then unsurprisingly inserted himself into things post-match as he lurked towards the edge of Spain’s trophy lift to ensure he was in the photo, despite Gianni Infantino trying to usher him away, after presenting the Spanish players with medals and the trophy.

Follow all of the fallout from the World Cup final in our live blog below

Government borrowing costs lifted higher and the value of the pound weakened amid caution from City traders ahead of John Healey’s appointment as the next Chancellor of the Exchequer.

Andy Burnham appointed the former defence secretary in a surprise move after speculation that Shabana Mahmood and Ed Miliband had been frontrunners for the role.

The appointment followed a largely steady session for the financial markets on Monday after Andy Burnham officially became the next Prime Minister.

open image in gallery Rachel Reeves lost the role of chancellor as part of Andy Burnham’s Cabinet reshuffle (Yui Mok/PA) ( PA Wire )

However, they took a downturn during the afternoon after Mr Burnham told reporters he would use “any flexibility” he could find within existing fiscal rules.

The yield on 10-year Government bonds, called gilts, moved eight basis points higher to 5.049% at the end of London trading.

It meant the cost of UK state borrowing had risen to its highest level for around two months.

The value of gilts decrease as the yield on them increases.

Mr Burnham said he will “stick to the fiscal rules” agreed by Sir Keir Starmer’s administration and added he will not be “taking risks with the economy”.

As the new Prime Minister started to make appointments for his first Cabinet, Rachel Reeves confirmed she had left the role of chancellor.

Mr Healey will be tasked with helping steer the country through a testing economic situation.

Growth remains weak, state borrowing is elevated, the national debt is at its highest level since the 1960s and the labour market faces continued pressure.

Caffeine lovers rejoice: The human body can safely handle an astonishing amount of coffee, according to a new statement from the American Heart Association.

Drinking up to five cups of black coffee each day appears to lower the risk of several cardiovascular conditions, including stroke, heart failure and heart disease. The latter is America’s top killer, accounting for over 919,000 deaths a year.

So it’s good news for the two-thirds of adults who drink coffee every day. Regularly consuming caffeinated beverages has also been linked to a lower risk of developing dementia and a reduced risk of cancer.

But consuming more than five cups - and exceeding the 400-milligram daily caffeine limit deemed safe by most experts - can be harmful to health, too, the association warned. Higher amounts may lead to seizures, sudden high blood pressure and breathing issues.

And beware of energy shots - which may contain 40-69 milligrams of caffeine per fluid ounce - between three and four times that of an eight-ounce cup of coffee.

Drinking up to five cups of black coffee each day appears to lower the risk of several cardiovascular conditions, including stroke, heart failure and heart disease ( AFP/Getty )

“Energy drinks, bars, gels and caffeine-based supplements often contain other added ingredients that may increase the absorption of caffeine, may accelerate its effects on the body, may raise blood pressure and increase the risk of cardiovascular harm,” the American Heart Association stated.

More research is necessary to investigate different health impacts of various types of caffeine products, the group added, noting that everyone responds to caffeine differently.

“What may be a reasonable amount for one person could cause unwanted effects, such as heart palpitations, anxiety or sleep disruption, in another,” Dr. Gregory Marcus, a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine, explained in a statement shared by the association.

“That’s why it’s important to pay attention to how your body responds to caffeine and talk with your healthcare team about what is right for you,” he said.

For some people, just a couple of cups of coffee can result in symptoms, like increased heart rate, heart palpitations, high blood pressure, insomnia, anxiety, nausea and upset stomach, headaches and the jitters, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration warns.

Toxic effects like seizures can occur when consuming around 1,200 milligrams, the agency says.

Fortunately, the average American only drinks around three cups a day - under the 400 milligram limit.

The hosts of The View have torn into Donald Trump over his appearance at Sunday’s World Cup final.

Trump was on hand to help present medals and trophies at the conclusion of the match, which saw Spain defeat Argentina 1-0 in extra time at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium. He then forced his way into the team’s winning photo, much to the chagrin of viewers at home.

During Monday’s broadcast, the women of The View launched right into dissecting Trump’s appearance.

“I will say it did seem like some people got a very chilly — like a ‘boo’ chilly reception from the crowd,” Whoopi Goldberg said. While showing viewers a photo of Trump crashing the Spain team photo, Goldberg added: “Can I just point out he looks like somebody inserted his picture?”

Ana Navarro interjected: “He inserted himself. But I mean, it’s like, I don’t know how this guy thinks that he’s not gonna get booed in a stadium that’s full of Latin Americans and Spaniards.”

open image in gallery The hosts of 'The View' ripped into Trump crashing the Spain team photo after their victory ( PA )

She continued, thinking back to the Argentina team walking across the field to accept their medals from Trump and Fifa president Gianni Infantino: “If these guys weren’t on this field, if they were standing in front of a Home Depot, Trump’s eyes would be racially profiling them.”

Navarro then launched into a laundry list of statements Trump has made in recent months about Spain, including calling them “bad people.” She also pointed out that in March, Trump said: “Spain is a loser.”

She then looked into the camera and smiled: “Oh no they’re not.”

When approached for comment, White House spokesman Davis Ingle told The Independent: “Ana Navarro is an extremely unlikeable, talentless hack with a poorly rated TV show who clearly suffers from a severe and incurable disease known as Trump Derangement Syndrome. I lose braincells every time I have the displeasure of hearing her speak.”

open image in gallery The hosts of 'The View' tore into Donald Trump's appearance at the World Cup final ( ABC )

For most of Sunday’s match, Trump could be seen behind bullet-proof glass, with First Lady Melania Trump and Barron Trump also sitting alongside him for the game.

Later on, Trump became part of the Fifa ceremony — as he did last year when Chelsea won the Fifa Club World Cup in the same stadium after victory over Paris Saint-Germain — joining Reece James at the heart of the celebrations to lift the trophy.

The cringe-worthy moment prompted Infantino to scurry toward Trump in a feeble attempt to move the president from the Spain team photo. Several snaps captured the president on the outskirts of the photo before he moved away from the celebrations.

Spain triumphed 1-0 after extra time thanks to Ferran Torres’ 106th minute goal.

News.title: India approves first dengue vaccine as cases surge in South Asia
News.content:
India has approved its first dengue vaccine as cases of the mosquito-borne disease surge in South Asia.

Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical’s dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India’s drug regulator, the Centre Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

The global threat posed by dengue has been rising for years, as climate change, urbanisation and international travel aid the spread of the mosquitoes that transmit it.

The approval comes as hospitals across South Asia grapple with a surge in dengue infections.

In Sri Lanka, health authorities reported 2,652 new cases on Sunday alone, taking the total to 76,044 dengue cases so far this year. At least 53 people have died.

Bangladesh is also suffering a major outbreak with over 9,000 cases and 30 deaths that has piled pressure on its health system even as it battles a measles epidemic.

Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.

Its symptoms include fever, severe muscle pain, and in severe cases, shock and internal bleeding that can be fatal.

Although mortality is relatively low, outbreaks place a substantial burden on health systems.

Takeda’s QDENGA jab is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It can be given regardless of previous dengue infections.

“The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades,” the company said in a statement.

News.title: Burnham’s plan to restore UK aid spending
News.content:
Andy Burnham is planning to reverse the cuts to Britain’s aid budget made by his predecessors Sir Keir Starmer and Rishi Sunak, according to reports.

A roadmap for returning the UK to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income (GNI) on international aid will be drawn up as part of a major shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), The Independent reported.

Ed Miliband is set to be named Foreign Secretary and put in charge of overhauling Britain’s international development aims, as well as prioritising climate goals, senior Labour sources said.

The aid spending plan was absent from Mr Burnham’s brief first speech as Prime Minister, in which he pledged to end rough sleeping and bring down the welfare bill in order to fund defence and council housing.

But it follows anger within the Labour Party over what was seen as a broken manifesto promise, when Sir Keir and Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, slashed aid spending to 0.3 per cent of GNI.

Senior Labour MPs have been lobbying for a return to the 0.7 per cent commitment, a target first established by the United Nations in the 1970s.

It has since become a key yardstick for international efforts to reduce poverty and tackle major health issues like the HIV/AIDS epidemic, vaccine access, and maternal mortality in poor countries.

News.title: The best bars and nightlife in Lyon
News.content:
While drinking in this gourmet city remains firmly rooted in the surrounding Rhône Valley’s ancient wine-growing heritage, new-gen addresses have embraced world cocktail culture in style. They’re using Lyon’s long-envied gastronomic know-how and rich bounty of local seasonal produce to create some sensational new drinks and food pairings as only the French can. Artisanal spirits meanwhile are increasingly fashionable: cornichon gin, Mezcal-fuelled soirées at chef Carla Kirsch’s gourmet tacos joint in Croix-Rousse, and the stunning Christian Drouin gin and pine-needle liqueur cocktail with stick of Comté cheese to stir I recently had at Hôtel Dieu’s Le Dôme bar all spring to mind.

Come the warmer days of spring and summer, the city’s fervent café-life spills onto pretty pavement terraces, while floating bars moored along Les Berges du Rhône (the landscaped river banks of the Rhône’s Rive Gauche or Left Bank) hum with after-dark dance parties and festivities. Clubbing remains fairly mainstream.

News.title: How to have the perfect holiday in France’s gastronomic capital
News.content:
Calling all bon vivants. This is your city. Within seconds of tucking into a traditional andouillette (tripe sausage) or modern vegetarian cuisine in a jam-packed bistro, admiring fine art in a Renaissance abbey, or getting delightfully lost in a traboule (secret passageway) used by 19th-century silk weavers, you’ll quickly realise that Lyon is a city that knows how to live well.

Enthralling, cinematic and richly storied, after living here for 10 years, I still find myself being surprised by a walled garden I never knew, a fresque (wall mural) suddenly popping up on a riverfront wall, a new museum or river boat route.

Street-smart Romans first spotted the city’s extraordinary topography, founding Lugdunum (Lyon’s predecessor) in 43BC on the sunny slopes of Fourvière. And to this day, this basilica-crowned hill above Lyon’s quaint Unesco-listed Old Town (Vieux Lyon) is the perfect perch for clocking the mighty Rhône and Saône rivers that wend their way so gracefully through the centre.

The city’s quays, landscaped with peaceful water gardens and floating bars, buzz night and day – while culture lovers can explore a bounty of museums. Then there’s the gastronomy: among France’s finest, thanks to the unfaltering creativity and sass of city chefs, both past and present.

News.title: The 16 best things to do in Lyon
News.content:
Few dedicated foodies make the pilgrimage to Lyon without dining once chez Paul Bocuse, be it at the late chef’s mythical, out-of-town gastronomic temple in Collonges-au-Mont d’Or (which lost one of its three stars in 2020, having held three since 1965) or at the more affordable Comptoir Paul Bocuse inside landmark covered market Halles de Lyon Paul Bocuse. Across the street, admire a larger-than-life portrait of the iconic chef, frescoed onto the side of a building. Inside the market, the moules glacées (cold mussel ‘soup’) at oyster and shellfish specialist Maison Merle and a gooey round of Saint Marcellin cheese from Fromagerie La Mère Richard are other local legends. Avoid buying fruit and veg here unless you have to – weekly outdoor food markets elsewhere in the city are cheaper.

To sample future talent in the Lyonnais kitchen, mingle with students over lunch, dinner or drinks and live music at La Commune – an innovative food court that hosts chefs aspiring to open their own restaurant in Lyon. Resident chefs cook up a storm at La Commune for maximum six months, meaning an ever-changing rollcall of epicurean excitement at this unique culinary incubator.

To extend the experience further afield, consider a road trip along a section of the Vallée de la Gastronomie, stretching 620km (385 miles). In Lyon, the gourmet route delves into the secrets behind chef Joseph Viola’s award-winning duck foie gras and sweetbread pâté en croûte (think French-posh pork pie) and the city’s distinctive offal-based bouchon (Lyonnais bistro) cuisine.

News.title: Spain win World Cup in triumph of football over Argentine thuggery
News.content:
Spain should have won far more comfortably, but the European champions lived up to the claim made by their coach Luis de la Fuente and proved they are the best team in the world, having beaten the favourites France in the last four.

Spain won this tournament for the second time, 16 years after the first. Now there is just one nation chasing a “second star”, the one beaten by Argentina in Atlanta last Wednesday.

If England ever want to win this again then here is the blueprint. This is how the game should be played. Get the ball, keep the ball, love the ball, move the ball. Try to play. Be brave and stay brave. It is not complicated, but it requires a re-education.

Maybe one day English football will grow up and cherish ball-players of their own, rather than Manchester City signing Rodri, who was magnificent here until he tired, or Arsenal with Martín Zubimendi, who successfully replaced him.

Rodri was named player of the tournament, in recognition of the football his nation played and the 30-year-old’s importance to to their system. He is their heartbeat and metronome. England do not just need to find a Rodri, but cherish whoever that is.

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan: Newcastle and Liverpool legend dies aged 75 as tributes pour in
Sports.content:
It has been confirmed that Kevin Keegan, the Newcastle and Liverpool legend, has sadly died at the age of 75 after a battle with cancer

Kevin Keegan has sadly passed away at the age of 75 following a battle with cancer, his family have announced.

It was confirmed back in January that the legendary former Newcastle manager was being treated for cancer, with Keegan himself revealing the disease was at stage four last month during an appearance at a fan event.

A statement released by Keegan's family on Monday afternoon read: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75. The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

"Kevin, a double Ballon D’or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin’s incredible medical team for all their support. "This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

Sports.title: 'I met my boyhood hero Kevin Keegan - his honesty and sense of humour struck me'
Sports.content:
They say that you should never meet your heroes.

Kevin Keegan, a legend of the game and a hero to millions, was the exception to that rule.

Growing up on Tyneside, he was my idol at school because of his exploits with Liverpool, England, Hamburg and then of course my beloved Newcastle United, where he was a player and then manager.

As a kid with black curly hair, I bought a full England kit and the red, white and blue wristbands worn by my hero back in the 1970s and 80s, when I was still at school.

‌



Keegan was ahead of his time, the first star of the modern era, promoting Brut on TV and competing on BBC's 'Superstars'.

When I started working for the Mirror in 1993, I met him when he managed England, and later when he was in club football at Fulham.

View 4 Images Kevin Keegan with his old Liverpool team mate, the late, great Ray Clemence (Image: Bob Thomas Sports Photography via Getty Images)

Kevin Keegan's final picture and brave public appearance before sad death aged 75 READ MORE :

Kevin Keegan: Newcastle and Liverpool legend dies aged 75 as tributes pour in READ MORE :

Keegan made a point of coming to meet George Cohen when I accompanied the 1966 hero to his old club to discuss the sale of Cohen's World Cup medal.

‌



Fulham bought it for £80,000 and displayed it at the ground where Cohen had played with such distinction.

Keegan took care of George that day, making us both feel welcome while discussing playing for England and his memories of 1966.

I was always struck by his honesty, his friendliness even when times were hard - and his sense of humour.

I met 'King Kev', as he was known on Tyneside, for the last time there for the unveiling of Alan Shearer's statue in 2016.

‌



View 4 Images Kevin Keegan receives his OBE on November 9, 1982 (Image: Popperfoto via Getty Images)

He gave a friendly hello, recognising me from our previous meetings and recalling his time with Shearer.

He had signed the Premier League's all-time top scorer for a then world-record £15m while he was manager.

Surrounded by fans at the unveiling, he never refused an autograph request, and was perfectly at ease with the public.

‌



In fact, he was in his element with supporters, talking about the game he loved.

Keegan had the common touch, which is why he remained such a hugely popular figure throughout his career, even when his stint as England boss came to an untimely end.

In his last public appearance on Tyneside, on May 31 at the New Tyne Theatre, he spoke openly of his cancer diagnosis with the courage which he had displayed throughout his playing career.

View 4 Images Kevin Keegan in 1982, when he played for England at the World Cup (Image: Bob Thomas Sports Photography via Getty Images)

‌



He had joked with his surgeon, a Liverpool fan, that he 'would never walk alone'.

No truer words were spoken; Kevin Keegan was loved by fans everywhere he went and never walked alone.

He told that last audience in Newcastle that he did not want a statue because he wanted to go back to St James' Park to see the supporters one last time.

Tragically, he was cruelly robbed of that return.

‌



But there may be a statue to him yet.

Sports.content:
Michael Carrick issues next Man Utd transfer demand as Premier League stars targeted

Manchester United have already been busy in the transfer market ahead of Michael Carrick’s first summer at the helm and the Red Devils boss is clear on what he wants next

View 2 Images Michael Carrick wants more signings at Manchester United (Image: Getty Images)

Michael Carrick remains determined to sign ANOTHER midfielder for Manchester United this summer. The Red Devils have already added to their options in the heart of the pitch over the past few weeks.

‌



Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos have arrived for a combined £85m from Aston Villa and Chelsea respectively. But it appears that Carrick is not totally satisfied yet.

‌



According to The Guardian, the United boss is still intent on signing a third midfielder to add to his options even further following the departuer of Casemiro. It remains to be seen who that man will be but it is unlikely to be be Atlanta’s Ederson.

‌



The Red Devils had agreed a deal for the Brazilian, only to pull the plug on a move. Away from midfield, United are also keen on adding to their defensive options, with a left-back a priority.

Every Premier League summer transfer as Man Utd, Arsenal and Liverpool splash the cash READ MORE :

Man Utd land £8m teenage star from Premier League rivals as they repeat transfer trick READ MORE :

Tyrell Malacia left the club at the end of his contract at the end of last season, leaving United needing more back-up. A couple of Premier League options have already been identified ahead of a potential move.

Newcastle’s Lewis Hall and Fulham star Antonee Robinson are among those. Hall has impressed at St James’ Park since his move from Chelsea.

‌



But having lost Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon this summer, Newcastle will not be keen on selling another key player. He remains under contract until 2029.

Robinson in the meantime has shone for Fulham over recent campaigns but being 29, is slightly older than United’s preferred profile.

View 2 Images Man United are interested in a deal for Lewis Hall (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Speaking after United’s opening pre-season defeat against Wrexham, Carrick was full of his praise for one of his summer arrivals. He said: "There’s loads of little positives to take from the game. I thought Andrey and Mason [Mount] did some really good things and connected really well. I could see some positives there.

"[At the] top end of the pitch, just because it is a week in, those sharp little movements and bright moments that you are looking for, they come as you progress through the weeks of training. That is what it is. There were good signs from Andrey on his first one, he’s getting in the rhythm and feel of it again, so it was good to see him in a red shirt.”

Carrick added: "As I said before the game, the boys have only been back together for 10 days or so. It was just about getting through today, looking for some positives, looking for some good things and knowing that it wasn’t going to be perfect.

Article continues below

"That is only natural for the first one. I think the most important thing is that everyone came through it in good shape. No injuries, so we can move on and take the next step next week.”

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan was an under-appreciated national treasure and a joy to be around
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan was an under-appreciated national treasure and a joy to be around

After his death aged 75, Mirror chief sports writer Andy Dunn pays tribute to Liverpool and Newcastle icon Kevin Keegan

View 3 Images Kevin Keegan, pictured during his time as England manager, as died aged 75 (Image: Owen Humphreys/PA Wire)

In my memory, there has been no character in football as irrepressible as Kevin Keegan. Simple as that. A joy to watch, a joy to be around. Infectious, funny, passionate and never one to take himself too seriously.

‌



Which - considering he twice won the Ballon D’Or and considering the proliferation of elite footballers who do take themselves so very seriously - deserved the highest praise.

‌



And as a player, Keegan really was truly elite. But it was hard to escape the feeling that, as odd as it sounds, Keegan’s contribution to football has been and remains slightly under-appreciated.

‌



He should have been a national treasure. For what he achieved as a player and for his warmth and generosity, he would have been knighted nowadays.

But to many of us, and to our parents, he WAS a national treasure. And he was an Anfield treasure, even though his place in Liverpool’s history books is nuanced.

Kevin Keegan dies aged 75 as family pay tribute to Liverpool and Newcastle icon READ MORE :

Kevin Keegan: Newcastle and Liverpool legend dies aged 75 as tributes pour in READ MORE :

He is one of the club’s greatest-ever players, that much is certain, but he left the club of his own accord, joining SV Hamburg in 1977 for a new challenge and a lucrative payday.

‌



Keegan did not just collect an array of medals during his time at Anfield - three league titles, two UEFA Cups, an FA Cup and a European Cup - he produced defining individual performances.

One of those was in the 1977 European Cup final when he destroyed Berti Vogts - acknowledged then as one of the world’s best defenders - in Liverpool’s 3-1 win over Borussia Mönchengladbach in Rome.

It was one of THE great displays in a European Cup final. Vogts would later pay tribute to the Machtig Maus, the Magic Mouse.

‌



View 3 Images Keegan has a nuanced place in Liverpool's history books (Image: Mirrorpix)

Ironically, another one of his great individual performances was in the 1974 FA Cup final against his beloved Newcastle United, when he scored twice in a 3-0 victory for Bill Shankly’s side. He was truly a talismanic player.

Can you imagine the fuss in this era if an English player won the Ballon D’Or twice in two years, as Keegan did in 1978 and 1979 when in Germany?

‌



Over half a decade, Keegan was the Lionel Messi or Cristiano Ronaldo of his time, but incredibly down to earth. He always had an amusing tale to tell us when the notepads were away and the voice recorders were switched off.

He told of the time when he was almost late for his Liverpool debut, a police officer not recognising the new £33,000 signing outside Anfield. He would laugh with is about the time he fell off his bike on the TV programme, Superstars.

Our relations with Keegan became strained during Euro 2000 when his relaxed regime at the squad's base in Belgium came under scrutiny, and when England failed to make it out of the group stage.

‌



But Keegan was that type of relaxed manager, a manager who treated his players to fish, chips and beer after a good win. But he never held our fierce criticism of England’s showing at the tournament against us.

View 3 Images Keegan was a brilliant player for England before later going on to manage his country (Image: Peter Robinson/EMPICS Sport/PA Wire)

And, of course, he gave the media a truly memorable moment with his ‘I’ll Love It’ rant at Sir Alex Ferguson in 1996 as his Newcastle United team surrendered a 12-point lead in the title race.

‌



Later generations of fans remember Keegan as much for that as they do for his brilliance on and off the field. And don’t forget, as Newcastle manager, Keegan moulded one of the most entertaining English club sides of recent decades.

He was a player and a manager who belonged - in a good way - to a bygone age. When football seemed a lot more fun.

Ahead of a schoolboy cup final, this correspondent felt compelled to get a curly perm, thanks to Keegan, who had been on Top of the Pops - yes, Top of the Pops - a few days earlier.

Article continues below

His song ‘Head Over Heels’ only made it to number 31 in the charts. For some time in English football, King Kev was number one, an irrepressible character who will be greatly missed.

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan's final picture and brave public appearance before sad death aged 75
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan's final picture and brave public appearance before sad death aged 75

Former England manager Kevin Keegan was a football icon for his achievements with Newcastle, Liverpool and beyond and he was well-known for his passion and good humour

View 3 Images Kevin Keegan made his final public appearance alongside Sam Allardyce (Image: INSTAGRAM)

Kevin Keegan was an inspiring figure on the pitch, in the dugout and away from football, and captured hearts across Yorkshire, Liverpool and Newcastle until the very end. His honesty, passion and good humour were standout traits for one of football's true icons.

‌



Keegan died aged 75 after being diagnosed with cancer, but was still active in the final months of his life. The former England boss is survived by his wife, Jean, and their children, Laura Jane and Sarah Marie.

‌



Even after being diagnosed with stage four cancer, Keegan made a number of public appearances, working alongside Peter Graves. It was his close friend who confirmed his passing.

‌



Graves wrote: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75.

"The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

Alan Shearer sends emotional goodbye to 'hero' Kevin Keegan as tributes pour in READ MORE :

"Kevin, a double Ballon d’Or winner, was a much-loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin’s incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

‌



Keegan took in an impressive England display during his final publish appearance. Working alongside Ray Parlour, David James and Sam Allardyce. In an Instagram post, Graves said that 'Keegan was a big fan of "Tuchel Ball"'.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Earlier in June, when Keegan revealed his cancer diagnosis publicly for the first time, he expressed his usual humour to deliver the tragic news.

‌



Speaking with Graves at the Tyne Theatre, Kevin revealed a discussion over his treatment. He said: "I was in a car accident and, through that, I had to have an operation. Whilst having the scan for the operation, they found out I had cancer.

"They said they had an absolute top doctor for fighting what you have got, which is stage four cancer. So I went to meet him. He’s a Liverpool supporter so I knew I wouldn't walk alone.

"He said, 'Kevin, this new treatment, I've got a tremendous strike rate'. I said, 'What's your strike rate?' He said, '33%'. I thought it would be 80%, 90%. 33%!? I'm still here at the moment.”

‌



Kevin Keegan: England and Liverpool legend dead aged 75

During another moment, Keegan revealed he also wanted to say farewell, having not had a proper opportunity during his second spell managing Newcastle. "I want to say goodbye. I didn't get the chance when I left last time…"

Tributes have poured in for the late Doncaster-born star. Alan Shearer posted on social media: "My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss [Crying emoji]."

‌



Jamie Carragher tweeted: "RIP Kevin Keegan. One of the greatest players this country has ever produced, trophies & goals galore, double Ballon d'Or winner shows he was an absolute giant of the English game.

"One of the most important men in making LFC [Liverpool Football Club] what it is today."

View 3 Images Kevin Keegan is a legendary figure on Tyneside (Image: Professional Sport/Popperfoto via Getty Images/Getty Images)

‌



Newcastle United offered a lengthy, heartfelt tribute. A club statement read: "Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager.

"He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters. As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James’ Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an Entertainer.

‌



View 3 Images Keegan was affectionately known as the Messiah at Newcastle (Image: Stu Forster/Getty Images)

"Above all that, Kevin forged an extraordinary bond with Newcastle, built on the roots of his father, Joe. He understood our people. He embraced the North East with a passion that was genuine and unwavering, and in return, he earned his rightful place in the hearts of millions.

"Kevin's impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him.

Article continues below

"At this profoundly sad time, we send our love and deepest sympathy to Kevin’s wife Jean, his family, friends and all who had the privilege of knowing and working alongside him. Today, we mourn the loss of a true giant of our history, and at the appropriate moment, we will carefully consider how we shape a lasting tribute to Kevin’s remarkable life and legacy. Rest in peace, King Kev."

Sports.title: Argentina in fresh punch shame after World Cup final as new footage emerges
Sports.content:
Argentina in fresh punch shame after World Cup final as new footage emerges

Spain's World Cup triumph descended into chaos as Argentina players and staff were seen throwing punches following the full-time whistle at MetLife Stadium

View 2 Images Roberto Ayala clashed with Dani Olmo

Argentina coach Roberto Ayala appeared to throw a punch at Spain's Dani Olmo during the chaotic scenes that followed the World Cup final. The defending champions suffered a 1-0 extra-time loss in New Jersey after Ferran Torres struck in the 106th minute.

‌



But the result only told half of the story. Enzo Fernandez was sent off just before the additional period for a second yellow card, while there were unsavoury scenes at full-time involving Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina.

‌



And now Footage has emerged showing Ayala, who is one of Lionel Scaloni's assistant coaches, swinging his right arm towards Olmo as they clashed. To his credit, the Barcelona star didn't react and team-mate Eric Garcia stepped in to play the role of peacekeeper.

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Former England goalkeeper Joe Hart labelled Argentina's behaviour 'disgusting'. He said: "There was one man on the pitch who did have class and that was Lionel Messi, who shook hands with every one of those Spanish players.

"The game's done. They could have absolutely no complaints about what happened today. Disgusting behaviour."

‌



Full list of Argentina's 27 dirty tricks in World Cup final as they ruin greatest match READ MORE :

Before he added: "Spain fully deserve it. They have been absolutely superb all tournament. They have dominated all game against a rigid, rugged Argentina. The best team has won this World Cup."

While fellow BBC pundit Wayne Rooney said: "Does it surprise you? It doesn't surprise me.

"We've seen this with Argentina before. It's just not the reaction you want. We've seen some of the reaction after knocking England out in the last round.

‌



"That's just sad. If you lose a game of football, be graceful and get out of there. It's really poor from them."

View 2 Images Paredes was sent off for an angry clash with Eric Garcia (Image: Getty Images)

Paredes was also sent off following the whistle, while Molina also appeared to throw a punch after the match. The latter took a swing at Rodri, while Paredes was spotted kicking Eric Garcia to the floor before pushing him back with a hand around his neck when the Barcelona defender attempted to confront him.

‌



He was also spotted in an exchange with Gavi and former Chelsea midfielder Craig Burley fumed: "Argentina were a complete and utter disgrace today, both with their performance and their antics.

"We expected the antics, we expected the thuggery, we expected the off the ball stuff, but we also expected a lot more on the ball, a lot more purpose... they were an utter shambles, disgusting, disgraceful. I'm so pleased Spain won. It was a disgusting performance [from Argentina]."

Sports.title: Brundle: The Hamilton-Russell penalty call and Antonelli's class of one
Sports.content:
Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix.

The Kimi Antonelli show, also known as the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix, took place in remarkably sunny and dry conditions throughout, if occasionally interrupted by an actual safety car deployment on lap one to clear a beached car, and a few more virtual safety cars to clear up high-tech litter from the racing surface.

The Circuit de Spa-Francorchamps has been developed and polished beautifully in almost every respect, even if in time-honoured fashion getting into and moving around the venue seems to have new systems and rules every day. To be fair, there is a huge area and a great many fans to be controlled.

As usual I was out and about trackside on Friday during practice and the cars looked very fast and impressive in front of the numerous grandstands. I've been racing here for 45 years, and I couldn't quite believe my eyes on the scale of the crowd.

It was enjoyable to watch the drivers jockey an excess of power over grip through medium-speed chicane exits, but like Silverstone there was a hidden story alongside the trackside 'wow', and the drivers were very restrained through the event not to complain too much about it.

We long ago lost Eau Rouge and Raidillon as corners to refined high-downforce cars with grippy tyres and a manicured racetrack, meaning from the turn one La Source hairpin to the long haul up to the turn five Les Combes chicane is effectively a straight.

Image: Kimi Antonelli rounds La Source during the race

But with the need to charge the hybrid batteries on this fast track, the longest on the calendar, just as with Copse, Becketts, and Stowe at Silverstone, as the engine is used to charge those batteries the arrival speeds into corners like Pouhon at Spa are dulled such that the corner effectively becomes a bendy straight too.

On such circuits we have lost the driver-defining, and thrilling, high-speed corners. It was the same in Suzuka.

Luckily in Budapest this weekend it will not be a problem at all, and normal service will be resumed, although there are no high-speed corners worth their name.

We have known for a while about these issues, and they are being addressed where possible for 2027 and again in 2028, but the last two races have unequivocally confirmed that we need a major power unit philosophy change much sooner than later.

There were always going to be teething problems reliability-wise but as we hurtle towards the summer break the words 'deployment issues' and 'no battery' are rather too prominent.

Russell's Mercedes problems and the 'racing incident' debate

George Russell is clearly not a direct descendant of the Alessandro Volta, Michael Faraday, Thomas Edison or Nikola Tesla families because he never seems to have the right battery power at the moment.

Whether that is missing straight-line speed compared to his team-mate Antonelli in qualifying, for whatever mystery reasons, or climbing the hill to turn five on the opening lap.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Drama at the start of the Belgium GP as George Russell's title hopes take a huge blow.

Antonelli got away well at the start and Verstappen's Red Bull launched unusually nicely too. But Max appeared to pull a cunning move by powering past before Eau Rouge at the bottom of the hill, but his post-race comments say that his car had too much battery deployment suggesting he had nothing to do with that cunning plan…

Both Mercedes of Antonelli and Russell started the race with less battery charge than needed, and it particularly hurt Russell on the long climb to the critical turn five braking point, and he was mugged by three cars including Lewis Hamilton.

George braked impressively late trying to make up for his poor arrival speed and was on the outside of Lewis, leaving racing room. Lewis, close behind Max, slid a little wide and contacted George who spun into retirement, and at the same time taking a massive hit to his championship comeback chances.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes driver George Russell spins after contact with Lewis Hamilton and his race ends on the opening lap, but was the Ferrari driver's penalty fair?

More referee leeway is given on the first lap with the pack inevitably in close company along with full fuel and sub-optimal brake and tyre temperatures. I called it a racing incident in commentary, unless the stewards were satisfied that Lewis had lost control of his car, which didn't appear to be the case.

George recovered to the pits by scooter and called it a racing incident whilst far more distraught about his ongoing power issues.

Ferrari called it a racing incident, I guess you could say they would, and most people I know agreed. But with whatever extra information the stewards had they applied a five-second penalty mitigated down from the standard 10 seconds. It perhaps cost Lewis a podium but that's speculative.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Oscar Piastri takes to his McLaren team radio to complain about contact with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc.

Later in the race, Charles Leclerc would squeeze Oscar Piastri in the T5 braking zone and there was contact which damaged Piastri's aero parts, to an extent. For me this was a clear movement in the braking zone which can mean anything from a warning flag to a full pit-lane drive through penalty in the guidelines.

The stewards, though, decided it was about relative front axle positions and who had the right to the corner. Leclerc's telling reaction when it was played out in the cooldown room tells us everything we need to know on that one.

The pit stops that did - and didn't - make the difference

Hamilton had a torrid weekend with an accident in practice, the five-second penalty with Russell, and nearly running one of his mechanics over in the pit stop through no fault of his own. That incident attracted a team fine rather than a race penalty and so Lewis was perhaps relieved to finish fourth, probably for the first time in his life.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The Ferrari pit crew were unable to tweak Lewis Hamilton's front wing level as the British driver knocked over a mechanic after being given the green light.

Piastri drove a spirited race to fifth despite his car damage although he lacked the same pace, which threatened to make the podium early on, after he swapped onto the hard compound tyres on lap 20 of 44.

Lando Norris drove beautifully all weekend but had to start 13th due to needing power unit control electronics beyond the allowance in the regulations, which is designed to keep costs down so that wealthy teams can't just throw new parts at the car every weekend.

Curiously McLaren chose not to use the virtual safety cars, or indeed a straightforward pit stop, until Lando eventually pitted on lap 30 to get rid of his starting hard-compound tyres. This left him with too much to do to catch Isack Hadjar who started his Red Bull from the back row of the grid, also due to numerous power unit penalties, to finish an impressive sixth.

Red Bull pitted Hadjar on lap one, and then again on lap two to cycle through the mandatory use of two different tyre compounds under cover of the Russell safety car, and then again under a virtual safety car on lap 20. Nicely done.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes Kimi Antonelli discusses his Belgian GP win and admits he's in a 'good position' after opening up a 45-point gap in the drivers' standings.

That same lap 20 VSC played out beautifully for Leclerc in his Ferrari as the time loss is only around 11 seconds when your rivals are lapping at reduced speed. Antonelli had pitted on lap 18 under full green conditions as Mercedes were covering off Red Bull's pit stop for Verstappen on lap 17.

Through all this Leclerc leapfrogged the pair of them and was now effectively leading, albeit with the yet-to-stop Norris ahead of him. Antonelli would hunt him down but perhaps not as rapidly as expected, Leclerc was driving beautifully.

'What a difference a year makes'

Eventually, and frankly inevitably given his speed throughout the event, the Italian teenager would take the lead, but Leclerc still wouldn't give up, and he finished second just two seconds adrift.

Verstappen would finish a solid third, Leclerc's safety car good fortune denied him a shot at second.

The final points went to Gabriel Bortoleto and Audi in eighth, Arvid Lindblad and Racing Bulls in ninth, and Franco Colapinto for Alpine in 10th. The safety cars played a role for and against throughout.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch from onboard Alpine's Franco Colapinto as he pulls off an incredible double overtake on Pierre Gasly and Liam Lawson at the Belgian GP.

What a difference a year makes. Antonelli never ran higher than 14th on his F1 debut here last year, but he was in a class of one this season.

Mercedes are on fire too, with their eighth victory of the season, which is one more than they won over the last four 'ground effect era' seasons combined. That combination will take some stopping from winning both championships in fine style.

Sports.title: 'He's got to get an answer!' - Russell 'knocked down' by mystery problems
Sports.content:
George Russell says he has been "knocked down" but will "get back up" after the latest setbacks to his world championship challenge at the Belgian Grand Prix

Having cut his title deficit to Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli from 68 points to just 25 points over the previous three rounds, benefitting from two reliability problems on the Italian's car, Russell dropped 50 points behind on Sunday at Spa-Francorchamps when his race lasted just five corners before a collision with Lewis Hamilton.

But Russell's post-race frustration at his early exit, and difficult race weekend as a whole, was aimed not at his former team-mate but instead towards weekend-long power issues on his Mercedes car that he said had left him vulnerable to such an incident on the first lap.

The Briton has been searching for stronger form for several months amid a failure to match Antonelli's pace on a consistent basis but, in a social media post on Monday, he resolved to keep fighting on in the championship chase.

"Knocked down, we get back up," Russell wrote.

"No matter how many times.

"So many tough moments this year but I will not stop fighting,"

Wolff explains Russell's power problems

While Mercedes are still working to get to the bottom of the mysterious straight-line speed issues afflicting Russell's car, team principal Toto Wolff explained after Sunday's race how two separate problems contributed to the Briton's difficult weekend.

On the first deployment issue in the sessions before race day - which Russell had initially hoped would be corrected by driving style changes but was not the case - Wolff said this had compromised the Briton's speed in the final sector of the long Spa-Francorchamps lap relative to Antonelli.

"The power units are so complex, in the way you harvest, the way you deploy, the interaction from the driver," said Wolff of 2026's new engines which feature a near 50-50 split between electrical and traditional internal combustion output.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix.

"We have a super strong package - championship-winning chassis and power unit, but we're still trying to give it our best to fix the reliability issue.

"And sometimes a new regulation (irregularity) happens. With George, over the weekend, there was definitely something on the engine that we have identified that meant he only had less energy to deploy into Turn 18 - that was the most visible.

"It's good that we spotted it here because in Budapest, which is not energy starved, it would have been more difficult to identify.

"But it still doesn't make it better for him. And that probably accounted for half the gap or a little bit more that he had to Kimi."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch from onboard with George Russell as he crashes out of the Belgian GP after contact with Lewis Hamilton.

All eight of the grid's Mercedes-powered cars were then hampered by a separate and "new" boost problem out of Turn One at the start of Sunday's race.

Andrew Shovlin, the team's trackside engineering director, said Russell's problems on lap one had been "more extreme" and so he was an effective sitting duck on the Kemmel Straight as the two Ferraris moved past him, with the Briton eventually spun into instant retirement at Les Combes due to contact with Hamilton.

Wolff added: "All Mercedes engines had a lack of energy out of Turn One, so that wasn't only George. It affected him more than Kimi, but also Kimi had that issue to a certain degree.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell pointed to an issue with the car as a reason for his collision with Lewis Hamilton during the Belgian GP.

"And that meant that he didn't come out at the end of the straight in P3, but P5.

"So, he lost his two positions, and then obviously the accident with Lewis."

'He's got to get an answer' - what now for Russell heading to Hungary?

Speaking during Sky Sports F1's post-race show in Belgium, Karun Chandhok suggested that Russell would want concrete engineering explanations before this weekend's race in Hungary as to what exactly was causing the confusing straight-line speed problems.

"I think he's got to go back and try to get clear answers from an engineering sense," said Chandhok.

"We've all had conversations this weekend with people from Mercedes, and the sense we're getting is that they don't have a clear answer.

"They've got to go back, they've got to look at the data, have a couple of days to digest it between now and Budapest, because he can't go on to the next race weekend with a four-tenth deficit in straight-line speed.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch all of George Russell’s unlucky moments so far this 2026 Formula 1 season.

"You're taking a pencil to a sword fight, so there's no point doing that. He's got to get an answer, and if it means they have to change the power unit and take a penalty, then maybe they have to do that to try to clear away this doubt.

"Because as a racing driver, arriving at a weekend having doubt in the package or the car you've got and whether you've got a fair fight, is an awful place to be. He will be looking for clear engineering-led answers, I think."

Russell said in interviews after the race that, having also run into technical issues earlier in the season most notably in China and, when leading, in Canada, he was now "numb to the disappointment".

Asked how he could keep his driver's spirits up, Wolff said: "You have to understand that the driver is very emotional when these situations happen. But on the other side, as a Formula 1 driver, you're part of a very elite group.

"I think it's quite an honour to drive a Mercedes. Sometimes we let ourselves down. And it's just the driver, but it's also us.

"It's valuable constructor points that we lose in our fight against Ferrari. So, I hope the numb feeling goes away. We will try to help to recreate optimism and positivity."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes driver George Russell spins after contact with Lewis Hamilton and his race ends on the opening lap, but was the Ferrari driver's penalty fair?

Wolff, who has known the 28-year-old Russell for over a decade, added: "I think all of the drivers, at least the ones that I have worked with, when they have difficult spells, and it happens to any sports person, you need to find a way of motivating or building up.

"George has his way, and I'm definitely trying to do that. I've known him for such a long time, I understand the frustrations, and the team is 100 per cent there."
