Sports.title: Did DeChambeau attempt to involve Trump in Open rules controversy?
Sports.content:
Bryson DeChambeau has been accused of wanting to involve United States President Donald Trump during his rules controversy at The Open, multiple media reports have claimed.

The two-time major winner was handed a two-shot penalty late on Friday night after officials reviewed footage and decided he had improved the area of his backswing by flattening down some long grass on Royal Birkdale's fifth hole.

Multiple reports claim DeChambeau allegedly threatened to call Trump during lengthy discussions with the R&A regarding the penalty, which dropped him from second place and one off the lead on Friday to tied-fifth and three back.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Scottie Scheffler defended Ryder Cup teammate DeChambeau after he was given a two-shot penalty

Sky Sports News has contacted the R&A, the White House press office and DeChambeau's management team for comment.

DeChambeau is a friend of Trump, serving on the President's council on sports, fitness and nutrition, making his last White House appearance in May, and has played golf with him.

Trump asked football's world governing body FIFA to review the red card shown to US forward Folarin Balogun during the World Cup, with the player's one-match ban subsequently being suspended, and DeChambeau wanted a similar intervention.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sam Burns said that 'there was not enough evidence' to penalise DeChambeau

While the call did not take place at the time, it is not known whether DeChambeau made contact privately, but on Saturday R&A chief executive Mark Darbon was asked whether the President had been in touch.

"No, I have not received a call from President Trump," he told BBC Sport. "Irrespective of which player this affected, it is the same decision - from a rules perspective it was clear cut."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Brandel Chamblee and Paul McGinley were critical of DeChambeau's actions in the rough on the fifth hole

Sky Sports News understands that DeChambeau visited Darbon in the championship office after his third round on Saturday, where his request to gain possession of his scorecard from the previous day was declined.

The R&A has also yet to comment on that issue. DeChambeau is next scheduled to feature at the LIV Golf League event in England, beginning at JCB Golf and Country Club on Thursday, although he is not listed for any pre-tournament media.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Jamie Weir delves into why DeChambeau was given a two-shot penalty

'A lot of ups and downs' - DeChambeau reflects on challenging week

DeChambeau making it through to the weekend ended a run of three consecutive major missed cuts and avoided the 'Bryson Slam' of missing all four in a season, eventually ending tied-14th and six strokes behind Ryan Fox.

The American refused to speak to the waiting media for the eighth successive major round, having also not given post-round interviews during his missed cuts at the PGA Championship and US Open.

"A lot of ups and downs this week, to say the least," DeChambeau said on Instagram. "But I'm proud of the way I fought through it.

"Thank you to all my supporters for carrying me through. Onwards and upwards from here. Congratulations to Ryan Fox on an incredible win!"

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Rory McIlroy spoke to the media after his third round of The Open and said he was not impressed with DeChambeau's actions

World No 1 Scheffler defended DeChambeau over the rules controversy, insisting his fellow American is "not a cheater", while Rory McIlroy described the incident as "performative".

"I won't pretend to be up here and defend Bryson," McIlroy said on Saturday. "I'm not particularly fond of him. I think a lot of it's performative. I think a lot of it's for attention.

"To hold the tournament hostage like that, and to have all of us, players, volunteers, everyone waiting on him to depart, I didn't feel like it was a great look."

Sports.title: Who is The Open champion Ryan Fox?
Sports.content:
Ryan Fox cut an emotional figure as he sat on a sofa inside the players' compound at Royal Birkdale.

He had just sunk an 11ft putt on the 18th, the toughest hole of the week, to card a birdie to win The Open.

Remarkable doesn't cut it.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fox explained his whole body was shaking as he lined up the putt on 18

Back home in New Zealand, fans stayed up all night eagerly watching Fox, the son of one of the country's greatest All Blacks and the grandson of a former New Zealand cricket captain, become only the second Kiwi to hoist the Claret Jug.

The 39-year-old, widely regarded as one of the most humble and self-effacing players on the PGA Tour, said his whole body was shaking at the enormity of the shot, but his cool and composed demeanour shone through.

A testament to his no-nonsense pace of play, it only took 22 seconds for Fox to rattle in a putt that would win him his first major title after his playing partner Sam Burns had wrapped up his round at Royal Birkdale.

Image: The New Zealand golfer said he never dreamed that he would go on to win The Open

Afterwards, a heartwarming moment unfolded backstage. Fox video-called his wife, Anneke, children, Isobel and Margot, and his dad, Grant, wiping the tears from his eyes as he celebrated his extraordinary achievement.

"I don't really know what to think at the moment," he said. "I spoke to my kids last night and they told me to bring back a trophy.

"I think this is a pretty cool one to bring back for them!"

"I used to get up in the middle of the night to watch this tournament back home," he added. "Just to be able to play in it and now to be the Champion Golfer of the Year, it's unbelievable."

Sport runs in his genes

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fox also equalled the lowest round in Open history with a third-round 62 at Royal Birkdale

Fox was born in Tokoroa, Waikato, in New Zealand's North Island, and following in the footsteps of his dad and grandad, he was a keen rugby union player and cricketer.

Sport ran in the family. His grandfather, Merv Wallace, was considered one of the best Kiwi batters of his time, playing 13 Tests for New Zealand, captaining the side on two occasions, going on to score 439 runs in his Test career.

His dad, Grant, was inducted into World Rugby's Hall of Fame in 2014 and is one of the finest goal kickers to have graced the game.

Image: Grant Fox (pictured left with George Bridge) enjoyed a glittering career with the All Blacks before going into coaching

The fly-half played his club rugby for Auckland and won 46 caps for the All Blacks, scoring 645 points during his international career.

Grant helped guide New Zealand to win the inaugural Rugby World Cup in 1987 and featured heavily during New Zealand's 2-1 series win over the British and Irish Lions in 1993.

"We've got a great history in our family," Fox said on Sunday afternoon.

Image: Fox said his family had a 'great history' in sport, but he was never pressured to follow the footsteps of his dad or grandad

"The other great thing is I had no pressure on me to follow in any of their footsteps. I was lucky enough to carve my own path there and had support from both my grandfather and my mum and dad through the whole thing.

"I don't know if this tops their achievements, but it's certainly right up there. There's no pressure on my kids going forward now!"

Fox pursues a career in golf

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fox attended the University of Auckland, and studied psychology, before pursuing a career in golf

After completing his high school studies, Fox chose to pursue a career in golf, having whittled his handicap down to two by the age of 16.

His parents had advised him to continue his studies, and he would enrol at the University of Auckland, where he began a bachelor's degree in law before switching to major in psychology.

But golf was his true love. He turned pro in 2012 at the age of 25 and would go on to win three times on the PGA Tour of Australasia.

Fox also cut his teeth on the Hotel Planner Tour before winning his DP World Tour card in 2016. He won his first title on the DP World Tour, claiming his first event at the ISPS Handa World Super 6 Perth in 2019, before going on to earn temporary membership on the PGA Tour in 2023.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fox turned pro in 2012 and would go on to win three times on the PGA Tour of Australasia

Including The Open, Fox now has five wins on the DP World Tour, including the BMW PGA Championship in 2023 and the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship in 2022, and won his first PGA Tour title last year at the ONEflight Myrtle Beach Classic, before winning the RBC Canadian Open.

But he never envisioned he'd win a major.

"I said to my team last night, you know, at dinner, if you'd have given me my career up till yesterday when I turned pro, I'd have jumped at that," Fox said.

"I don't know what to think now, to be honest. You dream of being a major champion."

'I wanted to do something special for Warney'

Image: The New Zealand golfer was 'great mates' with Australian cricket legend Shane Warne

In 2022, Fox dedicated his triumph at the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship to his late friend Shane Warne, who died in March of that year.

Fox and the Australian spin bowling legend, a low handicapper himself, had joined forces in the team element of the event in Scotland five times previously, last teeing up together at the 2021 event.

"The only person I can really think of at the moment is Warney," Fox said, after winning in 2022. "It definitely felt as if he was with me all the way around.

"It means a lot to win this event. We were great mates, and it's just a shame he's not here. I really wanted to try to do something special for Warney and I'm pretty proud to have been able to accomplish that."

The fourth Kiwi to win a major

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The 39-year-old is only the fourth New Zealand golfer to win a major

On Sunday, Fox became only the fourth player from New Zealand to win a major championship.

Sir Bob Charles was the first. He claimed victory at The Open in 1963 at Royal Lytham and St Annes, while Michael Campbell followed up in 2005 at the US Open.

Lydia Ko also boasts three major titles, with her most recent coming at the 2024 Women's Open.

"To be able to join them is amazing," Fox said. "To have my own little piece of history. I don't know if it's something I ever thought was possible, but we're here now."

A guy 'who never changed'

Image: Fox has been hailed as one of the most humble players in the sport and was credited for continually giving back to New Zealand golf

Fox has earned the plaudits from many within the golfing world for his attitude to the sport, life and never forgetting his roots.

Prior to his Open victory, PGA Tour of Australasia general manager Nick Dastey hailed Fox for "continuing to give back to Australian and New Zealand golf."

"The greatest thing I could say about Ryan is he hasn't changed from the moment he first turned professional to the moment now, and this won't change him either," Dastey told the DP World Tour.

"You know, he is just a fantastic human being. He is someone that, if we could model the professional golfer on, and someone that we would want as a tour member, he's it."

What's next?

The next PGA Tour event is the 3M Open at TPC Twin Cities in Minnesota, beginning Thursday, with early coverage on Sky Sports+ before switching to Sky Sports Golf at 7pm.

The 3M Open is part of a triple-header of live golf on Sky Sports, with the ISPS Handa Senior Open and ISPS Handa Women's Scottish Open also live. The women's major season then concludes with the AIG Women's Open from July 30-August 2, also live on Sky Sports Golf. Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract.

Sports.title: What does Rogers' move mean for Chelsea's squad?
Sports.content:
Morgan Rogers is set to join Chelsea in a British-record £117m from Aston Villa - and his arrival is set to have a knock-on effect for Xabi Alonso's Blues.

The England international - who arrived for his medical on Monday after returning from the World Cup - had also been linked with Arsenal, but he is set to arrive in the west of London instead.

Here, Sky Sports News reporters Kaveh Solhekol and James Savundra examine why Rogers is keen on the move and what the forward's imminent arrival could mean for the rest of the Chelsea squad.

Why Rogers and Chelsea wanted each other

KS: Some people may be surprised that Rogers has decided to swap Aston Villa for Chelsea, but the player really did have his heart set on moving to Stamford Bridge and once the bid materialised, he accepted it straight away.

Playing for Chelsea next season means he will not be playing in Europe. If he had stayed at Aston Villa, he would have been playing in the Champions League, but Chelsea are still a big club.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Morgan Rogers has been spotted arriving for his Chelsea medical after the Blues agreed a £117m deal with Aston Villa.

They have big ambitions and under their new manager Alonso, they are very serious about challenging for the big trophies again.

Rogers is obviously a fantastic player, we've all seen that, but he is also very physically imposing. There's been a feeling at Chelsea that one thing their side has been missing is some real physical presence and they've been trying to address that this summer. They've gone some way towards it by signing a player like Rogers.

How might Cole Palmer be impacted?

KS: I remember being at the game between Aston Villa and Chelsea last season and that was billed as being a game between Cole Palmer and Rogers - who was the better No 10? I think on the day, Aston Villa ended up winning that game and Rogers played really well.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League clash between Chelsea and Aston Villa.

So you have to ask the question - will Chelsea be able to have both Rogers and Palmer in the same side? The two players know each other well. They were together at Manchester City and Palmer's famous 'cold' goal celebration was first invented by Rogers. It'll be up to Alonso to see how he can accommodate both those players in the same side.

There are no indications that Chelsea want to sell Palmer, far from it. He's tied down to a very long contract and just before the end of the season, he gave a newspaper interview in which he said he was happy at Chelsea and was happy living in London.

There have been reports seeming to suggest that he may want to move back to the north west, that one day he wants to play for Manchester United, but I think he would cost so much that there are not many clubs who would be able to buy Palmer if Chelsea wanted to sell him.

What is the situation for Enzo Fernandez?

Image: Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez was sent off in Sunday's World Cup final (AP Photo/Frank Franklin II)

KS: Enzo Fernandez has come out on a few occasions and made it clear that he fancies a move to Real Madrid, but we had some sort of clarity on that a couple of weeks ago when the LaLiga club released a statement saying that they were not involved in any negotiations.

They had not made a move to sign Fernandez and if they did want to sign him, then they would do everything through the proper channels. Real Madrid have a very good relationship at the highest level with Chelsea, so I'm sure if they were interested in signing Fernandez, it would simply be a matter of picking up the phone.

I think what Chelsea would tell them is every player has his price and Fernandez's price is £120m. If you want him, that is what it's going to take to buy him. But as of yet, Real Madrid have not made a move for him to our understanding.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at the best goals Morgan Rogers has scored during the 2025/26 Premier League season.

JS: Fernandez's position remains largely unchanged despite the arrival of Rogers. Alonso confirmed his intention to keep the Argentine at his unveiling last week and noted to Sky Sports News that he was looking forward to working with the midfielder.

Having committed more than £100m to buy Fernandez in 2023, Chelsea would be looking to recoup at least a similar level of money to sanction a sale.

Real Madrid have ruled themselves out of the running to signing Fernandez - for now - which leaves few viable suitors.

The Argentine enjoyed success under Enzo Maresca, but is a move to Man City likely in a window in which City have spent £116m already on Elliot Anderson and given the tension between the clubs given the Maresca saga?

How might Rogers fit into Alonso's system?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol breaks down Chelsea's £117m deal for Morgan Rogers and what he could add to Xabi Alonso's side.

JS: Alonso refused to give any clues last week when it came to his playing system. His main success as a manager at Bayer Leverkusen saw Jeremie Frimpong and Alex Grimaldo dominate as wing-backs. If he adopts his preferred formation at Chelsea, Rogers is most likely to operate as a wide attacking midfielder.

Given the struggles of Alejandro Garnacho and Jamie Gittens last season and the presence of Palmer, you would expect Rogers to be favoured on the left.

There are real similarities between the positions picked up by Palmer, Rogers and to some extent Joao Pedro. Whilst the trio thrive in fluid positions rather than a strictly fixed structure, Alonso will need to lay out a clear framework with specific roles.

Are Chelsea sales required?

JS: Chelsea are Club World Cup champions. They have not always been world class on the pitch during the BlueCo era but they have been world-class sellers.

They have already ensured enough outgoings this summer to cover the £117m cost of Rogers. Chelsea raised around £130m from selling players like Marc Cucurella, Andrey Santos and Tyrique George and the sizeable compensation from Man City for poaching Maresca certainly helped too.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player After Andrey Santos' £50m move to Manchester United, here's a look at some of his best moments from last season with Chelsea

The likes of Reece James, Palmer and Joao Pedro are seen as untouchable assets, but other members of the first team squad will depart for sizeable fees - Garnacho, Nicolas Jackson and Trevoh Chalobah are likely to bring in another £100m if they go.

Despite not being in Europe this season, Chelsea will still be subjected to UEFA's stricter financial rules. Last summer, Chelsea entered into a four year settlement agreement with UEFA for breaching regulations and they'll look to demonstrate progress in showcasing financial sustainability following this window.

Chelsea brought in around £300m from player sales last summer and given the need to move on a number of defenders who are surplus to requirements and at least one striker, it could be another impressive summer of trading.

Where does this deal leave Arsenal?

KS: It's a long transfer window… but I'm not sure Arsenal would have been prepared to pay £117m for him.

Perhaps you could argue that Chelsea need him more at the moment - Arsenal are the reigning champions and they are in the Champions League as well.

A lot of these deals only happen when somebody puts their money where their mouth is. We can talk about the fact that Arsenal were potentially interested in Rogers, but it's Chelsea who made a bid and that has been accepted by Aston Villa.

Sports.title: Former England forward and manager Keegan dies aged 75
Sports.content:
Former England player and manager Kevin Keegan dies aged 75 after battle with cancer; Keegan's family announced in January he had been diagnosed with stage four cancer; legendary forward was twice named Ballon d'Or winner in 1978 and 1979

Sky Sports takes a look back at the incredible career of former England manager and legendary footballer Kevin Keegan, who has died at the age of 75

Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75.

It was announced in January that the former England player and manager had been diagnosed with stage four cancer, with his family revealing he was set to begin treatment.

"It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75," a statement from Keegan's family read.

"The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

"Kevin, a double Ballon d'Or winner, was a much-loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin's incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

England have announced that they will pay tribute to Keegan's life before their Nations League game with Spain at Wembley in September.

Image: It was announced in January Kevin Keegan had been diagnosed with stage four cancer

Keegan was considered one of the best players of his generation and enjoyed a stellar playing career, making almost 750 club appearances, lifting the First Division trophy three times with Liverpool and winning the Ballon d'Or back-to-back in 1978 and 1979 while playing for Hamburg in the Bundesliga.

Image: Liverpool's Ian Callaghan, Kevin Keegan and Ray Clemence parade the FA Cup

Image: Liverpool striker Kevin Keegan during a match with QPR

Seven years after his retirement, he took his first coaching role as manager of a struggling Newcastle team in February 1992. The Magpies were in danger of being relegated to Division Two but Keegan kept them up and then led them to the Premier League in his first full season in charge. Then, in 1996, he took Newcastle to within touching distance of their first top-tier title since 1927.

Newcastle were Premier League title favourites for most of that 1995/96 season, at one stage being 12 points clear of Manchester United. But a dramatic collapse from Keegan's side coupled with a Sir Alex Ferguson-inspired Man Utd winning 13 of their last 15, eventually saw Newcastle finish second by four points.

Late defeats at the hands of Liverpool and Nottingham Forest in the run-in saw United eventually haul them in. As the pressure mounted on a beleaguered Keegan, who was desperate to deliver the title to a passionate Newcastle fanbase, his infamous "I'd love it.." post-match interview after victory at Leeds, aimed at Sir Alex, among others, unfortunately characterised his time at St James' Park.

He would go on to manage England, for whom he had scored 21 goals in 63 games as a player, between February 1999 and October 2000 - resigning minutes after a 1-0 defeat to Germany in the last game played at the old Wembley Stadium.

Image: Kevin Keegan celebrates scoring against Scotland at Wembley in 1979

His time as national boss also saw England fail to get out of the group stage at Euro 2000, despite a 1-0 win over Germany, as defeats by Portugal and Romania piled on the pressure even before that defeat at the hands of Dietmar Hamann's free-kick four months later in the first qualifier for the 2002 World Cup.

A spell at Manchester City followed, which included promotion to the Premier League in 2002 as Division One champions, but Keegan left the club in March 2005, initially announcing his retirement from football.

Keegan made an emotional return to Newcastle in 2008, but only lasted eight months following tensions with the board and owner Mike Ashley.

Newcastle's statement in full on Keegan's passing

"We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply-loved figures in our club's history.

"Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.

"As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James' Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an Entertainer.

"Above all that, Kevin forged an extraordinary bond with Newcastle, built on the roots of his father, Joe. He understood our people. He embraced the north east with a passion that was genuine and unwavering, and in return, he earned his rightful place in the hearts of millions.

"Kevin's impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him.

"At this profoundly sad time, we send our love and deepest sympathy to Kevin's wife Jean, his family, friends and all who had the privilege of knowing and working alongside him.

"Today, we mourn the loss of a true giant of our history, and at the appropriate moment, we will carefully consider how we shape a lasting tribute to Kevin's remarkable life and legacy. Rest in Peace, King Kev."

'Giant of the game' - Tributes come in for Keegan

Alan Shearer: "My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss."

Jamie Carragher: "RIP Kevin Keegan. One of the greatest players this country has ever produced, trophies & goals galore, double Ballon D'or winner shows he was an absolute giant of the English game. One of the most important men in making Liverpool what it is today."

Liverpool FC: "We are deeply saddened by the passing of the legendary Kevin Keegan and mourn his loss. His indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on. Rest in peace, Kevin."

England national team: "We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away. Kevin earned 63 international caps and scored 21 goals between 1972 and 1982, before managing the Three Lions from 1999 to 2000. Our thoughts and condolences are with Kevin's family, friends and former clubs."

Thomas Tuchel: "As a young football fan, he was the first England superstar I can remember watching growing up.

"He won every honour possible and to be named the best player in the world two times was an unbelievable achievement. You only need to think how fondly he is remembered by supporters at his clubs to see what a man he was. Of course, he also had that special experience of playing, captaining and managing his country.

"My thoughts are with his family and friends today, and all the fans who loved to watch him play.

"I know we will pay him a full tribute when we welcome Spain to Wembley Stadium in September. We will be honouring a true hero of English football."

Southampton FC: "We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan.

"Kevin signed for the club in 1980 as the holder of the Ballon d'Or and brought great joy to fans at The Dell and across the football world. Our thoughts are with his family and friends at this difficult time."

Manchester City FC: "Everyone at Manchester City is devastated to learn our former manager Kevin Keegan has passed away, aged 75.

"Kevin was a transformative manager who brought optimism and vibrancy to City during his four-year spell in charge.

"The promotion campaign in 2001/02 will never be forgotten, and Kevin then established us once again as a top Premier League side in the years that followed. Our thoughts are with Kevin's family and friends at this very difficult time."

Former Newcastle interim co-chief executive Mehrdad Ghodoussi: "Devastated to hear about Kevin Keegan. Growing up watching football, he was one of the names that defined an era, a double Ballon d'Or winner, European Cup champion, England captain, and one of the most exciting players the game has seen.

"But what he did at Newcastle was different. He turned belief into something you could feel in the stadium. King Kev wasn't just admired, he was loved, because everything he did came from the heart. Rest in peace, Kevin. Thank you for everything you gave the game."

The English Football League: "The EFL is saddened to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan. A legend of the English game, Keegan will be remembered by generations of football fans for his impact as a player and manager. Our thoughts are with his family and friends."

Manchester United: "We are profoundly saddened by the loss of Kevin Keegan. A giant of English football, he was a cherished figure at the very highest levels of the game. Our condolences go to Kevin's family, loved ones and all those he inspired as a manager, player and person, on and off the pitch. Rest in peace, Kevin."

Former Liverpool striker David Fairclough: "Stunned. Such sad news Kevin Keegan has passed away. Absolutely devastated to hear such awful news. So many incredible memories of KK, I'm so lucky to have spent time and shared moments that have and will last a lifetime. Heartfelt condolences and love to Jean and family. YNWA."

Fulham FC: "We're incredibly sad to hear the news that our former manager Kevin Keegan has passed away. A legend of the game, Keegan led Fulham to the Football League Second Division title in 1999. He left Craven Cottage at the end of that season to focus on his duties as England manager. Our thoughts are with his friends and family at this difficult time."

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan, Liverpool legend and former Newcastle manager, dies aged 75
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan, the former England and Newcastle manager who was twice European football of the year and a stalwart member of Liverpool’s serial First Division and European champions in the 1970s, has died aged 75.

Keegan’s family revealed in January that he had cancer, and in June he revealed himself that it was stage four, the most advanced stage. “It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75,” read a family statement. “Kevin had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

“A double Ballon D’or winner, Kevin was a much loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin’s incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy.”

Keegan started his career at Scunthorpe before being signed for Liverpool by Bill Shankly for just £33,000 in 1971, “King Kevin” going on to win the First Division title three times as well as the FA Cup, the Uefa Cup twice and the 1977 European Cup. Keegan is the only British player to have won two Ballons d’Or.

The 5ft 8in combative “Mighty Mouse” was not, by his own admission, a natural talent but the son of a south Yorkshire miner trained hard, remained humble and never ducked a challenge, traits that endeared him to the Kop. “I learned so much from Shanks. He used to say: ‘If I was a road-sweeper, my street would be the cleanest in the borough.’ I took that to heart,’ he said.

View image in fullscreen Liverpool’s Ian Callaghan, Kevin Keegan and Ray Clemence parade the winning trophy after the 1974 FA Cup final between Liverpool and Newcastle at Wembley. Photograph: Liverpool FC/Getty Images

Keegan was twice named European Footballer of the Year while at the German club Hamburg and returned to England to play for Southampton and Newcastle before retiring as a player in 1984. He won 63 England caps, scoring 21 goals, playing at the 1982 World Cup and was also captain at the 1980 Euros.

Keegan was never one to hold back, his fiery temperament rarely far from the surface. He was memorably sent off for scrapping with Leeds’s Billy Bremner in the 1974 Charity Shield after boiling over and his volatile temperament and pugnacious intolerance of football’s machinations, real or perceived. “I don’t like people to deceive me and tell me lies,” he told the Guardian in 2018.

View image in fullscreen Kevin Keegan in 2008. Photograph: Michael Mayhew/Sportsphoto

He wrote newspaper columns, was one of the English game’s first players to have their own branded football boots, had a hit record (Head Over Heels in Love), and became an enduring star of the BBC’s Superstars. He was the public face of 70s aftershave Brut 33 with Henry Cooper. He became close friends with another of the game’s renegades, George Best. “I wanted so much to have his ability. His skill was unbelievable. I played against Cruyff, Beckenbauer, Maradona. But I still say Besty was the best I played against,” he told Simon Hatterstone.

Keegan retired from playing aged 33 and moved to Spain, where his two daughters grew up unaware he had been a footballer. “It was the best decision I made in my life,” he told the Guardian in 2011. “I was at the highest level and the only way was down. I call it the glass mountain – you can’t climb a glass mountain.”

In 1992, Keegan made his first step into management at his former club Newcastle, guiding them into the Premier League and to within touching distance of the 1995-96 title only to miss out to Manchester United. His finger-jabbing “I will love it” rant when Alex Ferguson’s mind-games got the better of him has become part of the English game’s lore.

After leaving St James’ Park in January 1997, a brief stint at Fulham followed before he became England manager in 1999, having initially taken on the job following Glenn Hoddle’s departure. Amid a disappointing Euro 2000 campaign, Keegan resigned on the back of defeat by Germany at Wembley Stadium, after just 20 months and 18 games, winning only seven of them – the worst win ratio of any England manager.

A spell at Manchester City followed, but Keegan left the club in March 2005, initially announcing his retirement from football, only to make an emotional return to Newcastle in 2008. That second spell lasted eight months following tensions with the board and owner Mike Ashley. In 2009 a tribunal awarded Keegan £2m damages for constructive dismissal.

Kevin Keegan’s infamous ‘I will love it!’ rant – video

He was made an OBE in 1982 for services to football, but Keegan’s unreconstructed opinions could offend. In 2023, his questioning the suitability of former England women’s internationals commenting on incidents in men’s international matches landed him in hot water. At a public event in Bristol, he told the audience: “I don’t like to listen to ladies talking about the England men’s team at the match because I don’t think it’s the same experience. I have a problem with that.”

Sports.title: More than a million people expected at Spain’s World Cup celebration in Madrid
Sports.content:
More than a million Spaniards, many still bleary-eyed and feeling a little delicate after the country’s historic World Cup victory against Argentina, are expected to descend on central Madrid on Monday night to welcome the triumphant national team home.

La Roja, who beat Argentina 1-0 in the final in New Jersey on Sunday night, were afforded the first of many heroes’ welcomes when they touched down at Madrid’s Barajas airport at 2.30pm local time on Monday.

Spain’s captain, Rodri, waved the trophy aloft as he emerged from the plane, his medal from the previous night around his neck. The team posed for a photo before heading into terminal four where hundreds of delighted fans, many in Spain strips and carrying the country’s red-and-yellow rojigualda flag, waited and hoped for a glimpse of the freshly minted champions.

The team’s first official stop is the Zarzuela palace, northwest of Madrid, where the players and staff will be received by King Felipe and Queen Letizia at about 4.30pm. After that, they are due to head to the Moncloa palace – the office and residence of the prime minister – for a meet-and greet with Spain’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, at around 6pm.

The victory parade will then kick off in earnest, with the team travelling into town by bus from Moncloa. The focus of the festivities, which will feature music and are expected to draw massive crowds, will be the Plaza de Cibeles just outside Madrid city hall.

Madrid’s mayor, José Luis Martínez Almeida, told Radio Nacional de España that the capital was working to give the team the homecoming they deserved. He also hailed the peaceful and joyous scenes that had greeted Spain’s victory.

View image in fullscreen Rodri carries the World Cup at Barajas airport on Monday. Photograph: Sergio R Moreno/GTRES/Shutterstock

“Even though there were thousands and thousands of people on the streets last night, there were practically no incidents in the city,” he said.

“We’re getting everything ready for tonight and the musical events should start at Cibeles from about 6pm, with the parade scheduled to start at 7pm – but all this is depends on various factors … The thing we’re focusing on is how to celebrate and greet a team that will live for ever in our memory.”

The victory – Spain’s second men’s World Cup win after their triumph against the Netherlands in South Africa in 2010 – was seen by hundreds of thousand of Spaniards who followed the match in bars, parks, fairgrounds, bullrings, and on giant screens in the centre of Madrid. The Spanish press have hailed it as “a unique collective experience” made possible by a young team that reflects all that is best about a modern, diverse and determined country.

The win has also been enthusiastically hailed by the country’s political class.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“WE ARE WORLD CHAMPIONS!!” Sánchez wrote in a social media post. “What an amazing national squad. Thank you, team.”

Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of Spain’s conservative People’s party, was equally free with the capital letters. “Well-deserved WORLD CHAMPIONS! Values, hard work, humility, and faith. You have made history. There are no limits for this team … Long live Spain!!!” he wrote on X.

Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, also offered his congratulations to the team for carrying “the flag of Spain so far and so high”.

The Spanish postal service, Correos, has announced the creation of a special stamp to commemorate what it called “one of the greatest achievements in the history of Spanish sport”. The red-coloured stamp will bear the word CAMPEONES and feature two stars – one for each of Spain’s World Cup victories.

Sports.title: The 2026 World Cup was full of spectacle, scandal and compromise | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Perhaps it’s too early, with the shreds of gold tape still fluttering through the New Jersey sky, to make a proper assessment. That will only come when everything has sunk in properly, when memories have had the chance to settle and shape themselves, when the consequences of certain events have become clear. But let’s try anyway to make some sort of assessment of where the World Cup that ended with Leandro Paredes grappling with Gavi ranks historically.

The Balogun Affair could yet have major consequences. At the moment, it feels that the world has moved on, but that’s the nature of tournaments. They have a momentum of their own, a drive towards the finish that tends to sweep everything else aside. But there can be little doubt that the bending before political pressure, sweeping aside 64 years of precedent to ensure a particular player could take the stage, just as Gianni Infantino had done with Cristiano Ronaldo, just as he had done in gerrymandering the qualification criteria for the Club World Cup to ensure Lionel Messi played, represents a milestone.

Perhaps in the future we will simply accept the principle that famous players get dispensation because making money is more important than justice or the good of the game – the prioritisation of revenue generation has been a feature of the 2026 tournament – or perhaps this will stiffen the sinews of opposition to Infantino; it’s been notable, for instance, how many British politicians – and some American ones – have taken to criticising Fifa and its president. An immediate consequence could be the expansion of the World Cup to 64 teams as Infantino looks to shore up his base, particularly given the damage US (and Canadian) immigration policy has done to his claims to be a champion of the global south.

Other issues that have sunk into the mulch of games will surely resurface. The treatment of Iran, for instance, was scandalous, and sets a worrying precedent. Ticket prices may be lower at the 2030 World Cup, but the idea that a reasonable proportion should be available to the regular fans who go to league football every week is now gone. The World Cup is no longer a mass movement but a luxury event.

The price paid by the host cities, similarly, will only become truly apparent in retrospect. That is financial, but it’s also social. In the US and Canada, there have been street sweeps of the homeless, people with very little deprived of what few possessions they have, ID and medication. In Mexico, there has been an outcry about water extraction and environmental damage linked to World Cup projects.

The Italian newspaper la Gazzetta dello Sport ran a double page on Saturday calling the World Cup a “disaster”, outlining certain major issues: ticket prices, Balogun, the weather, the increase in games, the decrease of rest. That may be an overstatement, but what followed really was a disaster as the newspaper found its ticket allocation for the final slashed from five to two. It’s not entirely clear whether the two were linked, but the idea that a media outlet could be denied access for rejecting the official narrative that this World Cup has been the greatest ever is dystopian.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk: World Cup Edition Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

That fitted the generally contemptuous attitude of Fifa towards the media at this tournament. While some venues – notably Houston and Atlanta – went out of their way to be welcoming, basic organisation and facilities were the worst for at least six World Cups. Quite understandably, nobody in the real world cares about journalists and whether the wifi works, but it’s indicative of a more general approach: fans are revenue units to be milked mercilessly; the media an irritating imposition.

The football, meanwhile, was good but not great. There were a number of fine and dramatic games – Brazil v Japan, Morocco v the Netherlands, England v Mexico, Argentina v Cape Verde, Norway v Côte d’Ivoire, Belgium v Senegal, Norway v Brazil, Argentina v Egypt – but unfortunately almost all of them were in the last 32 or last 16. The quarter-finals were not especially inspiring. Argentina’s win over England in the semi was thrilling and involved a collapse that will be discussed for years, but Spain’s win over France was almost too easy; Spain quickly established a degree of superiority over the French that was never really challenged.

And the final was dismal, an awful affair. The right team won, in their familiar bloodless way, but the grim spectacle was a direct consequence of the indulgence shown Argentina earlier in the tournament. The ending, inevitably, colours what went before, and drags this tournament behind 2022 and 2018, let alone the glorious World Cups of the 1980s or 1998. Posterity can judge where exactly in the middle rank it sits, whether above or below 2014 and 2006. It was not great but it was good and, beyond the Fifa bluster, that’s fine.

Sports.title: Tuchel is clinging to an outdated English style – he must let players take risks | Jacob Steinberg
Sports.content:
Only England can claim the bronze medal at the World Cup by beating France in a 10-goal thriller and end up even more annoyed with the manager. Yet emotions are still running high after the collapse against Argentina last week and it is going to take more than winning a game low on jeopardy for the criticism of Thomas Tuchel to die down.

Hiring Tuchel was centred around the promise that he would make the difference in the big games. When that fell down, all that was left was anger. It exposed the core emptiness of the appointment, of a rich federation covering up the flaws in its coaching development by trying to game the system by throwing money at an expensive outsider.

What is the Football Association’s vision? The initial idea was Tuchel providing a short, sharp shock and his tactical acumen helping England to get over the line. Then came a change after a successful qualifying campaign against modest opposition. The FA moved the goalposts by handing Tuchel a contract extension, and suddenly winning the World Cup did not seem quite as pressing.

Yet the idea of Tuchel as a project builder seemed far-fetched during the bitter recriminations after the defeat by Argentina. Criticised for his negative substitutions when England led, the German talked dismissively of English DNA, lamenting the lack of care in possession. Fair enough, you thought, because this has long been a weakness – only, hadn’t Tuchel caused some of the damage by leaving out most of the ball players from his squad? Would it have been different if Adam Wharton, Trent Alexander-Arnold and Cole Palmer had been around in Atlanta? Maybe not, but a lot of money has been spent on developing a different type of English player in recent decades.

Perhaps Tuchel was thinking of an old English DNA. But maybe this is part of the issue with employing a foreign coach whose focus is on winning by any means possible. This is the third time England have been down this road. There is an idea of the manager from abroad as a sophisticate. But Sven-Göran Eriksson was not as tactically adroit as Glenn Hoddle. Eriksson played a traditional 4-4-2 whereas Hoddle was flexible with his formations.

Tuchel, too, has struggled to build an identity. He seems taken with an outdated English style. Tuchel wanted to play like a Premier League team, with pace and physicality, but that has rarely worked for England. They tend to be outpassed in big knockout games, which is why there has been such focus in youth football in developing players more at ease with the dominant Spanish passing style.

View image in fullscreen England players look dejected after the semi-final defeat by Argentina. Photograph: Paul Childs/Reuters

Spain have just won another World Cup, their method too much for Argentina in a dour final, and for those watching from afar a big takeaway will surely be that the last two teams standing were led by homegrown coaches.

Luis de la Fuente and Lionel Scaloni have risen through the ranks and are part of a system. They have a feeling for their countries, a sense of the identity. Tuchel has been inserted in the hope he can cover up the FA’s failure to produce its own coaches. No male team led by a foreign manager has secured the World Cup and it should worry the FA when bringing in an outsider with a win-now mentality ends with the senior side using a very different style of play to younger age groups.

There is a view within youth coaching circles that Tuchel has taken England backwards at this tournament. The under-21s have won the past two European Championships by being brave on the ball. They have beaten Spain in consecutive tournaments and the demand from Lee Carsley is that his players take risks in possession. Tuchel finished the semi-final by lobbing balls towards Dan Burn. He played a pragmatic style and his England ended up unable to throw caution to the wind. This World Cup underlines that turning to celebrated coaches from the club game is not a recipe for success.

Brazil appointed Carlo Ancelotti but went out in the last 16. Roberto Martínez failed with Portugal after sticking with Cristiano Ronaldo. Mauricio Pochettino oversaw the USA side being humiliated by Belgium.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Scaloni came through the national setup before winning the World Cup with Argentina in 2022. Similarly De la Fuente won the European Under-19 Championship with Spain in 2015 and the European Under-21 Championship in 2019. He has brought players through and, having earned a promotion, won the senior European title in 2024.

View image in fullscreen Luis de la Fuente was a successful age-group manager before taking over Spain’s senior side and leading them to glory. Photograph: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

Spain show smooth progression. Players who beat Argentina in the final played youth football for De la Fuente. This is not to say that England’s next step should be to appoint Carsley, who did not seem as if he had the temperament for the senior job when he filled in as caretaker between Gareth Southgate’s departure and Tuchel’s arrival. Even so, Carsley is closer to the Spanish style and has shown it is possible for England teams to be risk-takers.

It is food for thought for the FA as it reviews England’s World Cup. As it stands, Tuchel will get another tournament. There are bridges to build but finishing third is not a sackable offence. In any case there is no other idea at the FA. Tuchel was not produced, he was bought. Hopefully he adapts during the Nations League. There should be a shift away from this physical style. But do not be surprised if the hired gun’s views on English DNA end up making him sound out of touch. It would not happen to Spain. De la Fuente knows their identity. He is part of it.

Sports.title: Hits, misses and Muppets: the star-studded World Cup half-time show nobody asked for
Sports.content:
Like hydration breaks and Donald Trump’s ability to get refereeing decisions overturned by simply phoning up the president of Fifa and complaining, the final half-time show is an innovation of the 2026 World Cup that comes with a degree of controversy attached. For one thing, its existence automatically means the World Cup final breaks the International Football Association’s 15-minute half-time mandate.

For another, its obvious antecedent lies in the NFL’s Super Bowl, where the half-time entertainment has mushroomed over the decades from a few marching bands to one of the big pop events of the year. To its detractors, it smacks of America not so much embracing the World Cup as imposing itself upon it.

View image in fullscreen Shakira performs during the World Cup final. Photograph: MB Media/Getty Images

But before you even got to the main event, there was more musical entertainment at the final to wade through, most notably the pre-match closing ceremony, a damp squib that neither the BBC nor ITV elected to broadcast live.

Anyone who hastened to iPlayer was rewarded not merely with Post Malone debuting what’s presumably the first single from his forthcoming album the Eternal Buzz, Chrome Heartbreaker (a pivot back to hip-hop-influenced pop after his recent diversion into country, should you be eagerly tracking the artistic vacillations of Post Malone’s career) and duetting with Swae Lee on their US chart-topper Sunflower, but also an online influencer-cum-professional wrestler called IShowSpeed performing Champions, a track that gained so much traction online that Fifa felt obliged to include it on the official Fifa World Cup album.

A frightful cocktail of thunderous drums and autotuned vocals, it featured lyrics that make your average football song sound as erudite and profound as the oeuvre of Leonard Cohen: “I take a breath and wait for the ref / This is the World Cup, put your hands in the air.” Alas, news of its social media virality clearly hadn’t reached the audience in the New York New Jersey Stadium. The deathly silence at its conclusion made you wonder if perhaps the TV broadcast couldn’t pick up the sound of the crowd, but no: some fireworks subsequently went off and they went audibly mental.

View image in fullscreen Three members of the Muppets’ house band the Electric Mayhem performed the White Stripes’ Seven Nation Army. Photograph: James Lang/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters

There was, it turned out, more to come. Jennifer Hudson sang the Star-Spangled Banner. Dutifully flogging a dead horse with all the professionalism he could muster, Robbie Williams performed the Fifa anthem, Desire, in the company of Laura Pausini and Nicole Scherzinger. The ballad debuted at the draw ceremony in December and – like all the musical entertainment at said event – it was overshadowed by the news that Fifa had apparently started making up awards in order to give them to Donald Trump. It vanished into obscurity thereafter, failing to chart anywhere in the world. Listening to it exhumed for another airing, you were forced to concede that the world had a point.

After all that, the actual half-time show felt like a comparative triumph. You could argue that the bar had been set pretty low without much dissent, but nonetheless, it zipped along, cramming a lot into its 11 minutes by the simple expedient of paring songs down to their bare essentials and swiftly cutting between artists. Madonna performed a version of her 2000 hit Music – reworked over a backing track immediately recognisable as derived from the Trammps’ Disco Inferno – on a vaguely Mad Max-ish vehicle piloted by Ronaldo and Ronaldinho.

Then the strains of the White Stripes’ Seven Nation Army rang out, ostensibly performed by three members of the Muppets’ house band the Electric Mayhem. There was no sign of their leader, Dr Teeth, but perhaps he was indisposed, being treated backstage after being exposed to Champions by IShowSpeed. BTS rattled through Dynamite, Shakira and Burna Boy played a truncated version of Dai Dai – the solitary World Cup song in recent memory to actually impact on the British charts – and Coldplay performed a song called Believe in Love accompanied by a children’s choir: the latter looks horrendous on paper, but was far less sugary in reality, undercut by the farty blast of a crowd of vuvuzela players.

View image in fullscreen Coldplay performed a song called Believe in Love accompanied by a children’s choir that was far less sugary than it could have been. Photograph: Tullio Puglia/FIFA/Getty Images

The solitary misstep might have involved allowing Justin Bieber to perform a downcast acoustic ballad, Everything Hallelujah – viral hit following his performance at Coachella or not, this perhaps wasn’t the moment for introspection – but no matter: if the half-time show wasn’t sufficiently head-spinning to convince the viewer it should be a regular occurrence at every World Cup final, it worked well enough to justify its existence at least this time. Although clearly not everyone felt the same way: “I thought it was crap,” offered Wayne Rooney, when pressed for his opinions by BBC presenter Gabby Logan.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi’s World Cup fairytale ends with pitiful Argentina as final villains | Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Sports.content:
Playing on the grandest stage in sport for the last time, Lionel Messi seemed almost certain to provide one last memorable moment in this World Cup final.

Yet as the sun ducked behind the west stand of New York New Jersey Stadium on Sunday, it became clearer and clearer that Argentina had lost the magic they had carried through this tournament. And as Spain gradually wrested control, one was left to confront reality: Messi, and Argentina, had finally run out of time, having long since given in to their worst instincts in a 1-0 defeat.

This final presented a stark contrast to the Argentina – and Messi – we observed in every other match of the tournament. Almost without exception, La Albiceleste have been the tournament’s most entertaining team, not so much for how they’ve scored their goals but for when they’ve scored them, offering a masterclass in dramatic timing. Twice they were nearly eliminated by badly outmatched opponents, results that only galvanized them.

Finals are frequently forgettable matches that fail to entertain but even by that lowly standard the pacing of things felt dreadful. Spain were suffocating defensively and – after a forgettable first half – finally worked their way into things in the second 45, eventually breaking through in extra time, quite expectedly. Argentina? They became the first team in the near century-long history of the tournament to fail to record a shot in regular time of a World Cup final. Even when handed an additional half an hour, they never threatened.

And Messi? Until this final, he had presented observers with one of the rarest opportunities in professional sport: a chance to witness greatness free of stakes, entirely devoid of any real pressure to perform. At 39, Messi has done his time and nobody could criticize his collection of hardware – as an individual or as part of a club or country. This defeat does nothing to sully a spotless legacy; a win would have only strengthened his claim as the greatest player in the history of the sport. To some Argentinians, the victory against England in their semi-final likely carries nearly as much weight as a victory in the final would have.

Yet it has to be said: Messi was rarely involved in this match, a far cry from the player who has sometimes carried his team this summer. Much of this, of course, is down to a Spain masterclass in defending. That alone is not always enough to contain the diminutive Argentina captain. But give Spain their due: they badly outclassed Argentina in every way, neutralizing even Messi. By the end Argentina had become what so many observers pegged them to be in the first place, sometimes unfairly: underhanded, dirty and desperate.

Time has almost always been irrelevant to Messi on the field, because he so frequently bends it to his liking to elude those who defend him. The manner in which he performs at age 39 has a similar effect, tearing open a rift in time itself and transporting observers back to his glory days at Barcelona and elsewhere. Time itself has not passed him by as much as he’s marched alongside it, occasionally trailing behind a step or two but always eventually pulling even with it again.

View image in fullscreen Spain kept close tabs on Lionel Messi, who had little impact on the final. Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty Images

Yet now we are left to face the unmistakable reality that Messi is done, with the World Cup at least – this is, it’s worth noting, what was said after he led Argentina to their first World Cup in nearly four decades in 2022 and what was assumed in 2016, when Messi briefly retired from the national team after Argentina’s defeat in the Copa América final. Back then, the dialogue surrounding this player was that he would never play for Argentina the way he did for Barcelona, or even rumblings that Messi himself wasn’t sufficiently Argentinian, having spent so much of his life in Spain. Both arguments feel laughable 10 years later.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It remains to be seen how Argentina’s performance will be perceived back home, where expectations were understandably high. The head coach, Lionel Scaloni, and even Messi had spoken at length before the final about how much they had already achieved. This final result, they implied, would do little to sully that sense of accomplishment.

This was, of course, before they took the field and more or less destroyed the game. Scaloni’s legacy, like Messi’s, was secure before this final, the coach having brought Argentina a third World Cup and a pair of Copa América titles, but this was a lost opportunity to solidify it. Two things can coexist: Scaloni is almost without question Argentina’s greatest coach, and this was one of his worst results and performances.

What feels much more real, though, is a sense of loss and disappointment after this pitiful final performance, which provided Argentina – and Messi – with a perfect opportunity to put the finishing touches on their fairytale. Instead, they turned from hero to villain – and needlessly so.

Sports.title: Melvine Malard hungry for trophies after joining Chelsea from Manchester United
Sports.content:
Chelsea have announced the signing of the France forward Melvine Malard from Manchester United on a four-year contract. The Guardian revealed last week that a deal was close for the 26-year-old, who has left United after three seasons for about £850,000.

Malard had one year on her contract and United were keen to keep the forward. However, once it became clear Malard wanted a move United decided to sell rather than lose a high-value player on a free next summer.

It is believed United will reinvest the fee, which is a record sale for the club, into the squad, with the transfer window open until 3 September.

United have made one summer signing, the full-back Andrea Medina from Atlético Madrid, but more incomings are expected after the departures of Leah Galton, Hannah Blundell, Sienna Wareing, Millie Turner, Lisa Naalsund and Malard.

“I’m so happy because I have a plan for my life and my career, and Chelsea were a part of that plan,” Malard said. ”My objective is to become better every single day and to win trophies. I know Chelsea always have that as an objective.”

The France international played under Chelsea’s head coach, Sonia Bompastor, at Lyonnes (formerly Lyon) and was recruited to their academy by Bompastor. “I have known Sonia since I was 14 years old, so it is great to work with her again,” Malard said.

It is understood Chelsea have been tracking Malard for some time. They have lost a number of players across the forward line, with the club record-goalscorer Sam Kerr and Guro Reiten departing for Gotham FC, Catarina Macario joining San Diego Wave and Johanna Rytting Kaneryd signing for Lyonnes.

Malard is Chelsea’s third signing of the summer, after the former Arsenal full-back Katie McCabe and the forward Manaka Matsukubo, who was with North Carolina Courage.

Malard spent seven seasons at Lyonnes, winning four Champions Leagues, three league titles and two Coupes de France. Her first season with United was on loan.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Last season she scored four goals in United’s run to a first Champions League quarter-final and six times in 18 Women’s Super League games.

Liverpool have signed the Japanese attacking midfielder Mao Itamura from Feyenoord. The 19-year-old, who won the Under-20 Women’s Asian Cup in April, was the Eredivisie player of the year last season in the Netherlands. She scored eight times and provided six assists as Feyenoord qualified for European competition for the first time, their third-place finish earning a place in the Europa Cup.

Itamura is Liverpool’s fifth summer signing, after Vivien Endemann, Sara Agrez, Mari Ward and Khiara Keating.

Sports.title: Rodri’s redemption story leaves stars in the shadow of Spain’s great controller | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
You don’t need to be long in the US before somebody, finding you’re here to cover “the Fifa” as so many Americans so demoralisingly call it, will tell you that the USA would obviously win it all the time if only their best athletes weren’t distracted by more local pursuits: American football, basketball, eating enormous sandwiches and the like. If you’re really lucky they’ll start shouting names at you with a detailed rundown of height, weight, sprint speed, what they can bench and other fascinating statistics.

At which you wonder whether the 5ft 7in Lionel Messi has ever done a bench press. Rodri probably has, but he’s still nobody’s idea of a great athlete. He’s tall without being physically imposing. He’s not quick. He ambles about games being in the right place. Occasionally he leans into people or passes the ball 10 yards. It would be difficult to put together a highlights reel of his performance in the World Cup final that would convince a neophyte that he was the defining player – but he was, and was rightly named player of the tournament as well.

This has been a World Cup in which individual stars shone. Kylian Mbappé topped the goalscoring charts, followed by Messi, Jude Bellingham, Erling Haaland, Harry Kane and Ousmane Dembélé. In the most heavily marketed World Cup ever, there were plenty of faces to market: “Look at this celebrity, scoring a goal!” But in the end the parade of goalscorers ended up marching in the shadow of the great controller.

Mauricio Pochettino made the point last year that there were two problems with a US system that in effect forces a parent who wants their child to play soccer to pay thousands of dollars a year to belong to a club. The first is that it means huge swathes of the population are excluded for basic financial reasons. The second is less obvious but perhaps almost as insidious: parents at the end of the year will demand to see progress, to know what they’ve got for their money.

The two most important attributes for an elite footballer – technical ability and tactical awareness – are extremely difficult to measure. And so coaches tend to tell parent that their charge has knocked a fraction off their sprint time, or is lifting 20 pounds more. That’s measurable; it satisfies the need to see a return on investment. The result is a focus on physicality rather than the nebulous but vital skills that define the best players, something reflected in how the US play. Carli Lloyd made a similar point, and a series of youth coaches I’ve spoken to over the past month have agreed.

View image in fullscreen Rori directs traffic in the Spain midfield during Sunday’s World Cup final. Photograph: James Lang/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters

There is no American Rodri, and perhaps in the present system there cannot be one. But then there is no English Rodri, or French Rodri, or Argentinian Rodri, or German Rodri. Rodri is a very Spanish type. He comes from the line of Sergio Busquets, and the closest player to him in the modern game is Martín Zubimendi. In an environment in which football is becoming increasing physical, they have found a role for the cerebral.

Much of what Rodri does is indefinable. He didn’t score a goal or register an assist at this World Cup. A pass completion rate of 93.2% is obviously very good, but it was only the 44th best in the tournament. Even if you filter out centre-backs, who play a lot of short simple, unpressured passes, Rodri is 18th. He ranked 22nd for tackles per game and 450th for interceptions. Even at fouling, at which, following in the proud Manchester City lineage of Fernandinho, Rodri is a master, has was only 97th. Although he completed a record 756 passes at this tournament, his great skill is simply being. By existing in the right spaces, Rodri lubricates and distributes and, by somehow combining that with a capacity to draw matter towards him, he discourages opponents from passing in his zone. He, as much as anyone, was the reason Lionel Messi was so little involved in the final.

Yet as recently as the end of the domestic season – which admittedly doesn’t feel that recent after 104 World Cup games, but was only two months ago – there were doubts about whether Rodri would ever be quite the same again. It was only 10 weeks after being named player of the tournament at Euro 2024 that Rodri sustained the anterior crucial ligament injury that kept him out for the 2024-25 season. City’s decline in his absence told its own story.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

His return was not straightforward. He struggled during the Club World Cup, forced off during the defeat by Al-Hilal. He started only 17 league games last season. Pep Guardiola suggested that the best of Rodri wouldn’t be seen until the World Cup. That’s been a recurring theme; most of the best players at this tournament were those who had not slogged through 50+ high-intensity games last season.

In that sense, Rodri’s is a great redemption story, a player returning after two very difficult seasons to add World Cup honours to his European award. But there’s also an undeniable irony that in a country that celebrates the individual like no other, in a World Cup that has relentlessly promoted celebrities, the defining player ends up being the most unflashy team-oriented candidate imaginable, the first non-creator to win the Golden Ball in 24 years.

Sports.title: 2026 World Cup team of the tournament: Harry Kane omitted and six Spain stars named in Gabby Agbonlahor’s XI
Sports.content:
2026 World Cup team of the tournament: Harry Kane omitted and six Spain stars named in Gabby Agbonlahor’s XI

The 2026 World Cup is officially over after an incredible five weeks of action, with Spain lifting the trophy for a second time.

But now the tournament is complete, it's a popular time for fans and pundits alike to put together their standout XIs.

5 Spain became world champions for a second time Credit: Getty

There were many starring performances, ranging from the world's best players to complete unknowns becoming legends.

Kylian Mbappe won the Golden Boot, while Rodri won the Golden Ball and Pau Cubarsi was handed Young Player of the Tournament.

Those three stars got the accolades, but do they all make the World Cup Team of the Tournament? And if so, who joins them?

Here's who Gabby Agbonlahor and Troy Deeney think deserve to be among the best 11 players of the summer:

Instagram star and Spain's defence

Agbonlahor, of course, started off with his defence, making a simple choice for his back four after selecting a star goalkeeper.

"There have been some good goalkeeping performances, but I have to give it to Vozinha," the ex-England striker began.

"Two clean sheets, five goals conceded, clean sheet against Spain, who went on to win the tournament.

"That just shows how good of a performance it was...a fantastic tournament and he got a load of Instagram followers."

He then moved on to his back four and simply selected the entire Spain defence, picking Pedro Porro, Pau Cubarsi, Aymeric Laporte and Marc Cucurella.

"Porro, I think he was fantastic, passion, determination...Cucurella is one of the best in the world, and Cubarsi and Laporte, how they played was incredible," Agbonlahor explained.

5 Cape Verde's Vozinha was one of the heroes of the 2026 World Cup Credit: Getty

'A credit to the nation'

He then moved on to his midfield, including Player of the Tournament, Rodri, and picking England's main man.

"Rodri went through a terrible knee injury...that was Ballon d'Or Rodri; those were the performances we've seen," he said.

"He's not been the same player since his injury, but any talk we were having of him going from City, now fans and Enzo Maresca will be saying no, Rodri will be starting with Elliot Anderson."

Agbonlahor then selected: "Alongside him I want Dani Olmo...Spain play to his strengths, behind the striker, receiving the ball, finding passes, I thought he was fantastic.

"And also in midfield, Jude Bellingham. Words can't describe how good he is, seven goals, one assist, the most goals by an English player at a World Cup.

"What he's proved to everyone is that he's a leader, a future captain, and he did everything in the tournament to get us over the line...the manager cost us...I thought he was a credit to the nation"

5 Bellingham made Agbonlahor's XI for his showing, but Kane was omitted Credit: Getty

Kane left out

Bellingham is the only England player in Agbonlahor's World Cup XI, as he opted against including Harry Kane in the team.

Kane scored six goals at the tournament and became the country's all-time top scorer there, but he didn't claim a place.

The Three Lions captain was snubbed amid some criticism for his performances, with three stars picked over him.

Agbonlahor explained: "The front three speak for themselves: Mbappe, 10 goals, four assists, Lionel Messi, eight goals, four assists, Erling Haaland, seven goals, zero assists.

"They were fantastic and it was a pleasure to see a World Cup where the top, top players turned up."

Agbonlahor's World Cup TOTT: Vozinha; Porro, Cubarsi, Laporte, Cucurella; Rodri, Olmo, Bellingham; Messi, Mbappé, Haaland.

5

Troy Deeney's Team of the Tournament

Similarly to Agbonlahor, Deeney couldn't help but have Spain dominate the defence in his best XI of the World Cup.

He also picked Cubarsi and Cucurella, adding in goalkeeper Unai Simon over Cape Verde's hero Vozinha.

On Simon and the Spanish defence, Deeney said: "He's been unreal... when you only let in one goal, that's frightening."

The former Premier League striker went on to select what he called a 'wildcard', with Lisandro Martinez being picked.

Martinez starred for Argentina ahead of the final, but he was unfortunately substituted with an injury in the showpiece.

In midfield, Deeney, of course, picked Golden Ball winner Rodri, but then selected a surprise name next to him.

He chose France's Manu Kone to slot into his team, as the 25-year-old impressed despite starting just half of Les Bleus' eight games.

Bellingham was also included in Deeney's team, like Agbonlahor's.

However, Kane wasn't snubbed for a second time, as the ex-Watford man picked the England captain for his line-up.

He was selected alongside Messi and Mbappe in the front line.

"Harry, Messi on the right, Mbappe on the left, Jude in the 10," he explained when picking his star-studded forwards.

Deeney’s World Cup TOTT: Simon; Porro, Cubarsi, Martinez, Cucurella; Kone, Rodri; Messi, Bellingham, Mbappe; Kane

Sports.title: Carabao Cup clash brought forward 24 hours due to unusual reason as statement released
Sports.content:
Bristol City have announced that their Carabao Cup first-round clash with Walsall has been moved forward for a rather bizarre reason.

The two sides had been due to get their seasons underway at Ashton Gate on Friday, August 7, but it will now be played 24 hours earlier to avoid clashing with the Bristol International Balloon Fiesta.

4 Ashton Gate will now host Bristol City's first game of the season 24 hours later than first planned Credit: Getty

On the same evening that the Robins and the Saddlers were set to meet, the annual local festival will get underway.

With over 500,000 expected to attend the Bristol spectacle between the Friday and Sunday, Bristol City were advised that the fixture could not take place over the course of the weekend.

The Balloon Fiesta is due to be held at the city's Ashton Court Estate, located just over two miles from the club's Ashton Gate stadium.

And after taking the disruption into consideration, the two teams will now kick off at 7:45pm on Thursday, August 6.

Save the date

Announcing the fixture change, Bristol City confirmed fans would be able to use their tickets originally purchased for the Friday night.

A statement read: "Bristol City can announce the Carabao Cup Round One match against Walsall will now take place on Thursday, August 6th at 7:45pm.

"Following discussion with multiple stakeholders, the decision has been made to avoid a clash with the Friday evening night glow at the Bristol International Balloon Fiesta.

"This will ensure easier travel for supporters and allow for attendance at this internationally renowned fiesta.

"We apologise to supporters who have already purchased tickets. All tickets purchased remain valid for the new date."

Meanwhile, Walsall apologised to supporters for any inconveniences caused, insisting the move was out of the club's control.

4 The Bristol International Balloon Fiesta is Europe's largest annual hot-air balloon event Credit: Getty

The Saddlers wrote: "Whilst the change is out of our control, we would like to send our apologies to supporters for any inconvenience this may cause."

New eras

Bristol City and Walsall will both be hoping to get their respective seasons off to a winning start when they meet in the Carabao Cup.

The cup tie comes just over a week before they begin their respective league campaigns on Saturday, August 15.

The Robins kick things off at home to Millwall at 3pm, while the Saddlers are away to Gillingham at the same time.

And both sides will be bidding to mount promotion charges this time around, after the two finishing 12th and 13th respectively last term, falling comfortably short of the play-off places.

Meanwhile for fans, the rescheduled Carabao Cup tie will be their first chance to watch their teams in competitive action under their new managers.

4 Bristol City hired Martin Skubala from newly-promoted Championship side Lincoln City Credit: Getty

4 Lee Grant will begin just his second managerial role at Walsall this season Credit: Getty

After Roy Hodgson took interim charge for the season's run-in, Bristol City then appointed Michael Skubala as their permanent manager.

Skubala swapped Lincoln City for Ashton Gate, after guiding the Imps to promotion to the Championship last term.

A new era will also be beginning at Walsall this season, who named Lee Grant at their new head coach ahead of the 2026/27 campaign.

The ex-Manchester United goalkeeper replaced interim boss Darren Byfield at the Bescot Stadium, with Mat Sadler the previous permanent manager before his sacking in March.

Meanwhile Grant's appointment as Saddlers' boss came just five months after he was relieved of his duties at Huddersfield.

Sports.title: Why UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin boycotted the World Cup final
Sports.content:
Aleksander Ceferin elected not to attend the 2026 World Cup final due to Donald Trump's intervention in the Folarin Balogun red card.

The UEFA President was nowhere to be seen at the MetLife Stadium as Spain were crowned champions of the world for the second time.

5 Ceferin made a very public statement to not attend the final Credit: AFP

As the leader of UEFA, he would have been expected to be in attendance, especially as a European nation were in the final.

However, after the White House intervened to get Balogun's red card suspended earlier in the tournament, he decided not to attend.

A report in The Times claims that the relationship between Ceferin and FIFA president Gianni Infantino is broken, and that this Balogun red card was the final straw.

What makes Ceferin's absence even more astonishing is that he is FIFA's Vice-President.

He is also reportedly annoyed at Somali referee Omar Artan being denied entry to the United States and for the treatment of the Iran national team throughout the tournament.
