Sports.title: BBC WIN the World Cup ratings war with ITV: Beeb boast a FOUR-times bigger audience than broadcast rival after ditching work from home studio for the New York final
Sports.content:
The BBC have declared victory over ITV in the World Cup ratings war - despite a difficult start to the tournament.

Daily Mail Sport understands the BBC's peak audience share advantage during the World Cup final - where Spain were crowned champions - was 4 times greater than ITV's, while its average audience share advantage was 4.06 times greater.

By comparison, the BBC's lead over ITV’s viewership in the 2022 World Cup final was 3.25 times higher for peak audience share and 3.4 times higher for average audience share.

The Beeb annihilated ITV's coverage of the final, increasing the gap between themselves and ITV from the previous World Cup.

Last night's final attracted a peak audience of 15.8million across BBC One and BBC iPlayer - giving the BBC 64% share of all TV viewing.

The BBC ditched their work-from-home studio in Salford for the World Cup final, presenting from inside the stadium

An average audience of 13.9 million tuned in across the BBC's coverage live from inside MetLife Stadium.

Meanwhile, ITV covered the game from their New York studio with the stunning backdrop of the Manhattan skyline.

The BBC did not send a studio panel to the States until the semi-final, with Wayne Rooney, Joe Hart and Micah Richards spending less than a week in the country.

Instead, they spent the first four weeks in Salford as part of cost-cutting measures to save licence payers' money.

Rather than having a swanky US studio - like ITV had - the BBC used an LED backdrop to display the skyline of whichever host city is staging the live match.

They claim their distant coverage has saved millions as part of Director of Sport Alex Kay-Jelski's cost-saving drive.

As a result, ITV had initial success in the ratings war. But for the business end of the tournament, the BBC reigned supreme.

On BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website & app, the final was streamed 11.1 million times.

Elsewhere, the BBC also enjoyed a bump to their tournament viewership with exclusive rights for England's exhilarating 10-goal bronze medal match against France.

An average audience of 10.8 million tuned in as the Three Lions secured their best finish in a World Cup since 1966.

Across the whole tournament, the BBC saw an overall reach of 42.8 million across TV viewing, while audiences streamed World Cup matches 237 million times on BBC iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app - more than double the 2022 World Cup.

Sports.title: Farewell to 'Mighty Mouse' Kevin Keegan - the diminutive pioneer who let his emotions run wild and was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world, writes OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
Farewell to 'Mighty Mouse' Kevin Keegan - the diminutive pioneer who let his emotions run wild and was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world, writes OLIVER HOLT

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Kevin Keegan, a kid from mining stock in South Yorkshire, a kid who started out at Scunthorpe United and went on to conquer Europe, was one of the greatest players English football has ever produced but it was the unquenchable passion that burned within him that won him such a prominent place in the hearts of the public.

Mighty Mouse, he was called as a player and it suited him. He was the little man who would never give up. He was the small guy who punched way above his weight. He was the lad who never bowed to anyone. He may have been slight of stature but he had the biggest heart that ever beat in the chest of an English footballer.

Sometimes, it feels as if time has dimmed the memory of quite what an outstanding footballer Keegan was and how he became a pioneer and a pathfinder, the first Englishman to play in a European Cup final with both English and foreign clubs, in his case Liverpool and Hamburger SV.

Sometimes it feels as if England’s mediocrity when he was at the peak of his playing career and the fame and affection he garnered in his managerial career, particularly at Newcastle United, have obscured the fact that he remains the only Englishman to have won the Ballon d’Or, the prize bestowed on the greatest player in the world each year, more than once.

Keegan won it in successive years during his time in Germany, in 1978 and 1979. For context, that puts him level with Franz Beckenbauer, Alfredo Di Stefano, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge and the Brazilian Ronaldo in the pantheon of the greats of the game. ‘I’m probably the most ordinary player to have won it twice,’ Keegan said in a recent interview.

But there was nothing ordinary about Kevin Keegan. Anybody who ever met him or ever watched him play or ever heard him giving a manager’s post-match press conference or ever saw him spending hours with fans desperate for a word or an autograph, knew that.

Liverpool, Newcastle and England legend Kevin Keegan has died at the age of 75 after a short battle with illness

Keegan (pictured in 1977 after winning the European Cup with Liverpool) is one of the greatest players English football has ever produced

Once, after his playing career was over, I sat opposite him on a stage at Westminster Central Hall, asking him questions in an interview organised by the newspaper I worked for then. I don’t remember the questions I asked, or the answers he gave.

What I do remember is how Keegan held the audience in the palm of his hand. They were rapt. After it was over, Keegan stayed until he had fulfilled every autograph request and spoken to every man and woman who wanted a word, who wanted to say that they had talked to one of the legends of the English game.

Keegan was an extraordinary man. He was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world. In a sport where players are told to keep their mouths shut and their emotions in check, he let his emotions run wild and people loved him for it.

His public profile rose even more when he competed in the BBC programme Superstars, which aired in the 1970s and 80s, and featured sportsmen battling it out against each other in series of different disciplines.

‘Superstar’ has become an overused term now but if ever a man fitted that description, it was Keegan. He was box office, from head to toe. The combination of the reach of television and the dynamism of his personality made him one of football’s first new age icons.

Even in the midst of everything he achieved on the pitch, what endeared him to people, and a huge part of the gift he leaves behind for us, was his heart and soul. His passion lit up his life. He could not contain it and we loved him for it.

His passion gave us some of the landmarks we remember him for. The fight with Leeds United captain Billy Bremner at the 1974 Charity Shield that got both men sent off and saw Keegan ripping off his shirt as he left the pitch.

What a different world it was then. ‘That looked very much like a right hook by Johnny Giles,’ commentator Barry Davies said when Keegan was flattened by a sweet right hand. Keegan pleaded for leniency for Giles. A few moments later, he was trading punches with Bremner. ‘This is a side of English football we do not want to see,’ Davies opined.

Keegan was beloved in Germany after moving to Hamburger SV in 1977. He won the Ballon d'Or twice on the continent

Keegan was an extraordinary man. He was a riot of colour and flame in a grey world

Keegan, who was born in Doncaster, had begun his career with Scunthorpe United before he was spotted and scouted by Liverpool manager Bill Shankly and established himself as the star player of the team that went on to win the European Cup, under Bob Paisley, in 1977.

That team was one of the great sides in the history of the English game. Let the names roll off your tongue: Ray Clemence, Phil Neal, Joey Jones, Tommy Smith, Ray Kennedy, Emlyn Hughes, Kevin Keegan, Jimmy Case, Steve Heighway, Ian Callaghan, Terry McDermott.

Keegan tormented the Borussia Monchengladbach captain Berti Vogts in that final in Rome and won the penalty in the 83rd minute that sealed a 3-1 victory for Liverpool and was the start of the club’s rise to being the most successful club in European competition in this country.

When Keegan moved to Hamburger SV that summer, many thought it would mark the end of Liverpool’s hegemony but they signed a player called Kenny Dalglish, who went on to emulate Keegan’s successes and more.

Then there was his bike crash in Superstars when he peddled furiously down the main straight of an athletics track at the start of a race against Belgian footballer, Gilbert Van Binst, wobbling from side to side as he desperately tried to keep up, before crashing to the tarmac on the first bend.

It was a nasty accident. Keegan, who was close to the height of his powers as a footballer at that point, sustained cuts and grazes but he still refused to give up. The race was re-started and Keegan won. It was the show’s greatest moment.

Keegan became a hugely successful manager and is particularly adored by Newcastle fans

Keegan pictured in 1995 with famous entertainers Ant McPartlin (L) and Declan Donnelly (R)

Then there was the most famous diatribe in English football history when, feeling the hot despair of Sir Alex Ferguson’s Manchester United closing in on the league title after they had overhauled his wonderful Newcastle United team, he snapped as he spoke to Sky Sports after an away win over Leeds United at Elland Road at the end of April 1996.

‘We’re still fighting for this title,’ Keegan almost shouted into the camera, his voice shaking with anger and his finger pointing and jabbing, ‘and he (Sir Alex Ferguson) has got to go to Middlesbrough and get something and I’ll tell you honestly, I will love it if we beat them. Love it.’

David Beckham has said since that when the United players watched Keegan’s rant, they knew they had won the league. They knew that Ferguson’s mind games had exploded in Keegan’s head and that the title was theirs.

But that only added to Keegan’s legend. There was something magnificently untameable about him, something beautifully unpredictable, something free and untrammelled. He was still Mighty Mouse.

And he is still adored in Newcastle. It may be, in fact, that he is adored there more than anywhere else. He is adored for the pride he brought to the city and the way he resurrected the club and for the thrill of the beautiful football the Geordies played under his management.

That team was made in his image and so it was brilliant and it was entertaining and it was breathtaking but it was also fragile. And it could not quite cope with the relentlessness of Manchester United. But every neutral was desperate for Newcastle to win the title that season. And that was mostly down to Keegan.

Keegan's 'I will love it' rant was a sign that he was cracking under the pressure of a title race with Manchester United - but it only added to his legend

In a sport where players are told to keep their mouths shut and their emotions in check, he let his emotions run wild

There was no artifice about Keegan. He did not bother to try to hide what he was feeling. Or what he was. It was all out there, everything worn on his sleeve. He would have been the world’s worst poker player. He was not a man for keeping his counsel. Or for keeping his cool. Again, we loved him all the more for that.

Keegan always burned hot. At his unveiling as England manager in 1999, Daily Mirror journalist Nigel Clarke, who was sitting on the front row of the press conference, coughed while Keegan was speaking. Keegan became convinced that Clarke was mocking him and demanded to know why he was coughing. A long stand-off ensued.

Before a game against Sweden the same year, Keegan told Paul Scholes to ‘go out there and drop a few hand grenades’. Scholes promptly became the first England player to be sent off at Wembley after two horrendous challenges on opponents.

At the end of his short reign as England boss, Keegan was preparing his team for the final game at the old Wembley on October 7, 2000, a World Cup qualifier against Germany, and he decided he was going to play Gareth Southgate, a central defender in midfield.

On the Friday night before the game on the Saturday, the news began to leak out. I was on a Sky programme called Hold the Back Page, hosted by Brian Woolnough and Jimmy Hill, and we began the show by discussing the Southgate plan with varying degrees of scepticism.

Keegan was incandescent. He asked the FA to phone Sky to demand that the programme be taken off the air. Sky, obviously, could not accede to that request and the show continued as normal. To no one’s great surprise, the Southgate experiment did not go well.

Keegan managed England from February 1999 to October 2000 but resigned from his post

Keegan scored 40 goals in 113 games for Hamburg, between 1977 and 1980

England lost the game 1-0 and Keegan was booed by a section of England fans as he walked off the pitch. He stopped to remonstrate with some of them at the entrance to the tunnel. When he reached the dressing rooms, he summoned FA officials, retreated to the quiet of the toilets, and promptly resigned. The FA tried to talk him out of it but he would not reconsider.

Keegan had been a sublime player at Liverpool and Hamburger SV and then, in the late summer of his career with Southampton and Newcastle. I say late summer deliberately. There was never anything autumn about Keegan. His football did not yellow and fade. After his last game for Newcastle, a testimonial against Liverpool, he was lifted from the St James’s Park pitch in a helicopter.

‘Auf Wiedersehen, Kev,’ a message on the scoreboard at the Gallowgate End read that day in May 1984. And now, it is time to bid him farewell once more. Auf Wiedersehen, Kev, and thank you.

Sports.title: FIFA launch investigation into Argentina's shocking World Cup final post-match behaviour... as new footage shows what really sparked final-whistle brawl
Sports.content:
FIFA will investigate the behavior of Argentina's bitter players after the World Cup final descended into violence following their defeat on Sunday.

The probe into the violent final-whistle scenes in New Jersey comes just as footage reveals the exact moment that sparked the ugly brawl.

The South Americans were outplayed by Spain in a drab encounter at MetLife Stadium, with Lionel Messi and his teammates unable to disrupt their rivals with the same aggressive, physical tactics that unsettled England in the semi-final.

Barcelona star Ferran Torres bagged the winning goal in extra time to seal Spain's second World Cup triumph – after first winning the trophy in 2010 – leaving Messi, 39, in tears at the final whistle.

However, the action continued following the final whistle as a brawl broke out between the two sides, resulting in a red card for Leandro Paredes.

The Argentina midfielder was sent off for grabbing Eric Garcia by the neck and punching Gavi in the face before pushing him to the ground in appalling scenes at full time.

FIFA is now set to open disciplinary proceedings into the red card issued to Paredes, with the role of other players and officials also set to be investigated, according to The Times.

Jaja, es Molina el que empieza todo pegando a Rodri. Hay que largar a todo el clan loser este ya, que encima de macarras, perdedores e insoportables, son malísimos. pic.twitter.com/Wk6C0fwABY — The Lion (@loloutlaw) July 19, 2026

FIFA is set to launch an investigation into the violent behavior of Leandro Paredes and other Argentina players after the World Cup final descended into violent scenes

The move came after ugly scenes at the end of the game which Spain won 1-0 after extra time

New footage has revealed that a punch landed on Spain captain Rodri sparked the brawl

Some of Argentina's players lost their heads as Spain's substitutes and staff ran on to the pitch to celebrate their victory.

Argentina's Nahuel Molina hit Spain captain Rodri in the torso as he was running by, resulting in the midfielder squaring up to his rival.

That saw players from both teams pile into the melee, before Paredes threw punches.

Elsewhere, 53-year-old assistant coach Roberto Ayala was also caught landing a punch on Spain's Dani Olmo at full time.

In the aftermath of the ugly brawl, DAZN Spain claimed Argentina defender Nicolas Otamendi complained to Rodri about La Roja's pre-match comments alluding to officiating concerns ahead of the final.

The South Americans had benefitted from a series of questionable decisions heading into the showpiece event, with the Manchester City midfielder raising concerns before the final.

'You and [Spain team-mate Aymeric] Laporte. Both of you,' he said to Rodri.

'You spent the time crying and complaining about the referees, my friend. But you shouldn't have spoken before the match, you know that? Didn't you see what he said this week?'

Argentina were thuggish throughout the World Cup final, just as they had been when they beat England in the semis.

Torres's 106th-minute winner came after Chelsea midfielder Enzo Fernandez was sent off in the 93rd minute following a reckless challenge on Pau Cubarsi – which summed up the South Americans' deplorable approach to the game.

por que el raton ayala le pegó una piña a dani olmo jajdjsjsjsj pic.twitter.com/ZNkBpPAcjU — Peñargrol (@CAPArgento__) July 20, 2026

Some of Argentina's players lost their heads as Spain's substitutes celebrated the win

Argentina manager Lionel Scaloni tries to intervene as Paredes clashes with Eric Garcia

Spain shared fears of roughhouse tactics from Argentina, and their concerns came to fruition with Enzo Fernandez sent off for a shocking challenge on Pau Cubarsi

Astonishingly, Fernandez complained about his dismissal for a second yellow, before attempting to get Chelsea team-mate Marc Cucurella sent off for covering his face while talking to Messi.

New laws state that footballers who cover their mouths when speaking to a player from the opposing team must be sent off, but replays showed Cucurella was simply scratching his nose as he spoke to Argentina's captain.

Paredes was also fortunate not to be sent off for a second bookable offense in regular time for a foul on the edge of the box which presented Lamine Yamal with a last-gasp free-kick before extra-time.

Following the game, the 2022 champions collected their silver medals from FIFA boss Gianni Infantino and US President Donald Trump on the stage but opted not to watch as Spain lifted the trophy – despite it being customary in finals of major tournaments.

Instead, the Argentina players, coaching team and staff walked over to the end where the majority of their fans were sat and turned their backs as their rivals celebrated.

Footage shows Spain players holding the World Cup trophy aloft as gold confetti explodes behind them, with the Argentina team facing the other way.

Argentina only had two shots in the entire match, with the first one coming in the 117th minute.

There were an estimated 1.5 to 1.8 billion viewers tuning in to watch the summer tournament's showpiece finale, which saw Trump take center stage during the trophy lift.

Argentina players decided to turn their backs to Spain's World Cup trophy lift on Sunday

Donald Trump took center stage as Spain lifted the World Cup trophy on Sunday afternoon

The President refused to step aside to allow the victorious Spaniards to have their moment in the spotlight.

Trump and Infantino handed out various awards to match officials and players, before officially welcoming the team up to the stage to lift the World Cup trophy.

The President presented the prestigious title to Spain captain Rodri, who took great pleasure in raising it aloft.

Much like when he presented the Club World Cup title last summer, Trump stood awkwardly alongside the Spain squad as they lifted the trophy and celebrated wildly.

It seemed as though, when Spain were about to perform the trophy lift, Infantino had attempted to usher Trump away from the players – though the President remained where he was.

He stood to the side of the team as the confetti cannons went off at MetLife Stadium, clapping and grinning while Infantino laughed off Trump's awkward cameo.

Loud boos had come from the stands when Infantino and Trump made their way onto the pitch, as fans made their feelings on the pair undoubtedly clear.

Fans noted that one Argentina star – Tottenham defender Cristian Romero – completely ignored the President as he collected his medal from Infantino.

It appeared as though Infantino attempted to usher Trump away – but the President remained where he was

In a video which swiftly went viral on social media, the Argentinian could be seen receiving his silverware from Infantino before waltzing past Trump on stage.

Meanwhile, the President also presented a trio of awards to Spain's stars, including the Young Player of the Tournament, the Golden Glove and the Golden Ball – which were claimed by Pau Cubarsi, Unai Simon and Rodri respectively.

There was a degree of irony in regard to Trump presenting Spain with the World Cup trophy, after previously launching a stinging attack on the country at a UN summit earlier in July for not contributing enough money to NATO.

'Spain is a terrible partner in NATO. They don’t participate. They don’t pay. I don’t want anything to do with Spain. Cut off all trade with Spain, please, including visits,' he said. 'Don’t even talk to them. They’re hopeless, bad people.'

Then, on his way back to the United States on Air Force One, Trump said Spain had tried to improve its standing with him.

'I did have issues, and ​I still do. But Spain, they came back all the way today. Spain was very generous today,' he said.

'They honored a request for lots of payments, and if they didn't, we wouldn't have even ⁠talked to them.'

Earlier in the day, Trump and his wife Melania were seen taking in the action inside a packed MetLife Stadium suite – alongside FIFA president Infantino, Canada's prime minister Mark Carney and Mexico's president Claudia Sheinbaum.

Wayne Rooney savaged the 2026 World Cup final halftime show as he described the performance as 'c**p' and said the 'best part was when it ended' live on BBC

The show delivered a spectacular mix of music, nostalgia and global star power, with the likes of Madonna, Justin Bieber, Shakira and the Muppets all performing under one roof

Trump also shook hands with Spain's prime minister Pedro Sanchez as Infantino stood beside them.

Spain's Queen Letizia and King Felipe VI also greeted the President. Javier Milei, the president of Argentina, reportedly watched the game from home due to 'superstition,' The New York Times reported.

Trump also waved at the crowd from behind the glass.

Inside the private suite, Infantino posed for pictures with the President's son, Eric Trump, his wife, Lara, and their children. Barron Trump also showed up for the big game.

The World Cup final also saw a bizarre half-time show, with Madonna, Coldplay, Justin Bieber, The Muppets and Shakira performing during the 27-minute interval, which was derided by Wayne Rooney.

'To be honest, mine [his highlight] was when it finished. I like a lot of those artists but to be honest I thought it was c**p', he fumed.

'I did honestly. It just didn't get me going. I wanted the football to be back on. It was a bit flat. I like Burna Boy, I like Shakira, I like Bieber but that was too flat.'

Sports.title: Argentina media label team 'polite and respectful' as FIFA launch brawl investigation
Sports.content:
Argentina media label team 'polite and respectful' as FIFA launch brawl investigation

Argentina players have been widely criticised for their behaviour after the World Cup but it appears that some members of the South American media don’t totally agree

View 2 Images Argentina players have been slammed for their behaviour after the final whistle (Image: Getty Images)

Argentina have been labelled as ‘polite and respectful’ despite triggering an angry brawl that marred the World Cup final. The South American side were aiming to become the first side since Brazil in 1962 to retain the trophy as they took on Spain in New Jersey.

‌



But it did not go to plan for the reigning world champions, with Ferran Torres’ goal seeing them defeated. The behaviour of a host of the Argentinian players was also the target of criticism.

‌



Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina were both involved in post-match scuffles, the former having been sent off for his part. Enzo Fernandez was also dismissed during the game for a woeful challenge on Pau Cubarsi.

‌



Despite that, newspapers in the South American nation believe that the team behaved well. A report from Argentine paper Clarin read: “As never before, the Argentine team displayed, both on and off the field, a range of values that are rare these days. From the pitch and beyond, they gave several lessons and showed the face of a country that we would like to see away from the football pitch.

FIFA launch investigation into Argentina after 'disgusting' World Cup final scenes READ MORE :

“A team that was polite and respectful, despite a few unfortunate isolated incidents in the last match; that didn't speak ill of its rivals or try to justify its own mistakes by blaming others.”

The response to Argentina’s behaviour is very different when it comes to the UK media. Speaking after Paredes’ red card, Wayne Rooney said: "Does it surprise you? It doesn't surprise me. We've seen this with Argentina before.

‌



“It's just not the reaction you want. We've seen some of the reaction after knocking England out in the last round. That's just sad. If you lose a game of football, be graceful and get out of there. It's really poor from them."

He added: "That's a reaction to them being outplayed, out-fought, out-thought on the football pitch, and then they resort to that at the end. It's poor from those two players."

View 2 Images Enzo Fernandez was sent off for Argentina in extra time (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Alan Shearer said: “Paredes threw two or three haymakers into someone’s face. He went for them. There is no place or space for that.

“We know how much it means to them and we know how much it hurts to lose, but there is a way to lose. Too many times we have seen that from Argentina. The reaction after the final whistle is terrible.”

Gary Neville also gave his take on the clash. He said: “They’re very competitive and I love that element of them, but (Paredes) has just been a disgrace for the last couple of games, and why the referees have allowed him to continue doing what he is doing…”

Sports.title: Josh Kerr slams 'appalling' prize money he receives for running the fastest mile ever
Sports.content:
Josh Kerr slams 'appalling' prize money he receives for running the fastest mile ever

Josh Kerr - the new fastest man over a mile - felt the financial reward he was given didn't reflect the magnitude of his achievement

View 2 Images Josh Kerr said he felt short-changed by the prize money he received (Image: British Athletics via Getty Images)

Josh Kerr criticised the $50,000 (£37.2k) bonus awarded to him for breaking the one-mile world record. Kerr's time of 3:42.66 was the quickest in 27 years, toppling previous holder Hicham El Guerrouj's by 0.47 seconds.

‌



The Scotsman sparked scenes of wild celebration in front of a sold-out crowd at the London Stadium. However, the financial reward didn't reflect the achievement in his eyes.

‌



He received the exact same sum from World Athletics as Moroccan El Guerrouj did in 1999. Once the dust had settled, Kerr called out the prize money situation.

‌



"It was a good day for me financially but $50,000 is a ridiculous number," he told The Times. "To get the same amount 27 years later is appalling, not to sound greedy.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! All the best sports news and much more on our dedicated Facebook page

Mile record-smashing Scot Kerr praised by track legend Steve Cram READ MORE :

Commonwealth Games 2026 athletes start arriving in Glasgow from around the world READ MORE :

"I know how much that took from investing in myself financially over the last eight years as a professional. I just feel like I’ve been a bit short-changed a little bit."

‌



World Athletics offer a $100k bonus (£74.5k) at flagship outdoor global championships but that sum is halved for Diamond League meetings. Kerr also admitted he had hoped to have "gone a little bit faster," although he was happy to have hit his goal.

View 2 Images Kerr smashed the 27-year world record (Image: Adam Davy/PA Wire)

"It was just incredible, that last lap," he told the BBC. "It was just me, my shoes and the track. I was absolutely deaf in the last 110 metres. I didn't take my foot off the gas, but I started to glide and I was like, 'Oh, wow, this feels incredible.'

Article continues below

"It's incredible because I'm slowing down. So, I was like, 'I better get to the line.' So crossing the finish line, seeing 42-something - anything - was my goal, so it was great.

"I am surrounded by amazing people and was just able to stay consistent, put the work in, and I knew I had 3:42 in me. I nearly lost it there at the end, but I got over the line.

"If I'm to leave my mark on this sport as a British legend, with the legends behind me and following in their footsteps, I have to put in those performances."

Sports.title: Alan Shearer sends emotional goodbye to 'hero' Kevin Keegan as tributes pour in
Sports.content:
Alan Shearer sends emotional goodbye to 'hero' Kevin Keegan as tributes pour in

Tributes have poured in after the sad news of Kevin Keegan's death aged 75 after a short battle with cancer

View 3 Images Alan Shearer has paid an emotional tribute to Kevin Keegan following the sad news of his death. (Image: PA Wire)

Alan Shearer has led the tributes to 'hero' Kevin Keegan after the former England, Newcastle United and Liverpool boss died following a short battle with cancer. The 75-year-old was diagnosed with stage four cancer back in January and has sadly passed away.

‌



A statement from Keegan's family read: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75. Kevin had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments. A double Ballon d’Or winner, Kevin was a much-loved husband, father and grandfather.

‌



"The family would like to thank Kevin’s incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

‌



Kevin Keegan dies aged 75 as family pay tribute to Liverpool and Newcastle icon READ MORE :

Donald Trump brutally booed at World Cup final as Spain and Argentina fans unite READ MORE :

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Shearer, who worked under Keegan for both club and country, took to social media to share an emotional goodbye. The Magpies legend said: "My Hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy Boss [Crying emoji]."

Keegan enjoyed an illustrious career as both a player and manager. His work at Newcastle United helped transform the Magpies into one of the best clubs in the country, and the Toon have also paid an emotional tribute.

‌



A club statement read: "Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters. As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James’ Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an Entertainer.

View 3 Images Keegan passed away after a short battle with cancer (Image: (Liverpool FC via Getty Images))

‌



"Above all that, Kevin forged an extraordinary bond with Newcastle, built on the roots of his father, Joe. He understood our people. He embraced the North East with a passion that was genuine and unwavering, and in return, he earned his rightful place in the hearts of millions.

"Kevin’s impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired wherever he went, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him.

"At this profoundly sad time, we send our love and deepest sympathy to Kevin’s wife Jean, his family, friends and all who had the privilege of knowing and working alongside him. Today, we mourn the loss of a true giant of our history, and at the appropriate moment, we will carefully consider how we shape a lasting tribute to Kevin’s remarkable life and legacy. Rest in peace, King Kev."

‌



King Kev would manage Fulham, England and Manchester City after leaving the Magpies, winning the Second Division with the Cottagers and the First Division with City.

"Everyone at Manchester City is devastated to learn our former manager Kevin Keegan has passed away, aged 75," a City club statement read. "Kevin was a transformative manager who brought optimism and vibrancy to City during his four-year spell in charge.

"The promotion campaign in 2001/02 will never be forgotten, and Kevin then established us once again as a top Premier League side in the years that followed. Our thoughts are with Kevin’s family and friends at this very difficult time."

‌



View 3 Images Steve Heighway and Kevin Keegan (R) celebrate with the FA Cup after Liverpool defeated Newscatle United in 1974. (Image: Mirrorpix)

Keegan was not just a decorated manager, but a brilliant player, winning the Ballon d'Or twice during his playing career and claiming just about every trophy there is to win during his time at Liverpool.

The Reds also paid tribute to Keegan and said: "We are deeply saddened by the passing of the legendary Kevin Keegan and mourn his loss.

‌



"His indomitable spirit and remarkable contribution will be forever etched in our history and his legacy will live on. Rest in peace, Kevin. 1951-2026."

Former Liverpool defender Jamie Carragher, meanwhile, tweeted: "RIP Kevin Keegan. One of the greatest players this country has ever produced, trophies & goals galore, double Ballon d'Or winner shows he was an absolute giant of the English game.

"One of the most important men in making LFC [Liverpool} what it is today."

Article continues below

England's official channel also paid tribute to the former Three Lions boss: "We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away.

"Kevin earned 63 international caps and scored 21 goals between 1972 and 1982, before managing the Three Lions from 1999 to 2000. Our thoughts and condolences are with Kevin's family, friends and former clubs."

Sports.title: Kevin Keegan dies aged 75 as family, fans and former players pay tribute to Liverpool and Newcastle icon
Sports.content:
Kevin Keegan, one of the most popular figures in English football, has died aged 75 after being diagnosed with cancer.

'King Kev' had an illustrious playing career and built one of the most popular teams of the Premier League eras at Newcastle United.

In a statement, his family said: "It is with immense sadness that we announce that Kevin Keegan has passed away at the age of 75. The former England player and manager had been battling cancer and was surrounded by his wife and daughters in his final moments.

"Kevin, a double Ballon D’or winner, was a much loved husband, father and grandfather. The family would like to thank Kevin’s incredible medical team for all their support. This is a hugely difficult time and they are requesting space and privacy."

‌



He leaves his wife of 51 years Jean and their children Laura Jane, 47, and Sarah Marie, 43.

Kevin Keegan: Newcastle and Liverpool legend dies aged 75 as tributes pour in READ MORE :

Alan Shearer sends emotional goodbye to 'hero' Kevin Keegan as tributes pour in READ MORE :

In a statement, Newcastle said: "We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club’s history.

"Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.

"As a player, he brought world-class talent, ambition and belief to St. James’ Park, helping to transform perceptions of what Newcastle United could be.

‌



"As a manager, he ignited our city. Kevin gave supporters hope and pride, and led a team whose style, spirit and passion captured the imagination of football fans around the world. He was so much more than an Entertainer.

"Kevin forged an extraordinary bond with Newcastle, built on the roots of his father, Joe. He understood our people. He embraced the North East with a passion that was genuine and unwavering, and in return, he earned his rightful place in the hearts of millions.

"Kevin’s impact will not be measured by appearances or results. It will live on in the memories he created with club and country, the dreams he inspired, and the generations of supporters around the world who fell in love with football because of him.

"At this profoundly sad time, we send our love and deepest sympathy to Kevin’s wife Jean, his family, friends and all who had the privilege of knowing and working alongside him.

‌



"Today, we mourn the loss of a true giant of our history, and at the appropriate moment, we will carefully consider how we shape a lasting tribute to Kevin’s remarkable life and legacy.

"Rest in peace, King Kev."

View 9 Images Kevin Keegan has died aged 75 (Image: Julian Hamilton/Daily Mirror)

Fellow Toon icon Alan Shearer simply added: "My hero. My manager. My friend. Sleep easy boss."

‌



Former Liverpool supersub David Fairclough said: "He made you feel fantastic. I was room mates with him for a number of games, and it was invaluable. There are not enough great things to say about Kevin Keegan. He was awesome."

One of the England legend's last appearances was on Tyneside in May where he told the audience: "They said we have a top doctor with this new way of fighting what you have got, which is stage-four cancer.

"He was a Liverpool supporter so I went to meet him. I knew I wouldn’t be walking alone, if you know what I mean." Keegan first revealed in January that he had cancer.

After a 'really tough time,' he felt well enough to commit to this appearance at the Tyne Theatre in Newcastle, the city that he loved and where the fans adored him.

‌



He joked that he couldn't form a dream strike partnership with Peter Beardsley and Chris Waddle as he "wasn't very fit at the moment."

Liverpool, for who Keegan made 323 appearances during the 1970s, said: "Liverpool FC is deeply saddened and mourning the passing of the legendary Kevin Keegan.

"The former Reds No.7, who appeared 323 times and scored 100 goals for the club across six seasons, died at the age of 75 on Monday after being diagnosed with cancer last year.

"The thoughts of everyone at the club are with Kevin's family and friends at this hugely difficult time.

‌



View 9 Images Keegan and David Beckham in 1999 (Image: Toby Melville/PA Wire)

One of just four Englishmen to win the Ballon d'Or, Keegan also represented Scunthorpe United, Hamburg, Southampton and Newcastle United during a playing career in which he was regarded as a hero wherever he went.

Keegan also received 63 caps for his country – 31 as captain – and netted 21 times. He then moved into management with spells at Newcastle (two), Fulham, Manchester City and the England national team.

Keegan's association with Liverpool began when he arrived from Scunthorpe as a 20-year-old in May 1971 .He endeared himself to fans soon after joining, scoring on his debut in the 1971-72 league opener against Nottingham Forest at Anfield.

‌



A forward partnership for the ages with John Toshack would blossom, and with it came success for the second of Bill Shankly's great Liverpool teams.

He was the standout performer again in the 1974 FA Cup final with a double at Wembley to down Newcastle, where in the future he would be known as 'King Kev'.

View 9 Images Keegan signed fellow Liverpool great Robbie Fowler for Manchester City in 2003 (Image: PA/PA Wire)

The 1975-76 Football Writers' Association Footballer of the Year award came on the back of another league and UEFA Cup double for the Reds.Keegan had signalled his intention to move abroad ahead of 1976-77, shocking the footballing world given his status.

‌



He signed off at Liverpool in the best way possible, though, by firing in 20 strikes en route to earning a third league winner's medal and lifting the club's first European Cup.

He won the Ballon d'Or in two of his three seasons at Hamburg and then returned to his homeland for the remainder of his time in football.

"'Liverpool made me, not just as a footballer but as a person'," Keegan said in 2011. "'The people I met – Shanks, Tommy Smith, Ian Callaghan, Ron Yeats – all these people you take something from.

"'The fans made me. When they started singing my name… what am I, five foot seven with Cuban-heeled boots? But [because of them] I was six foot six'."

‌



View 9 Images Keegan enjoyed a trophy-laden spell at Liverpool (Image: Mirrorpix)

The official England account added: "We are incredibly saddened by the news that Kevin Keegan OBE has passed away. Kevin earned 63 international caps and scored 21 goals between 1972 and 1982, before managing the Three Lions from 1999 to 2000.

"Our thoughts and condolences are with Kevin's family, friends and former clubs."

Manchester City said: "Everyone at Manchester City is devastated to learn our former manager Kevin Keegan has passed away, aged 75. Kevin was a transformative manager who brought optimism and vibrancy to City during his four-year spell in charge."

‌



"The promotion campaign in 2001/02 will never be forgotten, and Kevin then established us once again as a top Premier League side in the years that followed. Our thoughts are with Kevin’s family and friends at this very difficult time."

Hamburg, where Keegan won both of his Ballon d'Or crowns, posted: "Rest in peace, "Mighty Mouse".

Another of Keegan's former clubs, Southampton, posted: "Kevin signed for the club in 1980 as the holder of the Ballon d’Or and brought great joy to fans at The Dell and across the football world. Our thoughts are with his family and friends at this difficult time."

View 9 Images Keegan as manager of Newcastle in January 2008 (Image: Owen Humphreys/PA Wire)

‌



Fellow Liverpool legend Jamie Carragher added: "One of the greatest players this country has ever produced; trophies and goals galore. Double Ballon d'Or winner shows he was an absolute giant of the English game. One of the most important men in making LFC what it is today."

The son of a Geordie-born miner, he was a pioneer of the modern game, negotiating his own contracts, appearing in TV ads and moving abroad to further his career at the peak of his fame with Liverpool in the 1970s.

Keegan won the three League titles, two UEFA Cups, and the FA Cup, moving to Hamburg after winning the European Cup with the all-conquering Merseyside giants in 1977.

He was then twice voted European footballer of the year. In a 2013 interview, at the launch of his Soccer Circus business in Scotland, he said: "I have never been scared to do something new. I did the adverts, I did the record, I moved abroad, I have always been one of those people who say, 'Why not?' rather than 'Why?'".

‌



"I am very lucky in that I enjoy meeting people, it is a great help in life, not just business." It made him a hugely popular figure during his playing career, as England captain, and later as a manager, even as the national side struggled under his leadership.

With typical honesty, he stepped down after admitting that he did not think that he was good enough. He had stints in charge of Fulham, and Manchester City, but it was his two spells at Newcastle which defined his managerial career.

In the late 90s, he managed a United side nicknamed 'The Entertainers' because of their fearless brand of attacking football.

As a player, he was equally fearless, and famous for his Brut adverts with Henry Cooper, pop singles, curly perm, and an episode of the TV show 'Superstars', filmed in Bracknell in 1976, where he fell in a bike ride but got back on again despite being injured.

‌



View 9 Images Keegan was a legendary player for Liverpool in the 1970s and 1980s (Image: Liverpool FC via Getty Images)

In his 2018 autobiography 'My Life in Football', dedicated to his wife Jean and former Liverpool boss Bill Shankly - 'two people who have given me so much' - he wrote: 'It never ceases to amaze me how many people think that my lifetime achievements consist of, in rough order: the time I crashed off my bike in television's Superstars, my perm, and my top-40 record with Head Over Heels in Love."

He met Jean in 1970 while riding the waltzers in Doncaster; he told her that he worked at the steelworks as he thought saying he was a footballer would sound 'too flash'.

They married in 1975 after his £35,000 transfer to Liverpool. Born in Armthorpe, near Doncaster, in 1951, his grandfather, Frank, was a hero who saved lives in the 1909 West Colliery mining disaster in Co Durham.

‌



His family kept a photo of the 30 survivors; Kevin bore a striking family resemblance to Frank. From humble beginnings in Yorkshire, he went on to become a sporting hero to millions of football fans.

View 9 Images Keegan during his last game as England manager in October 2000 (Image: Ross Kinnaird/Allsport/Getty Images/Hulton Archive)

His dad Joe and uncle Frank loved Newcastle and told young Kevin all about their favourite players of yesteryear, Hughie Gallacher and Jackie Milburn.

Kevin was born at his aunt's house because it had electricity, making childbirth safer; his dad bought his first football boots after winning a bet on horses.

‌



At 15, he and two friends ran 50 miles from Nottingham to Doncaster, which he said prepared him for the physical demands of football.

He worked as an office clerk at Pegler Brass Works before a first professional football contract with Scunthorpe United as a 17-year-old. Three years later, legendary Liverpool manager Bill Shankly spotted his undoubted talent, signed him and converted him into a striker.

Forming a lethal partnership with Welsh striker John Toshack, Keegan scored 100 goals in 323 games before a British record £500,000 transfer to Hamburg.

View 9 Images Newcastle United fans hold a flag of Kevin Keegan prior to the Emirates FA Cup third-round match against Bournemouth (Image: (Annabel Lee-Ellis/Getty Images))

‌



He was their top scorer with 17 league goals when they claimed the Bundesliga title in 1978-79. He was European Footballer of the Year in both the 1977-78 and 1978-79 campaigns during his three-year spell. Keegan moved to Southampton in 1980.

He was the PFA Player of the Year in 1981-82 before making the switch to Newcastle in 1982, retiring as a player two years later.

He scored 21 goals in 63 appearances for England and captained his national side 31 times, making a late appearance in the 1982 World Cup in Spain after struggling with a back injury.

Joining Newcastle as manager in 1992, he led the club to the second-tier title and promotion into the Premier League in 1993. In 1996, his side let a 12-point lead slip before he famously said, "I would love it if we beat them", in an emotional live TV outburst during the tense run-in with Alex Ferguson's Manchester United.

‌



Keegan said friends had 'love it' as their ringtone and insisted that he was 'comfortable enough in his own skin' to see the funny side.

FIFA boss Sepp Blatter sent a fax to commend the Geordies' attacking football after the epic 4-3 defeat to Liverpool at Anfield in 1996.

Keegan left United in 1997 and took over at Fulham a year later, before being appointed as England boss in February 1999. He left that role in October 2000 following a 1-0 defeat by Germany in a 2002 World Cup qualifier, the final game at the old Wembley Stadium.

View 9 Images Keegan in action for England in 1979 (Image: Peter Robinson/EMPICS Sport/PA Wire)

‌



Keegan, though, returned to club management with a four-year spell at Manchester City prior to a short eight-month stint back at Newcastle in 2008. He left, and later successfully claimed unfair dismissal, after falling out with then club owner Mike Ashley.

He told how he secretly returned to St James' Park in disguise for a fan's party. Keegan had the common touch, and that is why he remained such a hugely popular figure throughout his career, even when his stint as England boss came to an untimely end.

He said of his approach: "I buy good players and let them play." His loved ones confirmed his cancer diagnosis.

In his life story, the legend of the game told fans: "I want people to dream about their football club.

‌



"We should all be dreamers at heart."

Sports.title: The people of Gaza watch the World Cup final amid the ruins of their homes
Sports.content:
The people of Gaza watch the World Cup final amid the ruins of their homes

Football fans, many of them children, stood amid the rubble of Gaza to support Spain as they beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time and many cheered for the Spanish team

View 4 Images Gaza refugees watching the World Cup final (Image: Getty Images)

An estimated 1.5 billion people tuned in to watch the World Cup final.

‌



But there can be few more devoted fans than the hundreds who gathered around giant screens showing the match next to the bombed-out buildings of Gaza.

‌



They stood amid the rubble of their homes to support Spain as they beat Argentina 1-0 in extra time. They cheered for the Spanish team because of the country's support for the enclave during the conflict with Israel.

‌



Giant screens, erected earlier in the tournament, have offered residents a welcome respite from daily hardships. Numan Abdullah, a Gaza resident who watched the match, said: “We came together to support Spain because it has stood by the Palestinian people for years."

View 4 Images The people of Gaza watch an earlier round of the World Cup in the US (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Argentina World Cup fate decided after calls to ban finalists from next tournament READ MORE :

FIFA launch investigation into Argentina after 'disgusting' World Cup final scenes READ MORE :

He said the gathering also carried a message of peace and solidarity with countries that stand with Palestinians. “We are a people who seek peace,” he added. Tragically, aid worker Mohammed al-Wahidi, who helped organise the screenings, died in an Israeli airstrike earlier this month.

View 4 Images The people of Gaza also watched the Egypt v Argentina game earlier this month

Al-Wahidi, 65, was an English teacher before the war but became a senior official with the Egyptian Relief Committee in Gaza. He worked for the Egypt-backed organisation that has played a prominent role in humanitarian relief efforts.

‌



Locals said that he became a familiar face in shelters across the territory because he preferred to remain in the field rather than directing operations from an office. As of late April, the UN had recorded the killing of at least 593 aid workers since the war began, including eight since Israel and Hamas agreed to a ceasefire 10 months ago.

View 4 Images The funeral of aid worker Mohammed al-Wahidi, who helped organise the screenings, and died in an Israeli airstrike. (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Aid workers set up the screenings of the World Cup games, in a bid to raise morale in the camps, especially among young children. The matches shown included the controversial 3-2 defeat of Egypt by Argentina.

Article continues below

The Israeli military launched a campaign in Gaza in response to the unprecedented Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on Oct 7, 2023. It saw 1,200 people killed and 251 taken hostage.

At least 73,118 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since then, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry. Their figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Sports.title: Why we are going to see less Rory McIlroy as golf superstar changes his priorities
Sports.content:
Why we are going to see less Rory McIlroy as golf superstar changes his priorities

The two-time Masters champion is taking another long break as he admits no longer being 'fired up' by regular events on the PGA Tour schedule

View 2 Images Rory McIlroy walks onto the first tee box on day four of the The 154th Open (Image: 2026 Getty Images)

Rory McIlroy was brilliant at The Open. Brilliant with the adoring crowds, brilliant with the media, brilliant with his playing partners.

‌



Even when it was clear he would not contend for the Claret Jug, McIlroy was one of the Championship’s main draw cards. Only Tommy Fleetwood, the local hero, drew as much attention.

‌



Rory is box office, wherever he goes. Scottie Scheffler is the world number one but McIlroy is the successor to Tiger Woods as golf’s poster player. Which is why his comments after his final round at Royal Birkdale will have alarmed PGA Tour executives. McIlroy is not just the most talented golfer out there, he is the most eloquent. And he gives an honest answer.

‌



Asked if he was not as ‘fired up’ by the PGA Tour as he once was, he replied: “Yeah, that is fair.” And he then elaborated, explaining his priorities have changed and that the new FedEx Cup format meant he could miss more tournaments.

Bryson DeChambeau shows true colours with response to Rory McIlroy taunts at The Open READ MORE :

Behind the scenes at Sky Sports Golf as plans for 2027 Open already put in place READ MORE :

He explained: “I think the change where it doesn’t matter where your are in the top 30 going into the Tour Championship … it’s like I just need to be in the top 30 going in there to have a chance to win a FedEx Cup.

"So why would I care about the first two?”

‌



It is a fair point. But it also shows McIlroy is becoming more and more selective when it comes to the business of competing in golf tournaments.

From the day he donned a second Green Jacket to the opening day of the 154th Open Championship, McIlroy played in five events. Five events in more than three months.

View 2 Images Rory McIlroy drew huge followings at The Open despite struggling for top form (Image: Warren Little/Getty Images)

‌



Look at the top five on the final Open leaderboard. In that same time, Ryan Fox played in nine events, Cameron Young in seven, Sam Burns and Scottie Scheffler in eight, and Tommy Fleetwood in nine.

Of those five events McIlroy played between his win at Augusta and his tied-40th place at The Open, two were majors. And the earliest McIlroy will return to the golf course will be on August 12, although judging by his comments on the FedEx Cup format, it is not an absolute guarantee he will start at the St Jude Classic on that date.

A back-to-back Masters champion and with six majors to his name - not to mention countless tournament wins worldwide and a personal fortune estimated to be around the £300million mark - McIlroy has earned the right to pick and choose when and where to play. But his performance at The Open made you wonder if his schedule could take a little away from his competitive edge.

Article continues below

McIlroy is so good that, even with a reduced schedule, he will be a prime contender for the lucrative end-of-season honours. He will be in the mix for the FedEx Cup and the Race to Dubai, that is for sure.

And when the next major comes around next April, you would not back against him making it three Masters wins on the spin.But it is clear golf is going to see less of its greatest player in the coming years, rather than more.

Sports.title: Argentina World Cup fate decided after calls to ban finalists from next tournament
Sports.content:
Argentina World Cup fate decided after calls to ban finalists from next tournament

Ugly scenes unfolded on the pitch after Argentina's World Cup final defeat to Spain

View 3 Images Argentina players conducted themselves poorly at the World Cup (Image: Marvin Ibo Guengoer - GES Sportfoto, Getty Images)

Argentina will automatically qualify for the World Cup 2030 despite calls for the nation to be banned from the next edition of the tournament. The 2022 winners failed to retain the World Cup trophy on Sunday at MetLife Stadium after losing 1-0 to Spain, thanks to an extra-time goal from Ferran Torres.

‌



Just as had been the case throughout their dramatic semi-final victory over England, Lionel Scaloni’s side were the weaker team across the 90 minutes but used dark arts tactics to even the playing field. That was clear to see with their overly-aggressive tackling, off-the-ball confrontations and attempts to get Spain’s players sent off.

‌



Having got away with various transgressions, Argentina themselves had midfielder Enzo Fernandez sent off for a second yellow card following a reckless challenge in stoppage time. The South American nation’s players then sparked a mass brawl after the final whistle blew, with several players landing blows on their Spanish counterparts in a shocking display of unsportsmanlike behaviour and lack of grace in defeat.

‌



JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

The unsavoury scenes, of which there were plenty against England too, disgusted much of the football world. Sections of football fans online have even called upon FIFA to officially ban Argentina from the World Cup in four years’ time due to their string of recent controversies.

However, Argentina have already booked their place at the next tournament without having to qualify, given they are one of an unprecedented six nations hosting at least one match in the 2030 edition, along with Spain, Morocco, Portugal, Paraguay and Uruguay.

‌



Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay will each host one match to honour the centenary of the World Cup. While the rest of the tournament will continue elsewhere, they don't have to go through the arduous qualification process in a special exception to the usual procedure.

View 3 Images There have been calls by some fans for Argentina to be banned from World Cup 2030 (Image: Rob Newell - CameraSport, CameraSport via Getty Images)

The 1930 World Cup, the first edition of the tournament, was played in and won by Uruguay. They beat Argentina in the final, while Paraguay have been included as the home of CONMEBOL, the first and only football confederation at that time.

‌



Argentina’s most ardent critics will be furious to learn the nation will still be involved, having taken to Reddit to call for their banning.

One user posted: "Their behaviour throughout this tournament should see Argentina banned from the 2030 World Cup. Maybe sitting a World Cup out will sort out their attitude." Another wrote: "They celebrated in English players‘ faces and then fought when they lost. Absolutely despicable… zero class."

A third chimed in with: "They should 1000% get banned for such poor behaviour," while a fourth added: "Exactly. Totally agree."

‌



Another pointed out: "Fully agreed. Show authority and ban foul behaviour. Political statements, violence and constant reckless play should be enough to earn them a disciplinary action."

With regards to Argentina and bans, midfielders Fernandez and Leandro Paredes will miss at least the next two international fixtures after being sent off. As Spain’s players ran onto the pitch to celebrate at the final whistle, Nahuel Molina appeared to throw a punch towards Spain captain Rodri's stomach too.

View 3 Images Argentina escaped punishment for holding up a controversial and political banner (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Paredes, who had already been yellow carded during the game and was lucky to escape a second booking, then seemed to punch Spain defender Eric Garcia in the throat before Argentina manager Lionel Scaloni ran over to separate the players.

Seconds later, Paredes turned his attention towards Gavi, throwing the Spain midfielder to the floor before shoving him in the face while grabbing his substitute's bib. Argentina coach Roberto Ayala also appeared to hit Dani Olmo in the throat.

After the victory over England in the penultimate round, Argentina’s players held up a controversial banner thrown onto the pitch by their supporters, which claimed the Falkland Islands belong to Argentina. Despite FIFA making it very clear that political statements had no place at the World Cup prior to the tournament, the Argentine players escaped punishment for that misconduct.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."
