Buenos Aires Takes the Lead with Multi-Artist Benefit

The centerpiece event, “Puente – Artistas por Venezuela,” takes over the Liverpool Club in Palermo on Saturday, July 11, from 9:00 PM to 3:00 AM.

More than 25 Venezuelan and Argentine performers will play across acoustic, band, and DJ sets, including Cesar Veloz, Andrés Cruz, and JOTA.

Liverpool Club, located on Cabrera Street in the trendy Palermo neighborhood, is a well-known hub for Buenos Aires’ independent music scene, making it a fitting stage for a grassroots-driven cause.

The lineup is carefully curated into three blocks: an acoustic segment featuring Mariangel González and Lulubelle, a band segment with groups like Guataca and Colibrí, and a late-night DJ set from Arnold Dica and others.

For foreign residents and visitors, this format offers a rare, immersive snapshot of the cross-border cultural ties that bind Argentina and Venezuela, two nations with a long history of artistic exchange.

A Second Buenos Aires Show Adds Star Power

A separate benefit, “Show a Beneficio de Venezuela,” is scheduled for Friday, July 17, at the Palermo Groove venue.

Argentine reggae icons Los Cafres and Fidel Nadal will headline, joined by Venezuelan acts like D Kumana and Raíces.

Los Cafres are one of Latin America’s most influential reggae bands, with a career spanning nearly four decades, while Fidel Nadal is a pioneer of Argentine reggae and a former member of the seminal punk band Todos Tus Muertos.

Their presence elevates the event’s profile and is expected to draw a large, diverse crowd, including long-term expats familiar with the local music landscape.

This show directs its proceeds to child-focused foundations Hogar Bambi, Fundana, and Ventura Orbit, organizations that provide shelter and support to vulnerable children in Venezuela, adding a targeted humanitarian layer to the musical effort.

Chile Joins the Global Venezuela Solidarity Concerts Movement

In Santiago, the global “Candlelight por Venezuela” series will feature a performance by the Parallel Quartet on July 30.

The exact Santiago venue has not been named, but the event is confirmed as part of a worldwide charity push.

The Candlelight series is an internationally recognized concept that stages classical music performances in intimate, candle-lit spaces, often in historic or unconventional venues.

For Chile’s capital, this represents a more formal, contemplative approach to fundraising, contrasting with the electric club atmosphere in Buenos Aires.

Investors and tourists in Santiago should watch for venue announcements from Fever, the platform that typically manages Candlelight ticketing, as these events often sell out quickly due to their unique ambiance.

Where the Money Goes: Direct Relief for Earthquake Victims

All ticket sales from the Puente concert will be delivered directly to families left vulnerable by the June tremors.

Meanwhile, the July 17 show directs funds to child-focused foundations Hogar Bambi, Fundana, and Ventura Orbit.

The Candlelight series in Santiago channels its proceeds to broader relief organizations working on the ground in Venezuela, ensuring aid reaches those in need through established humanitarian channels.

This multi-pronged funding approach allows donors to choose between direct family assistance, child welfare, or general disaster relief, depending on which event they attend.

For expats and international supporters, these concerts provide a transparent and culturally engaging way to contribute to a crisis that has received limited global media attention.

Background: A Region Responds to Sudden Tragedy

The June 2026 earthquakes struck Venezuela with little warning, destroying infrastructure and leaving countless families without shelter or basic services.

In the weeks since, grassroots solidarity movements have sprung up across Latin America, with artists leveraging their platforms to mobilize resources faster than many official aid channels.

Argentina and Chile are home to two of the largest Venezuelan diaspora communities in the world, a result of the country’s prolonged economic and humanitarian crisis over the past decade.

This diaspora has woven itself into the social and cultural fabric of host cities like Buenos Aires and Santiago, creating a deeply personal motivation for local artists and audiences to participate in these benefits.

For readers unfamiliar with the region’s dynamics, these concerts are not just charity events—they are a visible expression of the enduring bonds between host communities and their Venezuelan neighbors.

What It Means for Expats, Investors, and Travelers

For expats living in Buenos Aires or Santiago, these events offer a chance to engage with local culture while supporting a tangible humanitarian cause, with entry prices starting around US$10.

Investors with interests in the region’s entertainment or nonprofit sectors may see these large-scale, volunteer-driven benefits as a signal of strong community engagement and organizational capacity.

Tourists visiting either city in July can experience an authentic, emotionally resonant side of Latin American urban life that goes far beyond typical sightseeing itineraries.

Attendees should purchase tickets early through official channels, as venue capacities like Liverpool Club and Palermo Groove are limited and demand is expected to be high.

Beyond the immediate relief, these concerts help sustain a network of cultural solidarity that can be reactivated for future crises, making them a meaningful entry point for foreigners wanting to understand the region’s social resilience.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the main Venezuela solidarity concert in Buenos Aires?

The main event is “Puente – Artistas por Venezuela” on July 11 at Liverpool Club, featuring over 25 artists across acoustic, band, and DJ sets. It runs from 9:00 PM to 3:00 AM in the Palermo neighborhood, and 100% of ticket sales go directly to families affected by the June earthquakes.

How can I attend the Candlelight concert in Santiago?

The Santiago concert is on July 30 as part of the global Candlelight series, though the specific venue has not been announced yet. Interested attendees should monitor the Fever platform, which typically handles ticketing for Candlelight events, as these intimate performances often sell out quickly.

Where do the proceeds from these concerts go?

Funds go directly to Venezuelan earthquake victims, child welfare foundations, or general relief organizations depending on the event. The Puente concert sends money straight to affected families, the July 17 show supports Hogar Bambi, Fundana, and Ventura Orbit, and the Candlelight series funds broader relief organizations.

World.title: Tecnoglass Road Deal, Not Sale, Drives Barranquilla Growth
World.content:
Colombia · Companies

Key Facts —Joint project. Tecnoglass, Grupo Argos, and Barranquilla's mayor partnered on a road circuit. —Investment size. The deal involved COP 15,000 million (approx. US$4.6 million) in joint funding. —Job creation. Civil works lasted 12 months and generated around 150 local jobs. —Strategic goal. The project aims to improve mobility and attract a decade of new investment. —No sale. No real estate or glass manufacturing deal closed between the firms in July 2026.

Tecnoglass and Grupo Argos did not close a real estate or industrial sale in July 2026, but their actual joint infrastructure project is actively reshaping northern Barranquilla.

A Colombian manufacturer produces architectural glass and aluminum products for global markets.

The Real Barranquilla Project by Tecnoglass

The agreement, announced in June 2024, focuses on completing a key road circuit in northern Barranquilla, one of Colombia’s most important coastal industrial cities. It involves the Carrera 75A, Calle 98, and Vía 40 corridors, which are vital arteries for moving goods and workers through the city’s expanding northern zone.

The project is a three-way partnership between Colombian window and glass maker Tecnoglass, cement and infrastructure giant Grupo Argos, and the Mayor’s Office of Barranquilla. For foreign investors unfamiliar with the local landscape, Grupo Argos is one of Colombia’s largest conglomerates with deep experience in urban development, making this a significant public-private collaboration.

Funding, Jobs, and Long-Term Vision

The partners committed a joint investment of COP 15,000 million, which is approximately US$4.6 million at current exchange rates. Civil construction work was scheduled to last 12 months, a relatively fast timeline that signals strong coordination between the private companies and city officials.

The initiative was expected to generate about 150 jobs during the building phase, providing a modest but welcome boost to local employment. As a result, it aims to strengthen industrial, commercial, and residential development in the area, making the northern corridor more attractive for future projects.

Officials projected that better mobility would attract new investments in housing, industry, and commerce over the next decade. For expats and foreign businesses eyeing Barranquilla, improved road access can significantly raise property values and ease daily logistics in a city that serves as a major Caribbean logistics hub.

A History of Tension, Not a Takeover

The infrastructure deal does not signal a broader corporate merger. In fact, Tecnoglass and Grupo Argos have a history of public land-use disputes that have occasionally made headlines in Colombia’s business press.

Grupo Argos developed residential projects like ‘Portal del Norte’ next to Tecnoglass’s industrial complex. This proximity sparked controversy over zoning rules in the city’s northern expansion zone, as heavy manufacturing and residential neighborhoods typically do not mix well.

Because of these tensions, no credible sources report a new real estate or glass manufacturing deal closing in July 2026. The road project remains their primary joint venture, and it represents a pragmatic détente rather than a warm corporate embrace.

What the Road Means for Expats and Investors

For foreign residents and international investors, the completed road circuit directly improves connectivity between residential zones, industrial parks, and Barranquilla’s main logistics corridors. Shorter travel times on Vía 40, a major highway linking the city to port facilities, can reduce operational costs for businesses that rely on Colombia’s Caribbean export routes.

The project also signals that Barranquilla’s local government can successfully mediate between powerful corporate players with competing interests. This kind of stability is exactly what long-term real estate investors look for when evaluating emerging markets.

While US$4.6 million is a modest sum by global infrastructure standards, the strategic placement of these roads could unlock far larger private investments in the surrounding area. Expats considering property purchases in northern Barranquilla should watch for new residential and commercial developments along the improved corridors.

Tecnoglass's Separate Growth Path

Separately, Tecnoglass previously entered a joint venture with French multinational Saint-Gobain in 2019. That deal involved acquiring a 25% stake in Colombia’s Vidrio Andino glass facility, a move that expanded its raw material supply chain.

The partnership with Saint-Gobain also included building a new float glass plant in Barranquilla. This expansion is completely unrelated to the Grupo Argos road project, but it underscores Tecnoglass’s broader strategy of strengthening its manufacturing base on Colombia’s Caribbean coast.

What Happens Next

With the 12-month construction timeline now complete, attention turns to whether the promised wave of new investment materializes. City planners and both companies will be watching closely to see if developers move forward with housing and commercial projects along the upgraded corridors.

The road circuit also sets a precedent for how Tecnoglass and Grupo Argos can collaborate on shared infrastructure despite their history of zoning disputes. Future joint ventures are not guaranteed, but the successful completion of this project keeps the door open for further public-private partnerships in Barranquilla.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Tecnoglass sell part of its business to Grupo Argos in July 2026?

No. No credible reports support a July 2026 sale between the two companies. The only recent deal is a 2024 road infrastructure project carried out jointly with Barranquilla's mayor, and there is no evidence of any subsequent real estate or industrial transaction.

What is the joint project between Tecnoglass and Grupo Argos?

It is a COP 15,000 million (US$4.6 million) road circuit completion in northern Barranquilla covering Carrera 75A, Calle 98, and Vía 40. The project aims to improve mobility, reduce travel times, and attract new industrial and residential investment to the area over the next decade.

Why is there tension between Tecnoglass and Grupo Argos?

The companies have disputed land use because Grupo Argos built residential projects like 'Portal del Norte' right next to Tecnoglass's industrial complex in Barranquilla's northern expansion zone. This proximity raised concerns about zoning compatibility between heavy manufacturing facilities and residential neighborhoods.

World.title: Panama Buys Key US-Bound Oil Pipeline, Price Undisclosed
World.content:
Panama · Economy

Key Facts —Announcement date. July 17, 2026, by Panama's Ministry of Economy and Finance. —Current ownership split. The Panamanian state holds 59%, while U.S.-based NIC Holding Corp owns 41%. —Purchase price. Undisclosed; will be calculated using a pre-agreed formula based on audited financial statements. —Financing method. The buyout will be funded by the company's own cash flow, not through expropriation. —Strategic asset. The pipeline allows large oil tankers to bypass the Panama Canal, connecting the Caribbean to the U.S. East Coast.

Panama’s government announced on Friday it has begun the process to buy the remaining private stake in the Panama Petroterminal, a strategic trans-isthmus oil pipeline, aiming for full state ownership. The exact purchase price for the 41% share held by U.S. company NIC Holding Corp has not been publicly disclosed.

It operates a cross-country oil pipeline and storage terminal linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

A Contractual, Not Expropriation, Purchase

The Ministry of Economy and Finance confirmed the move is a contractual purchase under the 1977 Association Agreement, specifically Clause 10. It is not an act of expropriation, officials stressed, a crucial distinction for foreign investors watching the process.

The price will be determined by a pre-agreed formula based on the Panama Petroterminal’s audited financial statements. The government will use the company’s own cash flow and generated income to finance the deal, meaning no new public debt or extraordinary budget allocations are required.

Why Panama Wants Full Control of the Panama Petroterminal

President José Raúl Mulino’s administration cited three main reasons for the buyout. First, the state will capture all future dividends and economic value from the pipeline’s operations, rather than sharing profits with the private minority shareholder.

Second, full ownership tightens national control over a critical energy and logistics asset, reinforcing sovereignty. Third, the captured funds will support future investments in Panama’s energy, maritime, and logistics sectors, potentially strengthening the country’s position as a regional transport hub.

Strategic Role of the Trans-Isthmus Pipeline

The Panama Petroterminal was created in 1977 as a joint venture to handle oversized oil tankers that could not navigate the Panama Canal. It remains a key platform for the country’s logistics development and energy infrastructure.

The pipeline transports hydrocarbons from the Caribbean to the U.S. East Coast, bypassing the canal entirely. This function gives it critical strategic value for regional energy supply chains, as it offers a reliable alternative route for crude and petroleum products regardless of canal congestion or transit restrictions.

Background: A 50-Year Partnership Nears Its End

The Panama Petroterminal has operated for nearly five decades under a unique public-private structure established by the 1977 Association Agreement. NIC Holding Corp, the U.S.-based private partner, has been involved since the project’s inception, helping finance and operate the trans-isthmus system during a period when Panama was still consolidating its control over the Canal Zone.

The original agreement always contemplated a mechanism for the state to eventually acquire full ownership, which is why Clause 10 provides a contractual pathway rather than requiring hostile negotiations. For context, this model differs sharply from outright nationalizations seen elsewhere in the region, as it follows a pre-established legal roadmap that both parties signed decades ago.

What It Means for Expats, Investors, and Energy Markets

For foreign investors and expats living in Panama, the government’s emphasis on a contractual—not expropriation—process is a reassuring signal about respect for private property rights. The use of the company’s own cash flow to fund the purchase also suggests the state is not straining public finances to complete the deal.

From an energy market perspective, full state ownership of the Panama Petroterminal could lead to more predictable long-term operations, as the government will have undivided authority over maintenance and expansion decisions. However, international oil shippers will be watching closely to ensure that service continuity and competitive pricing remain in place after the transition.

Next Steps and Operational Continuity

The government guaranteed job stability for all current employees and continuity of supplier contracts. Uninterrupted service to customers will be maintained throughout the transition, a key concern for U.S. East Coast refineries that depend on the pipeline’s steady flow.

A final completion date for the transaction remains pending. The deal will close once the price is finalized through the agreed financial formula, moving state ownership from 59% to 100% and ending the nearly 50-year public-private partnership.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Panama Petroterminal?

It is a trans-isthmus oil pipeline and terminal system created in 1977 as a joint venture between the Panamanian state and U.S.-based NIC Holding Corp. The facility allows large tankers to move crude oil and petroleum products from the Caribbean to the U.S. East Coast, bypassing the Panama Canal entirely—a critical function for vessels too large to transit the waterway.

How is Panama paying for the private stake?

The government will use the Panama Petroterminal's own cash flow and generated income to finance the buyout, meaning no new taxes or public borrowing are required. The purchase is a contractual process under Clause 10 of the 1977 Association Agreement and is explicitly not an expropriation of the U.S. owner's shares.

Why hasn't the purchase price been disclosed?

The exact transaction value will be calculated using a pre-agreed formula based on the company's audited financial statements. Until those audits are completed and the formula is applied, the final dollar figure remains confiden

tial. This method was designed decades ago to ensure a fair, transparent valuation rather than a politically negotiated number.

How Lula 2026 Alliances Reshape the Electoral Map

Brazilian President Lula has secured regional coalitions with heavyweight center parties like the PSD, MDB, and PSB. This broad front covers every region except for one holdout, Minas Gerais, where negotiations continue.

Meanwhile, right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro of the Liberal Party (PL) has defined alliances in only 14 to 15 states. He remains deadlocked in the Northeast and lacks consensus in key battlegrounds like Goiás and Espírito Santo.

A Coalition Built on Center-Party Muscle

Lula’s strategy relies on sharing campaign platforms, called “palanques,” with powerful regional allies rather than running only Workers’ Party (PT) candidates. For example, in Pernambuco, he backs popular Recife Mayor João Campos of the Brazilian Socialist Party (PSB).

In Amazonas, the alliance supports Senator Omar Aziz of the Social Democratic Party (PSD). In Pará, it is Hana Ghassan of the Brazilian Democratic Movement (MDB).

This approach helps Lula tap into local political machines.

Flávio Bolsonaro's Narrower Path

Flávio Bolsonaro’s PL is betting more on its own party candidates, expecting to launch at least 11 gubernatorial bids. However, his coalition is limited to the PP, Republicans, and Podemos in just a handful of states.

As a result, his national reach is weaker. He faces impasses in six states, including Alagoas and Maranhão, which blocks his expansion in a region where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, previously showed strength.

What the Numbers Mean for October

Securing 25 state platforms gives Lula control over local resources and guaranteed media time when official campaigning starts on August 16. The first-round vote is set for October 4.

Because party conventions run from July 20 to August 5, the alliance map is nearly final. The only unresolved piece is Minas Gerais, where both camps await a decision between potential allies Marília and Cleitinho Azevedo.

Background: Why State Alliances Matter in Brazil

In Brazil’s sprawling federal system, gubernatorial candidates act as powerful local campaign managers for presidential hopefuls. They mobilize voters, organize rallies, and share precious television and radio advertising time during the official campaign period.

For foreign investors and expats, this patchwork of state-level deals is often more telling than national polls. A presidential candidate who lacks a local ally in a key state can be virtually invisible to voters there, no matter how strong their national message.

The Political Backdrop to Lula's Coalition Push

Lula’s alliance-building did not happen overnight. It reflects lessons learned from the bruising 2022 race, when he narrowly defeated Jair Bolsonaro in a runoff that exposed deep regional divides.

Back then, the PT struggled to find allies in several agricultural heartland states, forcing Lula to campaign with a thinner ground game than he wanted. This time, his team started negotiating much earlier, offering cabinet positions and federal budget commitments to centrist governors in exchange for their public backing.

The result is a coalition that looks more like the broad centrist fronts that dominated Brazilian politics in the early 2000s than a traditional leftist ticket.

What It Means for Expats and Investors

A Lula victory built on such a wide centrist coalition likely signals policy continuity rather than sharp leftward swings. The heavy reliance on PSD and MDB governors suggests a pragmatic governing style that markets generally find reassuring.

For expatriates living in Brazil, the alliance map also hints at local stability. States with defined, broad-based coalitions tend to experience smoother transitions and less political noise, which can affect everything from public services to local business climates.

How the Electoral Calendar Unfolds from Here

With party conventions wrapping up by August 5, the campaign enters a critical phase where television and radio slots become the most valuable currency in Brazilian politics. Lula’s 25-state network guarantees him a dominant share of this free airtime, dwarfing what Flávio Bolsonaro can muster with his narrower alliance map.

For ordinary Brazilians, this means the president’s face and message will be far more present in daily life between August 16 and the October 4 vote. In a country where television still shapes voter decisions, especially among lower-income households, that visibility gap could prove decisive long before any ballots are cast.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which parties are part of Lula's 2026 coalition?

The main allies are the PSD, MDB, and PSB, along with the PP, PDT, União Brasil, and Republicans in specific states. This broad front spans the center and center-left, giving Lula a reach far beyond his own Workers' Party.

How many states does Flávio Bolsonaro have alliances in?

As of July 2026, Flávio Bolsonaro has defined pre-candidacy alliances in only 14 to 15 states, far behind Lula's 25. His Liberal Party has struggled to build bridges with centrist governors, especially in the Northeast.

When is Brazil's 2026 presidential election?

The first round of the general and gubernatorial elections is scheduled for October 4, 2026, with official campaign ads starting August 16. Party conventions to formally nominate candidates take place from July 20 to August 5.

World.title: Ministry of Immigration recognizes immigration officers at Philip Goldson International Airport for outstanding service
World.content:
Ministry of Immigration recognizes immigration officers at Philip Goldson International Airport for outstanding service

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Ministry of Immigration, Governance and Labour recognized the dedication and professionalism of Immigration Officers stationed at the Philip Goldson International Airport.

The Ministry hosted an appreciation ceremony where Minister of Immigration, Governance and Labour Kareem Musa, and Director of the Department of Border Management and Immigration Services, Lawrence Thompson, presented awards to outstanding officers.

“As the first representatives of Belize that returning Belizeans and international visitors encounter upon arrival, professionalism and courteous service is vital,” the Ministry said.

Their work ethic ensures a welcoming experience while maintaining the integrity and security of Belize’s borders.

The officers recognized were:

Outstanding Contribution: Tricia Gillett, Immigration Clerk I

Best Attendance: Bobby Flowers, Immigration Assistant I

Most Improved Officer: Eladio Pop, Immigration Clerk II

Most Productive Officer (Arrival): Herman Martinez, Immigration Clerk I

Most Productive Officer (Departure): Triana Bennett, Immigration Clerk II

Minister Musa congratulated the award recipients for their dedication and encouraged all officers to continue delivering the high standard of service expected at Belize’s primary international gateway.

Director Thompson also commended the recipients for their professionalism and commitment, emphasizing that their work reflects the values and mission of the Department of Border Management and Immigration Services.

The Ministry extended congratulations to each award recipient and thanks all Immigration Officers at the Philip Goldson International Airport for their continued service to Belize and the travelling public.

World.title: International Moon Day celebrates human achievement and the future of space exploration
World.content:
International Moon Day celebrates human achievement and the future of space exploration

By Zoila Palma: International Moon Day is being observed today to commemorate one of humanity’s greatest achievements — the first human landing on the Moon during NASA’s Apollo 11 mission in 1969.

The United Nations General Assembly established the annual observance in 2021 through Resolution 76/76 on international cooperation in the peaceful uses of outer space.

The day highlights the achievements of countries involved in lunar exploration. It also serves as a reminder of the importance of international cooperation as nations continue developing new missions to explore Earth’s closest celestial neighbor.

The 2026 observance follows the historic Artemis II mission, which saw four astronauts complete a journey around the Moon and return safely to Earth.

The mission, carried out in April, marked one of the farthest human spaceflights ever completed and reinforced the message that global cooperation can help achieve extraordinary milestones.

World.title: Young Belizean athletes carry national pride to Costa Rica Tennis tournament
World.content:
Young Belizean athletes carry national pride to Costa Rica Tennis tournament

By Zoila Palma: Two young Belizean tennis athletes are representing the country at the CONTECA U10 Tournament in Costa Rica, where they will compete against some of the region’s best young players.

The Belize team includes 9-year-old John Habet and 10-year-old Armaan Sugnani, who are traveling with Coach Ismar Amaya Jr. for the Central American Tennis Confederation competition.

The Belize Olympic and Commonwealth Games Association extended best wishes to the athletes, encouraging them to embrace the opportunity to gain international experience, build friendships, and make Belize proud on the regional stage.

World.title: International News: Taiwan warns of rising Chinese vessel activity, plans Pacific supply route drills
World.content:
International News: Taiwan warns of rising Chinese vessel activity, plans Pacific supply route drills

By Zoila Palma: Taiwan has reported a sharp increase in Chinese coast guard and research vessel activity around the island, raising concerns in Taipei that Beijing may be testing strategies to disrupt vital supply routes in the event of a conflict.

Taiwan Coast Guard data showed 55 sightings of Chinese government vessels in June, compared with 30 in May and 25 during the same month last year, Reuters report.

The figures represent an 83% increase from May and a 120% rise compared with June 2025. The data does not include activity near Taiwan-controlled islands close to China. Taiwanese officials said the growing presence of Chinese coast guard vessels highlights Beijing’s expanding use of maritime forces to reinforce its territorial claims.

Taipei has accused China of using “lawfare” by attempting to establish a legal justification for operations around Taiwan.

Officials said the increased patrols could be linked to preparations for a potential blockade scenario aimed at cutting off Taiwan’s Pacific supply routes and limiting access to allied support.

A senior Taiwan Coast Guard official said the government has developed contingency plans with the navy, including tabletop exercises and live drills, to protect the island’s maritime lifelines.

World.title: International News: WestJet expands Belize service with new non-stop Winnipeg route
World.content:
International News: WestJet expands Belize service with new non-stop Winnipeg route

By Zoila Palma: WestJet has announced a major expansion of its winter 2026 schedule, including the launch of a new non-stop flight between Winnipeg, Manitoba, and Belize City, Belize, providing Canadian travelers with another direct gateway to the Jewel.

The weekly service will begin on December 14, 2026, further strengthening Belize’s air connectivity with Canada during the peak winter travel season.

The airline said the new route is part of its strategy to meet growing demand for warm-weather destinations across Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean.

The Winnipeg-Belize City service complements WestJet’s existing flights from Toronto and Calgary, giving Canadian visitors even greater access to Belize’s beaches, barrier reef, rainforests, and cultural attractions.

The new Belize route is one of five destinations being added to WestJet’s winter network, alongside new non-stop services between Calgary and Mérida, Mexico; Winnipeg and Punta Cana, Dominican Republic; Regina and San José del Cabo, Mexico; and Ottawa and Liberia, Costa Rica.

WestJet also reaffirmed its position as the leading Canadian carrier serving Belize this winter. The airline said it plans to increase capacity on several of its most popular routes, with additional announcements expected in the coming weeks.

World.title: International News: Canada to temporarily bar foreign travelers recently in Congo over Ebola concerns
World.content:
International News: Canada to temporarily bar foreign travelers recently in Congo over Ebola concerns

By Zoila Palma: The Canadian government announced Sunday that it will temporarily deny entry to foreign nationals who have been in the Democratic Republic of Congo within the previous 21 days as part of new border measures aimed at reducing the risk of Ebola entering the country.

The restrictions, which take effect on July 20 at 11:59 p.m. EDT, come despite the World Health Organization’s recommendation against imposing travel or trade restrictions on Congo, where officials continue to battle a major Ebola outbreak, Reuters report.

Canada’s Public Health Agency said the temporary measure is intended to protect public health, although it acknowledged that the risk of Ebola spreading to Canadians remains low.

The World Health Organization has repeatedly warned that travel restrictions can stigmatize affected communities and complicate efforts to control outbreaks.

The agency maintains that Ebola is spread primarily through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person and estimates the risk of international transmission from Congo remains low. As of July 15, Congo had recorded more than 2,100 Ebola cases, including 828 deaths.

World.title: International News: Spanish Aid vessel delivers medical supplies to Cuba as humanitarian crisis deepens
World.content:
International News: Spanish Aid vessel delivers medical supplies to Cuba as humanitarian crisis deepens

By Zoila Palma: The Spanish humanitarian organization Open Arms has delivered seven tons of humanitarian aid to Cuba after its sailing vessel, Astral, arrived at the Port of Havana on Sunday.

The shipment, destined for the Juan Manuel Márquez Pediatric Hospital, includes solar panels, replacement batteries, and medical supplies aimed at strengthening critical healthcare services amid Cuba’s worsening economic and energy crisis, telesur reports.

The aid is part of the “Heading to Cuba” campaign, launched by Open Arms alongside more than 150 political and social organizations.

The vessel completed a 6,200-mile journey after departing Barcelona in May.

According to Open Arms, the mission was financed through donations from more than 4,000 supporters, raising over €160,000 (US$182,816).

The equipment will provide energy autonomy for the hospital’s intensive care unit, intermediate care unit, and clinical laboratory, helping to ensure essential medical services remain operational during frequent power outages.

World.title: Government of Belize expresses solidarity following ferry tragedy in Guyana
World.content:
Government of Belize expresses solidarity following ferry tragedy in Guyana

By Zoila Palma: On July 18, 2026, a ferry which departed from Georgetown, Guyana, carrying 116 passengers and 17 crew members, capsized in rough waves.

The latest reports indicate that 67 persons have been rescued, and a massive search-and-rescue effort is currently underway for those who remain missing.

“On behalf of the people of Belize, Hon. John Briceño and the Government of Belize extend prayers of hope for the safe rescue of those still missing off the coast of Guyana and offer comfort to the families awaiting the return of their loved ones,” a statement from the Government of Belize expressed.

The thoughts of the people of Belize are with the people of Guyana as they grapple with this tragedy.

World.title: More traffic headache coming for motorists in Liguanea
World.content:
Sewer upgrade work underway on Retreat Avenue off Old Hope Road on Saturday. The work will shortly be extended on Old Hope Road to its intersection with Wellington Drive. Naphtali Junior

MOTORISTS in the Liguanea area of St Andrew should brace for major traffic disruptions this summer as the National Water Commission (NWC) undertakes the renovation of sewage infrastructure along Old Hope Road

Speaking during a recent meeting of the Jamaica Observer Press Club at the newspaper’s headquarters in St Andrew, Minister of Water Matthew Samuda said the work forms part of the Government’s ongoing programme to strengthen resilience through upgrading the county’s water and sewage network.

He explained that work on Munroe Road and Wellington Drive, which led to traffic snarls in the area for weeks, is now complete, allowing work to begin on the stretch of Old Hope Road that runs through Liguanea, Matilda’s Corner, and Seymour Avenue.

Samuda told Observer editors and reporters that work along that corridor was deliberately postponed to avoid disrupting students travelling to sit their various examinations.

“We didn’t start last month because we didn’t want to run the risk of a child being stuck in traffic trying to get to their PEP [Primary Exit Profile] exams at St Peter and Paul, or a child trying to get to Campion to do their CXC [Caribbean Examination Council] exams along that particular space. We expect to start in the coming week or so,” said the minister.

World.content:
Dayton Campbell

On Monday, 13 July 2026, the Jamaica Observer published an article entitled ‘Dead girl’s ghost haunts Dayton’.

The Observer acknowledges that the headline was capable of conveying the false impression that Dr Campbell had some association with, or responsibility for, the rape and murder of Diane Smith. The Observer acknowledges that any such implication is entirely false.

Dr Campbell was an infant when Diane Smith was raped and murdered. He has never been implicated, suspected, or connected in any way with that tragic crime.

The Observer further acknowledges that Dr Campbell did not repeat or endorse any allegation connecting any person to the rape and murder of Diane Smith, whether debunked or otherwise.

The Jamaica Observer sincerely apologises to Dr Campbell for the distress, embarrassment, and reputational harm occasioned by the publication and withdraws any defamatory imputations arising therefrom.

World.title: Puzzling double murder in Mandeville
World.content:
An undated photo of murder victim Deneekia Pounall, 24, Knox Community College nursing student and resident of Heartease district in Manchester .

MANDEVILLE, Manchester — Even as police here have launched a manhunt for a gunman who posed as a passenger in a taxi before disembarking the vehicle and killing two passengers on Saturday, detectives are struggling to make sense of the incident as up to press time they had not determined a motive for the attack.

“It is senseless…He paid his fare and got his change and the vehicle drove off and he just fired shots on it. The motive is not clear, because why would you shoot up a vehicle with seven people,” a senior police source told the Jamaica Observer on Sunday.

Police identified those killed as Deneekia Pounall, 24, a nursing student at Knox Community College, a resident of Heartease in the parish, and her neighbour 21-year-old Sadefa Henry.

According to the police, about 7:30 pm on Saturday, Pounall and Henry were seated in a Toyota Voxy operated as a public passenger vehicle on the Mandeville to Royal Flat route when a man, who was a passenger in the vehicle, disembarked at a section of Caledonia Road commonly referred to as Horseshoe Curve.

The man reportedly opened fire on the seven occupants of the taxi, hitting the two who were seated at the back of the vehicle.

They were taken to the Mandeville Regional Hospital where Pounall was pronounced dead on arrival, while Henry later succumbed to his injuries.

Residents of Heartease told the

Observer on Sunday that Pounall and Henry lived in neighbouring apartments at a property in the community.

“She was such a calm girl. She nuh talk, and the guy was quiet and humble, so this incident is quite puzzling,” said a resident who requested anonymity.

The double murder has increased the number of homicides reported in Manchester to 20 since the start of the year.

Just last week acting head of the police’s Area Three, Senior Superintendent Shane McCalla, predicted that fewer than 94 murders will be recorded across Manchester, Clarendon, and St Elizabeth by year end, following the launch of Operation Reset last month.

“We are trending upwards in the murder and aggravated assaults, so Operation Reset was primarily designed to address this…and in terms of the acquisitive crimes, we are trending down by 104. This is our commitment to the High Command that Area Three will deliver in December,” he told the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s High Command last Wednesday at the Mandeville police station.

McCalla gave a breakdown of murders statistics down the years in Area Three. He said in 2023 there were 189 murders, in 2024 there were 150 murders, while 94 murders were recorded last year.

“Year to date we have 58 [murders]. Despite seeing some issues where St Elizabeth is concerned… I am convinced and I am committing to you that we will end under the 94 [in December],” he vowed.

World.title: Sumfest history
World.content:
Mavado (left) and Vybz Kartel share the Sumfest stage. (Garfield Robinson)

For 18 years it remained one of dancehall’s biggest unanswered questions: Could the music that once divided a nation ever become the force that united it?

Shortly after 2:00 am on Sunday that question was answered inside Plantation Cove as a Taste of Reggae Sumfest delivered an experience of history-making proportions.

Vybz Kartel and Mavado stood shoulder to shoulder on the festival’s grand stage, writing a new chapter in one of the most defining narratives in dancehall culture. The showdown was far more than an exhibition of hit songs. It was the closing of a circle that began during the combative Gully/Gaza era — a rivalry that shaped an entire generation of dancehall fans and forever altered the genre’s landscape.

Dressed for battle, but performing in brotherhood, both deejays were ready to give fans exactly what they asked for.

Without hesitation, they reached back into the catalogue that made them icons. Serving up songs such as

The Real McKoy, Real Deal, Send A Hell, the entertainers elicited loud cheers of approval from the sold-out crowd.

The tension that once defined the rivalry had given way to celebration.

“This a history innu,” Mavado declared.

“Memba dat,” Kartel responded before embracing his long-time rival.

“We ago gi unnu supm unnu never see yet,” Kartel continued.

For two hours they spewed hit after hit from their arsenal of songs.

For Professor Donna Hope, one of Jamaica’s foremost authorities on dancehall culture, the significance of the moment extended well beyond nostalgia.

“Eighteen years later… We have been through many things, they’ve been in exile in different ways, they lost things, they gained things, and so the energy was different,” she reflected after the performance. “Gaza/Gully in 2008 was a very combative energy but Reggae Sumfest 2026, it was different. Their performance reminded people that dancehall culture is alive and well and Vybz Kartel and Mavado are powerful artistes that have matured and now understand the mission and are carrying it out.”

Even while revisiting songs born from lyrical warfare, the two men frequently completed each other’s lyrics, laughed together, and embraced the shared legacy they helped create. Records that once encouraged fans to choose sides became reminders of just how deeply both artistes have shaped modern dancehall.

Mavado confidently held his own with crowd favourites, including Weh Dem A Do, Top Shatta Nah Miss, Chat Too Much, Warn Dem, and Amazing Grace.

Kartel answered with equal force, unleashing anthem after anthem through Gaza Army, Broad Daylight, Kill Dem All, Done, Weh Dem A Go, Murder Informa, and Never Scared.

Female fans were delighted with selections including Love Dem, Picture Me & You, Beg You (A Touch), and Come Home, while Mavado countered with Squeeze Breast, Bicycle, Ever Blessed, When You Feel Lonely, and Never Believe You.

The surprises continued as Mavado invited Stacious to recreate their hit Come Into My Room, while Kartel called on Gaza Hindu to perform Spice’s verses on Ramping Shop and Virginity.

“It’s a good feeling to be back on a Sumfest stage,” said Stacious. “Tonight I’m here not just as an artiste, but as a fan of dancehall who lived through the era where Gully/Gaza did a run road… Mavado hasn’t performed in Jamaica for a while so I was happy to witness that return and be a part of it… [I]t’s always fun when we connect…” As they got ready to draw the curtains on their historic set, the clash songs and romance anthems gave way to messages of gratitude and faith as the deejays delivered Hope and Pray, God Is the Greatest, The Messiah, and Thank Yuh Jah. Then came the perfect ending. Their first collaboration, Happiest Days. “This a the first song me and him ever do,” Kartel reminded the audience. “Listen to it good and see how everything come full circle.” Few closing songs could carry greater symbolism — history, legacy secured!

World.title: Rastafari ganja rights review
World.content:
From left: Sancia Bennett Templer, permanent secretary, Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce; Delano Seiveright, minister of state in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce and chairman of the Cannabis Industry Development Taskforce; Delroy Chuck, minister of justice and constitutional affairs; and Olivia “Babsy” Grange, minister of culture, gender, entertainment and sport, engage meeting attendees (out of picture) following Thursday’s high-level ministerial consultation on Jamaica’s sacramental cannabis framework at the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs.

THE Government on Thursday opened consultations on the country’s sacramental cannabis framework during a high-level policy meeting at the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs.

Justice Minister Delroy Chuck; Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia “Babsy” Grange; minister of state in the Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs Marisa Dalrymple-Philibert; and minister of state in the Ministry of Industry, Investment and Commerce Delano Seiveright led the talks with senior technocrats from the ministries.

The discussions were convened following recommendations of the Cannabis Industry Development Taskforce, chaired by Seiveright, which identified the need for a coordinated consultation on policy and operational issues affecting Jamaica’s sacramental cannabis regime.

The meeting considered the existing legal and administrative framework with the objective of providing greater clarity, consistency, and certainty while safeguarding the religious freedoms provided under Section 7C(2)(a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act, which makes provision for members of the Rastafarian community to possess ganja.

The meeting discussed matters relating to the recognition and oversight of sacramental organisations, approved cultivation lands and spaces, cultivation and possession limits, transportation arrangements, enforcement protocols, and the need to clearly distinguish sacramental cannabis activities from Jamaica’s regulated, commercial cannabis industry.

Jamaica’s commercial cannabis industry is regulated exclusively by the Cannabis Licensing Authority (CLA) under the Dangerous Drugs Act and its Regulations, with no other entity having legal authority to license or regulate commercial cannabis activities.

There have been growing concerns surrounding the misuse of the sacramental framework to facilitate unlawful activities, as well as persistent confusion about what the law permits.

In recent times there have been repeated allegations from Rastafarians about facing prosecution over their use of ganja, despite the provision in law for its sacramental use.

Recently the

Jamaica Observer reported the case of Westmoreland resident Troy Harrison who had charges of possession of ganja and dealing in ganja against him dropped in the Westmoreland Parish Court.

The Crown offered no evidence on both charges on the basis that Harrison is a member of the Rastafarian community and therefore entitled to possess and use ganja for sacramental purposes.

“Some police continue to want to interpret the law how they want to,” attorney-at-law Marcus Goffe, who represented Harrison, told the

Observer.

“The Rastafari community is fed up with the continual targeting and unfair prosecution of members of the community for ganja, despite the 2015 amendments to the Dangerous Drugs Act intended to recognise and protect the community’s rights. It is clear that the narcotics police are not fully aware of the extent of Rastafari’s ganja rights or how they are to approach, investigate, determine, and resolve the rights of Rastafari in relation to ganja,” charged Goffe, who was then on a mission to have the seized ganja returned to Harrison.

Against charges such as the ones made by Goffe, the high-level meeting led by the Government ministers also explored mechanisms to strengthen coordination among the various ministries, the CLA, and the Jamaica Constabulary Force.

A significant part of the discussions focused on the possible transfer of responsibility for the operational governance and administration of sacramental cannabis matters to the Ministry of Culture, recognising the fundamentally religious and cultural character of the sacramental regime.

Ministers agreed that the proposal should form part of the ongoing consultation process as the Government works to strengthen governance; improve inter-ministerial coordination; and provide a clearer, more effective framework that protects legitimate sacramental rights while preserving public confidence, public safety, and the rule of law.

World.title: END OF THE ROAD
World.content:
Spain’s Rodri (left) and Argentina’s Lionel Messi fight for the ball during the World Cup football final match at the New York/New Jersey Stadium in East Rutherford, United States, on Sunday.

EAST RUTHERDORD, United States (AFP) — Ferran Torres scored a dramatic extra-time winner as Spain defeated holders Argentina 1-0 to win the World Cup on Sunday and shatter Lionel Messi’s dreams of a triumphant farewell to football’s greatest stage.

Barcelona striker Torres lashed home a thumping finish in the 106th minute to reward a dominant display by Spain against an Argentina team who failed to register a single shot on target in 120 minutes.

A star-studded crowd of 80,663 that included US President Donald Trump packed East Rutherford’s MetLife Stadium to see if Argentina captain, Messi, could crown his glittering career with a second World Cup victory.

But the 39-year-old maestro — almost certainly playing in his final World Cup game — was reduced to irrelevance as Spain took control early on against an Argentina team who committed cynical fouls throughout.

The South Americans’ skulduggery ended with midfielder Enzo Fernandez being sent off after a brutal challenge on Spain defender Pau Cubarsi in stoppage time.

For long periods, though, it looked as if Argentina may somehow hold on for a penalty shoot-out as Spain struggled to make the breakthrough.

But after Nico Williams had a goal controversially disallowed in extra time, Spain struck.

A lofted cross to the back post by Pedro Porro found Williams who nodded into the path of Torres to crash home the goal that clinched Spain’s second World Cup title after their maiden 2010 triumph.

“Ultimately, the goal belongs to 47 million people — not just me or the 26 players,” goal hero Torres said, referring to Spain’s approximate population.

“At the end of the day, all finals are tough; when you’re up against Messi, there’s a certain nervousness, but we always believed in our football and in ourselves.”

There were ugly scenes after the final whistle as Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes triggered a melee by grabbing Spain defender Eric Garcia around the throat in a skirmish that saw Spanish substitute Gavi thrown to the floor.

Messi, meanwhile, was seen with tears streaming down his face after receiving his runners-up medal in a ceremony headed by Trump — who was subjected to deafening boos and catcalls as he walked onto the pitch alongside FIFA President Gianni Infantino.

Trump and Infantino later presented the World Cup trophy to Spain Captain Rodri, the midfield general who had orchestrated La Roja’s superb win.

“We have won everything, and that is wonderful,” Spain Coach Luis de la Fuente said of his team. “They are a generation of footballers who are a source of pride for Spain.”

Before Sunday’s final, many pundits had predicted a technically inferior Argentina would seek to disrupt Spain’s smooth game with cynicism.

There was an early sign of the South Americans’ cynical game plan early on when Alexis Mac Allister went flying in with a studs-up challenge that struck Dani Olmo’s ankle.

Mac Allister escaped an early yellow card, although after Slovenian referee Slavko Vincic only awarded a foul.

Spain made their presence felt moments later, though, with Alex Baena poleaxing Messi with an elbow to the back that again escaped sanction.

Argentina continued to test referee Vincic’s patience with a series of niggly challenges, and Nicolas Tagliafico was lucky not to be cautioned after raking Lamine Yamal’s calf in a clumsy challenge.

Eventually, though, Vincic did reach for a yellow card, with Lisandro Martinez booked for a cynical challenge on Mikel Oyarzabal.

The final’s controversial half-time show featuring Madonna, Shakira, and Justin Bieber stretched to 27 minutes, but did little to upset Spain’s rhythm.

The Spanish piled on the pressure in a lopsided second half as Argentina hung on grimly.

De la Fuente sent on Pedri and Ferran Torres for Fabian Ruiz and Oyarzabal, and the chances continued with Argentina in full siege mode.

Pedri and Cubarsi both lashed long-range shots that Emi Martinez failed to grasp at the first attempt, but somehow Argentina continued to hold on.

The arrival of substitutes Williams and Mikel Merino gave fresh life to Spain’s attacking momentum, and the onslaught continued.

Fernandez’s reckless red card left Argentina down to 10 men heading into extra time.

Martinez had one last save deep in stoppage time when Yamal’s superb whipped free-kick was clawed wide.

The Spanish dominance continued in extra time. And it looked as if Spain had made the breakthrough when Williams slid a low finish into the net, but referee Vincic blew for a marginal foul on Nicolas Otamendi.

But the breakthrough came with Torres’ winner.

Argentina made a desperate last raid on Spain’s goal, but La Roja held firm to seal victory.

World.title: Nickeria Smickle: Redefining success for the next generation of Caribbean women
World.content:
Founder and chief executive officer of A-List Marketing & Entertainment Group Nickeria Smickle.

NICKERIA Smickle built a company, rebuilt communities after a hurricane, and now wants to prove that there’s more than one way to make it.

Ask Smickle for her formula and she won’t give you a business-school answer, instead she says, “faith, hunger, and a touch of delusion”.

It is a deceptively simple recipe for a woman who has spent the last six years proving that the most successful people are often the ones bold enough to begin before anyone else believes in them.

Smickle is the founder and chief executive officer of A-List Marketing & Entertainment Group and a 2026 Ignite Caribbean 30 Under 30 honouree in entrepreneurship and philanthropy.

But the title she is most interested in expanding isn’t her own. It’s the definition of success itself.

The instinct to give showed up early. At nine years old Smickle was selling candies at school and sharing her lunch money with classmates who had none. At 18, she rode the bus from Mandeville to Kingston to shoot photography at events and volunteer wherever she was needed. By 24 she was running a business and executing her own charity initiatives.

“My passion for service has always been at the core of my journey,” said Smickle.

Long before the company, that meant painting rooms for homeless women and children, joining community outreach, and showing up for beach clean-ups. The scale grew. The instinct never changed.

What sets Smickle apart is not just what she has built, but what she believes. Her argument is direct — not every child is meant to become a lawyer, teacher or doctor, and the ones who become musicians, painters, beauty professionals or entrepreneurs deserve to see their path celebrated too.

She is putting structure behind the belief. In late 2025, she registered the Anchor of Love JA Foundation in honour of her late mother. Its flagship project is Jamaica’s first school tour dedicated to non-traditional careers in the arts and entertainment, designed to show students that success can take a shape no one ever drew for them.

The philosophy is matched by a record. Through A-List Marketing & Entertainment Group, Smickle’s back-to-school programme in the west Kingston community of Tivoli Gardens reaches more than 700 students every year, from early childhood through tertiary level, and employs residents from the communities it serves.

Her annual Gift of Hope Christmas outreach, in partnership with Dolla Financial Services, brings toys, food, and essentials to families across Kingston each holiday season.

When Hurricane Melissa devastated western Jamaica, she answered with a three-phase relief effort. Phase one, with PROVEN Wealth, delivered supplies to Petersfield, Darliston, and Water Works in Westmoreland. Phase two, Joy to the West, sent her team out of Kingston before sunrise on December 24, 2025, to support young mothers at the Women’s Centre of Jamaica Foundation in Savanna-la-Mar; students at Llandilo School of Special Education; and families on Crooke Street, where a community space became a day of games, bounce houses, and supplies.

Phase three, now in development, will re-roof homes for the families hit hardest.

For all the work, Smickle is candid about how rarely she stops to acknowledge herself. “I want to say something I do not say often: I am proud of myself,” she declared. “I’m proud that I did not give up and proud that I kept believing in my vision even when others questioned it.“

She is already looking past the milestone. By 2030, she plans to expand to the United States and the Caribbean, growing both the business and the foundation that carries her mother’s name.

“Entrepreneurship is not only about building a successful company; it is about building stronger communities,” she said. “Success is measured not by personal achievements alone, but by the number of lives uplifted along the way. For the dreamers, the believers, and the ones bold enough to begin, this one is for you.”

World.title: EU bets fossil fuel lobby is crying wolf over supply shock warnings
World.content:
Instead, it has issued new guidelines advising EU countries’ governments to hold off on fining offenders for three years. While that doesn’t officially remove the requirements, it would suspend enforcement to give companies more time to comply. The guidelines, first reported by POLITICO, were made official Monday after months of speculation. Member countries will discuss them Wednesday.

The Commission’s gamble is that companies are raking in so much money from selling to Europe — especially as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz sends energy prices soaring — that they won’t kill a lucrative trade just because of some legal uncertainties.

The executive is also confident that compliance won’t be a problem in the first place, and has reassured diplomats that its three-year “grace period” for penalties will stand up in court if member countries implement it properly. Last week it issued further guidance to help companies prove the emissions intensity of cargoes — a key detail they say has been missing.

“People will come to their senses” over the summer, said one EU official, granted anonymity to speak openly. The guidelines “will make it clearer how and when to comply, and it will become clearer that most importers can comply and will comply rather than lose their sales in a liquid global gas market.”

It’s true that business is booming for companies exporting to Europe. In the first 100 days after the U.S. and Israel’s attack on Iran, the EU paid an additional €62 billion for energy supplies, according to the Jacques Delors Institute. In particular, the bloc massively increased its imports of jet fuel and liquefied natural gas from the U.S., one of the most vocal opponents of the methane rules.

The conviction that companies won’t abandon Europe was illustrated in a meeting of EU ambassadors last week, during which the Commission told member countries that it would be best to wait until 2028 to assess the impact of the rules, instead of tearing them open on the basis of industry speculation, according to two diplomats briefed on the meeting.

World.title: Inquiet des usages de l’IA par les députés, le Parlement européen a une solution
World.content:
“Le Parlement n’a pas été épargné par les erreurs liées à l’IA et les contenus trompeurs générés par IA”, a observé Brando Benifei, député européen du groupe des Socialistes et démocrates qui a dirigé les travaux du Parlement sur l’AI Act, la législation phare de l’UE encadrant cette technologie. “Les députés européens doivent montrer l’exemple à mesure que les règles de transparence prévues par l’AI Act entrent en vigueur.”

Ce projet met en lumière le dilemme auquel est confronté le Parlement à mesure que l’IA générative s’intègre dans son travail. Quelque 2 100 personnes utilisent quotidiennement l’IA, soit environ 20% de l’ensemble des effectifs.

Ses dirigeants souhaitent que les responsables publics cessent de mettre des documents parlementaires sur des plateformes publiques non contrôlées, mais ils craignent également que cette technologie ne nuise à la qualité du travail législatif et n’introduise des erreurs ou des contenus trompeurs dans le processus démocratique. Ils ont soupçonné que les parlementaires et leurs assistants utilisaient déjà l’IA après une recrudescence d’amendements nécessitant une traduction, des styles de rédaction révélateurs et des références parfois fantaisistes à des lois qui n’existent pas.

Les présidents des commissions ont demandé au secrétaire général du Parlement, Alessandro Chiocchetti, d’élaborer des lignes directrices concernant l’utilisation de l’IA par les parlementaires. Celui-ci a répondu que cette question pourrait plutôt relever de la commission des Affaires constitutionnelles, qui devrait alors modifier le règlement intérieur de l’institution afin d’introduire des règles plus strictes.

Aujourd’hui, les députés européens ne sont pas tenus d’indiquer si leurs amendements, questions ou autres travaux parlementaires ont été élaborés à l’aide de l’intelligence artificielle.

Barry Andrews, président Renew de la commission du Développement, a affirmé qu’il était déjà évident que certains députés européens utilisaient l’intelligence artificielle pour rédiger des questions parlementaires, des discours et des amendements.

World.title: EU hits China’s Alibaba with €550M record fine over illegal products
World.content:
The finding that AliExpress failed to check and tackle these risks "is very dangerous for our consumers, but it’s also unfair for those companies that are complying with all our rules," Virkkunen said.

The record fine is the third one imposed under the Digital Services Act so far. It comes two months after Brussels hit rival marketplace Temu with a €200 million bill over similar breaches. “We were looking at the duration and the seriousness of these failures when deciding the size of the fine," Virkkunen said, recalling that Temu had so far only been sanctioned for failing to check its service for illegal products sold in Europe properly.

The Commission opened a probe into AliExpress in March 2024 over suspected breaches of the DSA, including also on the platform's transparency on advertising and recommender systems. Many of these suspected breaches were already settled in a series of commitments in June 2025.

In its new findings, the EU assessed that AliExpress failed to "evaluate whether it had sufficient staff to review potentially illegal products," leading to "overcharged" moderators having "only like 10 or 20 seconds to review the illegal product," a senior Commission official said in a briefing ahead of the announcement. It also failed to assess how its recommender and advertising systems "exacerbate" the spread of illegal products and relied on compliance checks that "could easily be circumvented through mis-categorization."

AliExpress has until Oct. 20 to come up with an "action plan" to address the infringements, which lasted at least until June 2025, or face additional penalties.

A spokesperson for AliExpress said in a statement that the company will appeal the EU's decision, calling it a "disproportionate fine [which] ignores our sound risk management framework and the significant, proactive enhancements we have made." They added: "AliExpress has been and continues to be committed to meeting our obligations to consumers."

This article was updated to include a comment from AliExpress confirming it will appeal the decision.

World.title: America’s reassurance mission at Farnborough
World.content:
Europe’s biggest airshow of the year is set to open this week under the specter of two wars, with the Pentagon facing doubts it can hit a trillion-dollar budget topline and if it will play nice with NATO nations increasingly confident about going it alone.

The show that spans more than five million square feet — enough to fit 78 football pitches or 1,350 Concordes stacked wing to wing — has been running since the end of World War II and will launch tens of billions of dollars worth of deals. But with the U.S. delaying arms sales and hanging onto more weapons, the feeling is in the air that American credibility — especially their ability to clarify what they want from Europe and to meet demand — is on the line here at Farnborough.

“There's no question that the primary subtext to this air show, last year's air show, I'm sure next year's air show, is going to be the geopolitical issues and the transatlantic issue in particular, and a lot of anxiety about what that means on both sides,” said a U.S. industry official. “Europe is far from a monolith. You have European countries that would absolutely like to push full on the gas to build an organic defense industrial base. You have others that are very clear they want to continue to buy American kit.”

“We still argue that we make the best stuff in the world, and everybody wants it,” added the official, who, like others, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “But the Europeans are worried if they can get it.”

Scar tissue: Even as top European officials acknowledge they will need America’s help rearming, some are chafing at the Trump administration’s suggestions that the continent shouldn’t try to replace the U.S. defense industry’s role — even as the Pentagon is signaling that it is removing some U.S. forces from Europe.

“The U.S. is moving the goalpost while demanding Europe take ‘primary responsibility’ for its own defense while opposing the industrial-policy tools to do it,” said Oscar Jonsson, a specialist from the Swedish Defence University. “Most European states figured that buying American won’t reverse the trend of U.S. withdrawal, and it will only prolong an overdependence on the U.S. It’s not unlikely that there will be a compromise with some more buying American, but it’s only a slight delay to the structural shift.”

World.title: Pistorius makes fresh push for Hegseth meeting after spring setback
World.content:
The plans are still being prepared and the individual meetings depend on the minister’s final schedule.

The German defense ministry declined to comment on the plans. However, it would be Pistorius’ second attempt this year to secure a dedicated meeting with Hegseth in Washington.

The German minister abandoned the U.S. leg of a planned North America trip in May after a meeting with Hegseth could not be arranged. Pistorius went ahead with the Canadian portion of the trip, while Hegseth traveled to the Shangri-La Dialogue security conference in Singapore.

The episode was a setback for Berlin as it sought direct access to the Trump administration during a period of growing uncertainty over Washington's military role in Europe.

Pistorius and Hegseth have met before. Most recently, both were at the NATO Summit in Ankara. And during a formal Pentagon visit in July 2025, the two discussed the future of U.S. forces in Europe and Germany's interest in the American Typhon long-range missile system as well as Tomahawk missiles.

Those questions have only become more pressing. Hegseth announced in June a six-month review of U.S. troop deployments in Europe, while Washington has already reduced some of the military capabilities it makes available to NATO. Pistorius has warned that any American withdrawal must be coordinated with European allies to avoid dangerous gaps in the alliance’s defenses.

World.title: Attacks on Ukrainians in Poland rise, police data show
World.content:
The number of nationality-motivated attacks in Poland is steadily increasing, according to data provided to the Polish press by the National Police Headquarters.

 

This month has already seen widespread coverage of a vulgar attack on teenage girls from Ukraine on a municipal bus in Bielsko-Biała. An adult man verbally abused, threatened and insulted the girls for no other reason than that they were speaking Ukrainian.

And this is just one of 180 incidents that were reported to the police in the first half of 2026.

Alarming figures on attacks

Data shows that the scale of aggression against Ukrainians in Poland has risen sharply.

In 2024, Ukrainians living in Poland filed 267 reports of alleged hate crimes. In 2025, that number rose to 275. The 180 reports filed in the first half of 2026 already represent an increase of more than 30% compared with the same period last year, and nearly 35% compared with 2024.

Political blame game

Politicians are trading accusations over who is to blame for the rise in attacks.

Interior and Administration Minister Marcin Kierwiński wrote on X: "Kaczyński, Braun and Czarnek are doing a great deal to ensure that the brown wave spreads across Poland. The victims are both Poles and foreigners. I have a message for all those who have fallen in love with hatred: the police will always respond firmly. Zero tolerance!".

Opposition Law and Justice (PiS) spokesperson Rafał Bochenek said that "Every form of violence and aggression, both physical and verbal, especially against vulnerable people, including children, should be unequivocally condemned and the perpetrators held to account."

He argued that Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Interior and Administration Minister Marcin Kierwiński bear responsibility for such attacks: "Donald Tusk and Marcin Kierwiński have not only deliberately downplayed the rise in aggression on Polish streets so far, they are directly responsible for the brutalisation of public life in Poland".

Polish-Ukrainian relations deteriorate

Ukrainian activist Natalia Panchenko, from the organisation Stand With Ukraine in Poland, sought to ease tensions between Ukrainians and Poles in a Facebook post following the case in which teenage Ukrainian girls were subjected to abusive comments on a municipal bus in Bielsko-Biała.

"The state is fighting xenophobia. Poland stands for the rule of law. Law enforcement agencies, the courts and the law operate here. That is why we should seek to hold the individual perpetrator to account, rather than projecting his actions onto an entire nation. I know many Poles who have been helping Ukraine for years. (...) Some idiot on a bus is not the whole of Poland. Just as any criminal among Ukrainians is not the whole of Ukraine," she wrote.

World.title: Emergency farming law: reintroduction of two banned pesticides splits political parties
World.content:
French MPs are due to vote on Monday evening on the emergency agriculture bill, whose final version was approved last Thursday by a joint committee (CMP). A piece of legislation whose adoption is far from a foregone conclusion.

 

Of the 78 articles contained in the bill, one in particular is splitting France’s political forces: the reintroduction, by way of derogation, of acetamiprid and flupyradifurone – two pesticides banned in France but authorised in the European Union – for certain struggling sectors.

Last year, the bill put forward by Senator Laurent Duplomb, which already envisaged the return of acetamiprid, ran into strong public opposition, leading to a widely supported petition. The provision was ultimately struck down by the Constitutional Council.

A divisive bill, even within the government

In an effort to rally his troops ahead of the vote, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu convened a meeting at Matignon on Monday with the main representatives of the government coalition (Renaissance, MoDem, Horizons, LR), the centrist Liot group, as well as ministers Annie Genevard, Monique Barbut, Mathieu Lefèvre and Laurent Panifous.

The Minister for Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, said on Saturday that the reintroduction of banned pesticides remained "the main sticking point".

"To make this bill fail out of ideology, calculation or fear would utterly dash farmers’ hopes", argued Agriculture Minister Annie Genevard.

Renaissance MP Prisca Thevenot says that "it is urgent that [the bill] be passed and implemented" but that "out of 78 articles there is one that raises questions" and puts the legislation "in mortal danger". She is categorical: "Acetamiprid must not appear in this bill."

Prisca Thévenot listens to Emmanuel Macron during a meeting of the Council of Ministers, on Friday 21 July 2023 at the Élysée Palace in Paris AP Photo/Christophe Ena, Pool

Prisca Thevenot had previously recalled that the government could "always table an amendment to delete acetamiprid" before Monday’s final vote.

The secretary-general of Renaissance, Gabriel Attal, had also urged "the government to table a deleting amendment" for the article concerning acetamiprid, according to a Les Républicains (LR) MP speaking to AFP.

Late on Monday afternoon, people close to Sébastien Lecornu nonetheless confirmed that Matignon was not proposing to scrap this derogation, preferring to let Parliament "decide" the matter.

The current version of the bill is backed by the Rassemblement national (RN) as well as many right-wing and centrist MPs.

By contrast, most Horizons MPs "seem to favour removing acetamiprid", according to a source close to the talks. As for MoDem, while one source indicated that "the acetamiprid totem continues to raise questions for some MPs", no common position has yet been made public.

Environmental concerns

A year after the revolt against the Duplomb law, this new bill is once again dividing French society, at a time when the climate context is sharpening anxieties over environmental protection.

For the environmental association Générations Futures, bringing back banned pesticides would mark "the Senate’s deadly U-turn".

Conversely, the president of the Confédération générale des planteurs de betteraves sucrières (CGB), Franck Sander, believes that the reauthorisation "in a targeted and regulated way" of flupyradifurone "is an essential condition for our competitiveness when all the indicators are flashing red".

Related Study links exposure to agricultural pesticides to cancer risk

The reform of water storage for agricultural irrigation, provided for in the emergency agriculture law, is another source of contention. Several protests against this measure are planned this week, including a demonstration on Monday evening at Les Invalides.

Annie Genevard nonetheless considers this reform a "common-sense" measure. "If we give up on this emergency agriculture law, we condemn the French to imported food. I will not accept that", she said on X.

The vote on this bill in the National Assembly, ahead of its passage to the Senate on Tuesday, comes as recent heatwaves have pushed environmental issues back to the forefront of French concerns.

Almost a third of them (32%) now consider environmental protection a priority issue, according to a poll carried out for La Tribune Dimanche, a 12-point increase.
