World.title: Moscow targeted by drones while Russia bombards Kyiv
World.content:
Ukraine fired more than 400 drones toward Moscow in its latest major attack on the Russian capital, the city's mayor said Monday.

The blitz came hours after Russia bombarded Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities with ballistic missiles in a relentless cycle of tit-for-tat strikes that make a settlement to end Moscow's more than 4-year-old all-out invasion appear a distant possibility.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said the onslaught lasted from late Sunday until early Monday, local time, with most downed far from the city and 85 intercepted near it.

Moscow regional Governor Andrei Vorobyov said 10 people were wounded by Ukrainian drones, while several residential buildings and civilian infrastructure facilities were damaged.

The attack started a fire at the Yuzhnye Vrata industrial park, about 30 kilometres south of Moscow, while a Russian news outlet also reported that an oil depot in Podolsk, about 20 kilometres south of Moscow, was on fire after being struck.

Recent Ukrainian drone attacks are bringing the conflict closer to home for residents of the Russian capital. (Reuters)

Ukrainian forces hit logistics facilities and an oil depot in the Moscow region, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, adding that Kyiv's forces hit two vessels belonging to Russia's so-called shadow fleet transporting sanctioned oil and four dry cargo ships in the Black Sea.

A drone struck a passenger bus in Shebekino in Russia's Belgorod region bordering Ukraine, killing five people — four women and a boy — and injuring 23 others, according to acting Gov. Alexander Shuvayev.

It was not possible to independently verify either side's claims.

Russia steps up ballistic missiles

Ukraine's long-range drone technology has evolved during the war, posing a problem for Russia, whose huge land mass is hard to protect fully. Kyiv's forces have aimed especially at Russian oil facilities, causing fuel shortages and embarrassing Russian President Vladimir Putin.

How Ukraine is breaking through defences to bring war home to Moscow Ukraine's growing arsenal of locally-produced long-range drones are getting increasingly sophisticated, allowing Kyiv to increasingly strike targets across Moscow.

In May, the Russian Defense Ministry said air defences downed 1,054 Ukrainian drones in a 24-hour period.

In response, Russia has turned towards greater use of its ballistic missile stocks, taking advantage of a Ukrainian shortage of intercepters.

Ballistic missiles fly faster than the speed of sound and can reach Kyiv in minutes, giving air defences little time to react and civilians to reach shelter.

"Russian forces have launched more ballistic missiles against Ukraine thus far in July than Russia reportedly produces each month," the Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said late Sunday.

"Russia appears to be dipping into its stockpiles to continue increasing the number of ballistic missiles it launches against Ukraine, as these missiles have a higher success rate than drones and cruise missiles," it noted.

Ukraine's air force said Russia fired two missiles and 94 long-range drones at Ukraine overnight. It said air defences jammed or intercepted 81 drones, while nine drones and a missile caused damage at nine locations.

Ukraine is testing Russia's air defences with drones, while the Kremlin is turning to ballistic missiles that are harder to intercept. (Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Russia's Defense Ministry said Monday its forces struck fuel tanks in the southern Ukrainian port of Odesa overnight.

A Russian strike on Pavlohrad in Ukraine's central Dnipropetrovsk region injured 13 people, according to military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha. Eleven people were hospitalised, including a 13-year-old girl, he added.

Cargo ship attacked

Ukraine's Sea Ports Authority said a cargo vessel under the flag of the West African country of Guinea Bissau was hit by Russian forces on Sunday shortly after it left the port of Odesa, killing 10 of its crew, including five sailors from Syria.

India's foreign ministry added that another four of the victims were Indian nationals, adding that India "condemns such attacks".

Eight people were rescued from the ship, which was carrying Ukrainian corn, it added.

Syria's General Authority for Borders and Customs said it "strongly condemns the repeated attacks targeting commercial vessels with Syrian sailors and crews aboard in Ukrainian ports and nearby maritime areas in the Black Sea, and the resulting deaths and injuries among Syrian sailors."

The Syrian statement did not mention Russia.

Moscow has built relations with the new Syrian government since former President Bashar Assad was ousted in December 2024 in a rebel offensive led by now-interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa.

Zelenskyy faces protests

Mr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said he would hold "key talks" Monday as he tries to defuse a domestic political crisis, after last week's government reshuffle exposed a deep split between the military's old guard and young innovators over how to fight the war.

The Ukrainian president needs to reassure Ukrainians that sacrificing 35-year-old Mykhailo Fedorov as defence minister and keeping faith with 60-year-old Soviet-trained Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi as armed forces chief won't derail the fight against Russia.

Days of street protests in favour of Mr Fedorov and against Mr Syrskyi followed Mr Zelenskyy's reshuffle.

AP

World.title: Spouses of people with dementia have higher risk themselves, study finds
World.content:
Spouses of people with dementia have a higher risk of developing the condition, but the level of risk can vary depending on income and how many children the couple has, a new study has found.

Research published in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) today studied almost 1 million people in Taiwan to examine dementia risk among married couples and what factors might alter that risk.

The researchers found female spouses had a 74 per cent higher risk of all types of dementia if their partner had it, while male spouses had a 69 per cent increased risk if their partner had the condition.

Similar associations were found when researchers studied Alzheimer's disease and vascular dementia separately.

The reasons for these associations, the researchers said, may come down to three overlapping factors:

Assortative mating: The tendency for people to choose partners who are like themselves and have similar education levels or socio-economic background.

The tendency for people to choose partners who are like themselves and have similar education levels or socio-economic background. Shared lifestyles: Partners often have similar dietary habits, exercise patterns or cognitive reserves. Emerging evidence also suggests oral health may be similar in couples and contributes to cognitive outcomes.

Partners often have similar dietary habits, exercise patterns or cognitive reserves. Emerging evidence also suggests oral health may be similar in couples and contributes to cognitive outcomes. If the partner is also a caregiver, this can cause high stress, sleep loss, and social isolation. All of which are risk factors for dementia.

About 1 million people were studied to examine the dementia risk among married couples. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)

Previous research has established spouses who are primary caregivers often have worse mental health and may develop dementia more often, but co-author of the JAMA study, Chi-Shin Wu, said these past studies had some limitations.

"Many were based on relatively small or regional samples [and] our study included spouses in general and did not assume that every spouse was the primary caregiver," Dr Chi-Shin told the ABC.

"This allowed us to examine dementia risk at the household level rather than attributing the association solely to caregiving."

The researchers used data from Taiwan's National Health Insurance research database, which covers nearly 99 per cent of the population, and identified dementia diagnoses among married individuals between 1998 and 2022.

To make a comparison, they also found married couples where neither had any recorded dementia diagnoses at the same point in time.

They took into account the couple's incomes, the number of children they had, their geographical locations and comorbidities like cardiovascular or mental health.

Simone Reppermund, an expert in cognitive disorders from the Centre for Health Brain Ageing at the University of NSW, who was not involved in the study, said it moved the dial on better understanding the condition.

"The researchers controlled for a lot of factors that are important to control for, which is a real strength of this study, and still the risk of dementia was a lot higher," Dr Reppermund said.

The researchers say spouses should be aware but not alarmed by the findings. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)

Once the researchers accounted for extra risk, such as age, they found the increased risk corresponded to an additional 2.75 cases of dementia per 100 women and 3.49 cases per 100 men over five years.

How children and income change risk

The researchers found the risk of dementia was lower for spouses who had more children or a higher income.

Dr Chi-Shin suggested this could be because lower-income households have fewer resources to pay for support, so the spouse has more caregiving stress, while those with fewer children had less potential family support.

"However, because we did not directly measure caregiving responsibilities, intensity or stress, this interpretation remains suggestive rather than conclusive," he said.

Dr Reppermund said income was also a proxy for how well educated someone was, with higher levels of education being a known protective factor against dementia.

But she said people should not assume that having more children always equated to a lower dementia risk.

"The present study showed that number of children played a modifying role, but it depends on the quality of the relationship … the children might be overseas or there might be no relationship whatsoever."

The study's authors acknowledged their research had several limitations, including that they could not analyse the spouses' lifestyle factors such as diet, exercise, smoking, social isolation or hearing.

The World Health Organization recently updated its dementia guidelines to establish the modifiable risk factors for the condition, which can be attributed to 45 per cent of dementia cases.

The risk factors include hearing loss, air pollution, obesity, vision impairment and poor sleep.

Modifiable dementia risk factors: Air pollution

Diabetes

Hypertension

Traumatic brain injury

Early/premature menopause

Obesity

Physical inactivity

Unhealthy diet

Smoking

Stroke

Depression

Cognitive inactivity

Social isolation

Hearing loss

Vision impairment

Poor sleep

Harmful alcohol use

HIV

Dyslipidaemiea Source: World Health Organization

Dr Reppermund said future research must dig deeper into what life looks like for couples where one person has dementia.

"We need to work out whether it's lifestyle that has more of an impact than caregiver stress," she said.

Dr Chi-Shin said spouses should be aware but not alarmed by the research.

"An increased risk is not a certainty, and our observational study does not show that caring for a partner causes dementia. Spouses should not feel blamed for caregiving or assume that they will inevitably develop dementia," he said.

Dr Chi-Shin said spouses must not overlook their own health and continue to look after their sleep, mood, social connections and cardiovascular conditions such as hypertension and diabetes.

They should also access respite care when possible so they can recharge, he added.

At a policy level, Dr Chi-Shin said dementia care must focus more on supporting the household, not just the diagnosed individual.

If this story has prompted any questions or concerns, please call the National Dementia Helpline 1800 100 500 (24 hours, 7 days a week) or visit dementia.org.au.

World.title: Iran-backed Houthis declare maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia
World.content:
The Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia, in a move which could put even greater pressure on international energy supplies.

In a statement, the Houthis military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group would enforce the blockade against its "criminal Saudi enemy" effective immediately.

He said the Houthis were acting in response to Saudi Arabia's "oppressive siege" on Yemen over the past 12 years, and promised the rebels would respond to "any foolish act" by their neighbour to break the restrictions with force.

The war between the US, Israel and Iran sent shockwaves through energy markets given the decision by Tehran to block the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil supplies flowed.

About a fifth of the world's oil supplies flowed through the Strait of Hormuz before Tehran blocked the passage when the war broke out. (Reuters)

While smaller Gulf states such as Kuwait, Bahrain and Qatar suffered major disruption to their exports as a result, Saudi Arabia had been able to use its geography to its advantage and pump oil from its large port precincts on the Persian Gulf to facilities on the west coast.

That allowed it to send shipments out through the Red Sea instead — providing a vital lifeline for the Saudi economy and relieving some, but not all, of the pressure on global oil supplies.

The East-West pipeline, as it is known, had come under attack by Iran at the height of the war.

Blockade expected to target Saudi exports in Bab el-Mandeb Strait

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait is located between Yemen and Djibouti on the Horn of Africa. (Getty Images: Gallo)

The new blockade announced by the Houthis suggested the group would target ships carrying Saudi exports transiting through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — the narrow waterway between Yemen and the Horn of Africa, acting as the gateway to the Red Sea.

It is not clear whether it will cause further disruption to shipping in the area, given the Red Sea also feeds into the Suez Canal.

Yahya Saree's post about the maritime blockade on X. (X: Yahya Saree)

The Houthis have previously attacked ships transiting through in protest over the Israel-Gaza war — a move which forced global shipping companies to take massive detours to avoid the area.

The Houthis and the Saudis have been in conflict for more than a decade, as civil war ripped Yemen apart and the Saudis formed a coalition to try to restore the Yemeni government's rule.

A truce brokered in 2022 had largely held until last week, when the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Yemen's main international airport in a bid to prevent an Iranian plane landing there.

In response, the rebels fired missiles at the Kingdom.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps had threatened to use the Houthis to block the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, as fighting between the US and Iran intensified last week.

World.title: Trump says Iran will 'pay' as US names two soldiers killed in Jordan
World.content:
The United States has identified two soldiers killed while defending against Iranian missile and drone attacks in Jordan, with US President Donald Trump saying the Islamic Republic would "pay" for the killing of US personnel.

Three service members were killed in action over the weekend, taking the American military death toll in the war with Iran climbs to 17.

The Pentagon said 1st Lieutenant Tyler James Feehan, 25, of Hawaii, and Private Isabella Gonzales, 19, of Texas, were killed while supporting the US-led mission against Islamic State in Jordan.

Israel says Iran launched missiles towards Jordan The US warns its citizens to stay away from air and sea ports at Aqaba in southern Jordan, hours before Israeli authorities announced that Iranian missiles had been launched towards the city.

US Central Command said the pair died on Friday while defending against Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks. It has not disclosed how they were killed.

A third service member remains missing after the attack, with Central Command saying "unidentified remains" had been recovered from the site and were undergoing examination.

Mr Trump, in a post on his Truth Social platform, vowed to avenge the killings, saying: "Every time Iran kills an American Soldier they will pay for that killing many times over!"

"This directive has been passed on to Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Daniel Caine, and every Leader in the Military."

The latest deaths underscore the widening reach of the conflict, with US forces stationed across the Middle East increasingly exposed to Iranian retaliation despite not fighting on the ground inside Iran.

President Donald Trump has defended the military campaign as necessary to prevent Iran from developing nuclear weapons, saying the latest US strikes were carried out "in honour" of the fallen troops.

The conflict began on February 28 when the United States and Israel launched strikes targeting Iran's nuclear and missile programs and allied militia groups.

People stand on a bridge destroyed after a strike in Hormozgan province, southern Iran. (AP Photo: Iranian Students' News Agency)

The first American fatalities came days after the war began, when an Iranian drone strike on a civilian port in Kuwait killed six US soldiers from an Iowa-based logistics unit.

A seventh soldier later died from injuries sustained during an Iranian missile attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia.

In March, six service members were killed when a KC-135 refuelling aircraft supporting operations against Iran crashed in Iraq.

On Saturday, another US service member was killed in northern Iraq while carrying out a controlled detonation of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian drone. A second service member was injured.

Separately, the US military said a Navy pilot died after a helicopter crashed into the Arabian Sea earlier this month during what it described as an emergency landing not believed to be caused by hostile action.

Iran claims strikes on US military assets

The Muwaffaq Salti air base, east of Amman, had been targeted, according to unverified video on social media. (Supplied: Planet Labs PBC)

Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Monday they had launched fresh attacks on US military assets across the Middle East after another night of American air strikes on Iranian cities.

The Guards said they targeted Jordan's Aqaba airport, military facilities in Kuwait and positions in Syria with ballistic missiles.

Sirens sounded in Bahrain, while Kuwait's military said it intercepted hostile drones during the attacks.

Iran also claimed two oil tankers had exploded while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz, though Reuters could not independently verify the claim. Separately, British maritime authorities said a commercial vessel had been struck by an unidentified projectile off the coast of Oman.

Israel says Iran launched missiles towards Jordan The US warns its citizens to stay away from air and sea ports at Aqaba in southern Jordan, hours before Israeli authorities announced that Iranian missiles had been launched towards the city.

US Central Command said it had conducted a ninth consecutive night of strikes aimed at degrading Iran's ability to threaten commercial shipping through the strategic waterway.

The conflict has also expanded to attacks on civilian infrastructure.

Kuwait said one of its desalination plants had been struck for a second consecutive day, causing a fire. Desalination facilities provide most of the drinking water for Gulf nations, raising concerns about water security across the region.

Iran has accused the United States of previously striking one of its own desalination plants and has threatened to retaliate against similar facilities elsewhere in the Gulf.

Iranian authorities say at least 50 people have been killed and more than 500 wounded in US strikes over the past three weeks, while the broader conflict has killed thousands of people, mostly in Iran and Lebanon.

Both sides leave door open to diplomacy

Despite the escalating violence, both Washington and Tehran indicated they remained open to renewed negotiations.

Search for Strait of Hormuz alternatives Gulf countries and oil companies have been finding ways to bypass the choke point.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States would continue targeting Iran while it threatened international shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, but said Washington remained open to a diplomatic solution.

Iran's Foreign Ministry also said diplomacy remained "a tool through which we pursue our national interests, just like war", signalling talks had not been ruled out.

The renewed fighting has also pushed oil prices above US$90 a barrel and driven US petrol prices above US$4 a gallon, adding to political pressure on Mr Trump ahead of November's congressional midterm elections.

ABC/wires

World.title: Andy Burnham becomes British PM, provides AUKUS hints in first speech
World.content:
Andy Burnham has pledged to provide immediate cost-of-living relief for Brits and "do politics differently" in his first speech after becoming prime minister.

Speaking outside his new official residence at 10 Downing Street shortly before 1pm local time (10pm AEST) on Monday, Mr Burnham also gave his clearest signal yet he does not plan to alter the AUKUS defence partnership, in which Australia has already invested billions of dollars.

Mr Burnham officially rose to the United Kingdom's top political office on Monday, after a weeks-long process to replace the unpopular incumbent Sir Keir Starmer as Labour Party leader.

The new PM spoke without a lectern, something that represents a significant break with British tradition, and was surrounded by supporters on Downing Street.

Mr Burnham acknowledged the fact he was the country's seventh prime minister in 10 years.

"We will make this moment a circuit breaker for Britain," he said.

Andy Burnham makes a point to reporters on Downing Street. (Reuters: Temilade Adelaja)

Foreign leaders, including Australia's Anthony Albanese, were quick to congratulate Mr Burnham, a former long-time MP who had until last month served as the Mayor of Greater Manchester.

Now, he is in charge of the world's fifth largest economy.

"I look forward to working with you to strengthen our partnership and promote security, resilience and prosperity in the years ahead," Mr Albanese posted on social media.

While Mr Burnham has said little about foreign policies in the past few weeks, he did say on Monday Britain would honour its "defence commitments to international partners" in the clearest sign yet he does not plan to try and tinker with the AUKUS pact.

Signed in September 2021, AUKUS is set to cost Australia at least $300 billion over the next three decades. The UK has had five PMs since the deal was inked, and concerns have been raised that Britain is struggling to keep up with its end of the bargain.

Later on Monday, Mr Burnham spoke to US President Donald Trump on the phone, and invited him to Manchester. President Trump has previously mocked Mr Burnham as the "mayor of some town".

Andy Burnham and King Charles pose for a photo in Buckingham Palace's Chinese Dining Room on Monday. (Reuters: Aaron Chown/Pool )

Unlike in Australia, British prime ministers are not sworn in. Instead, they meet the monarch to take part in an ancient ritual called "kissing hands" (once there was an actual kiss, but these days it is just a conversation).

Mr Burnham arrived at Buckingham Palace about 12:05pm. His meeting with King Charles III took place in the Chinese Dining Room, a few minutes after Sir Keir had been there to tender his resignation.

After his meeting, Mr Burnham travelled to Downing Street where he made his address.

"Later this year, I will bring forward a new plan for Britain, a 10-year plan laying believe we all want Britain to be, wherever we're coming from, whatever party we support," Mr Burnham said.

"But I can do something to give people some breathing space now, some help with the cost of living. And I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them."

Mr Burnham, a former minister in the Brown and Blair governments, has twice stood unsuccessfully to be Labour leader in the past.

Amid Sir Keir's plummeting approval ratings, Mr Burnham returned to national politics via a by-election last month.

As part of his platform, he plans to decentralise power from London and put key services under state control. He said on Monday he would "put people at the heart of everything I do".

"Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again. The moment we bring back hope," he said.

Sir Keir Starmer and his wife Victoria were all smiles outside downing street. (Reuters: Kevin Coombs)

Earlier, Sir Keir gave his final address outside Number 10 Downing Street, the prime minister's official residence, where he said, "My work here is done."

"I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything we have achieved," he said.

Of Mr Burnham, he said: "I wish him every success; he has my full support."

Sir Keir had been Labour leader for more than six years and had won a landslide general election victory two years ago.

However, he had become so unpopular in the UK, his position was seen as untenable by many Labour colleagues and when Mr Burnham returned to Westminster as an MP, he resigned a few days later.

Sir Keir's cabinet overhauled

Mr Burnham's front bench will look vastly different to Sir Keir's.

Justice Secretary and Deputy PM David Lammy, was sacked immediately. The former foreign secretary was a close ally of Sir Keir's.

Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, was also dumped. In what was widely considered a surprise move, she will be replaced by former defence secretary John Healey.

Tony McNulty, a former Labour MP who is now a political scientist at Queen Mary Unviersity London, said Mr Burnham would have plenty of issues to deal with on day one as PM.

"He's going to try and rebuild the broad coalition that is the Labour government. He's already said as much and some of his early appointments point to that," Dr McNulty told 7.30.

"On the policy side, he's had people from the centre right and the centre left working together [already]."

He said Sir Keir's government had done a lot of behind-the-scenes work that would likely make things easier for Mr Burnham. But the public perception was that Labour had not delivered on changes it promised.

The significant gains made by right-wing, populist Reform UK party at May's local elections, led by Brexiter and anti-immigration campaigner, Nigel Farage, was the nail in the coffin for Sir Keir and one of the many reasons why many inside the Labour Party saw no other option but to change leaders mid-term.

Britain's newly appointed Prime Minister Andy Burnham delivers his speech outside 10 Downing Street. (Reuters: Isabel Infantes)

Dr McNulty said Mr Burnham would get a "short honeymoon" period after coming to office.

"I learned when I was a politician that the one thing in short supply, quite rightly, from the public, is gratitude," Dr McNulty, who was in parliament between 1997 and 2010, said.

"They want to know what you're going to give them tomorrow, not what you've given them already, so we shall see but I would be optimistic for Labour at the moment."

Mr Burnham has already announced he will relocate part of the PM's office to Manchester as part of his push to decentralise power.

But Jill Rutter, a former Whitehall civil servant and senior research fellow of the think tank UK in a Changing Europe, said making government less London-centric would be easier said than done.

"The issue of devolution is that it might make sense. I mean, successive governments have now actually built a bit of a consensus that we need to move power out of Whitehall, but it's quite difficult," she told 7.30.

"It's quite tricky. You've got to build up capabilities in the authorities that you're going to devolve power to, to take on tasks that are currently being managed centrally, but what it isn't is a quick fix.

"So, it doesn't deliver you a magic upturn in growth overnight and that's really what Andy Burnham desperately needs to help solve his problems, get him out of the fix he finds himself in."

World.title: Hundreds march on Pine Gap in secretive site's biggest protest in decades
World.content:
Arrernte traditional owners in Central Australia have delivered a letter to the front gates of Pine Gap demanding the return of their land, during the biggest protest outside the secretive military base in decades.

Located in Alice Springs, Pine Gap is a joint Australian-US defence facility that gathers intelligence from a network of surveillance satellites around the globe, and has long attracted controversy over how its intelligence is used.

Protesters called for the facility to be closed and for the return of traditional owners' land.

This afternoon about 300 people gathered near the front of the secretive spy base to raise their concerns over its role in US military operations, including many who had travelled to Alice Springs from across the country to take part.

The turnout made the rally — organised by a range of anti-war, pro-Palestinian and land rights activists — the largest at the site since 1987, when more than 1,000 demonstrators marched up to its gates.

People travelled from all over Australia to attend the protest. (ABC News: Will Green)

NT Police set up a traffic stop a few kilometres from the site to check drivers and passengers' identifications before they were allowed to continue, and about 200 metres from the high-security gated entrance another police blockade stopped people from getting any closer on foot.

As the group moved in unison toward the police barricade, holding signs and flags, they called out a series of chants, including "shut it down", "close Pine Gap" and "always was, always will be Aboriginal land".

Protesters carried signs, placards and flags as they marched towards the site. (ABC News: Will Green)

Among the protesters was New South Wales Greens senator David Shoebridge, who said he was concerned Pine Gap was a "foreign military base set up for the interests of a foreign military" which he believed was "lurching towards right wing politics, not respecting international law".

"We're letting them use our land, this key real estate, I think [to] commit some of the worst atrocities we've seen," he said.

The protest was organised by a range of groups including anti-war, pro-Palestinian and land rights activists. (ABC News: Will Green)

"This is perhaps one of the most secure and peaceful places on the planet, except for the presence of Pine Gap, which brings danger into the heart of our country.

"US bases are targets and the US is quite happy to have their front line in other people's nations."

The protest was the biggest at Pine Gap since 1987. (ABC News: Will Green)

He also backed strong calls in the crowd for the land to be handed back to traditional owners.

When the group neared Pine Gap, Arrernte traditional owners accompanied by a small group of protesters carried a letter to the gates and delivered it senior police officers.

Security was tight outside Pine Gap, with police setting up multiple road blocks outside the top-secret site. (ABC News: Will Green)

The document outlined their calls for their land to be returned and for their need to access sacred sites and rock art inside the facility.

It also demanded compensation for decades of occupation of the site.

Arrernte traditional owner Felicity Hayes told the crowd she wanted her land back, with her words met with resounding applause and cheers from the group.

Hundreds gather in Alice Springs ahead of Pine Gap protest Hundreds of activists have gathered in Alice Springs to join Arrernte traditional owners ahead of a planned protest against the joint Australian-US military base at Pine Gap.

"My country's a sacred place. It's a sacred place for me and my family and for everybody in Australia," she said.

" We don't want Pine Gap to ever exist on our land. "

The demonstration bookends a three-day gathering of activists and academics in Alice Springs designed to draw attention to the role of Pine Gap in global warfare.

The protest's organisers did not rule out returning again, and said they would be demonstrating against Australia's AUKUS agreement with the US in September.

World.title: Alleged murderer denies killing woman, says he knew 'something was wrong'
World.content:
A man accused of murdering a woman in Adelaide's southern suburbs has told a court he is not to blame for her death, and instead alleged the crime was committed by the victim's ex-wife.

Warning: This story contains content some readers may find distressing.

Johnathan Paul Parker, 51, is standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court after pleading not guilty to murdering 38-year-old Krystal Marshall at her Aldinga Beach home in October 2023.

However, at the start of the trial, he pleaded guilty to destroying her remains by setting them on fire.

On Monday, Parker took the stand in his defence and told the court that Anastasia Marshall — Krystal Marshall's ex-wife — was responsible for her death.

He said he had attempted to cover up the crime because he was in an "intimate" relationship with Anastasia Marshall and he "was in love with her".

The court previously heard that Parker, Krystal Marshall and Anastasia Marshall were all living at the same house.

Krystal Marshall's body was found at the scene of a house fire at Aldinga Beach south of Adelaide, prompting a murder investigation by SA Police. (gofundme)

Parker told the court that on October 19, 2023, the trio had an argument before Krystal Marshall's alleged murder.

"I went out and had a couple of cones just to chill out … just to remove myself from the situation," he said.

He added that it "wouldn't have been 10 minutes" before he walked back into the home and asked Anastasia Marshall if the two had stopped arguing.

"Anastasia looked at me, I don't know how to explain it as such, but the way that she looked at me … something was obviously very wrong," he said.

"I opened up the door and I seen [sic] Krystal's body face down on the bed.

"I don't remember exactly how her arms were. But all I remember is seeing her face was down on the bed."

The 51-year-old also told the court that his "mind went to mush" after he confronted Anastasia Marshall.

"I walked back into Anastasia's room and said, 'What the f*** have you done?," Parker told the court.

"She looked at me and said, 'What does it matter? She's dead'."

Krystal Marshall's body was found inside the Aldinga Beach home. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

Parker also told the court that he was not sure why he "thought to use fire" a day later — on October 20 — but that he was "trying to disguise what had happened".

"I just soaked a heap of wood in accelerant," he said.

"I put that over Krystal's body, then I used the last of the accelerant and tipped it over the bed.

"I can't remember how I lit the fire … I know there were some candles in the hallway."

When asked by his barrister Bill Boucaut KC, Parker said his motivation to set Krystal Marshall's body on fire was to protect Anastasia Marshall.

"I was in love with her still, very much, and I started to feel I wanted to protect her from that situation," he said.

"I thought that she loved me."

He added that Krystal Marshall and Anastasia Marshall had a "tumultuous relationship" and "they argued a lot".

"It was common knowledge that they didn't get along that well," Parker told the court.

"They went from just yelling to bumping chests."

Prosecutor asks if evidence 'made up'

In cross examination, prosecutor Jim Pearce KC asked Parker how he knew that Anastasia Marshall had allegedly killed Krystal Marshall if he had not explicitly been told.

Parker told the court that it was the "way she looked at me".

Mr Pearce then asked: "Was there something evil in the way she looked at you?"

"Yeah," Parker responded.

"On what you're telling us, you had no idea how Krystal had died, did you?," Mr Pearce then asked.

Parker responded: "That's correct."

Johnathan Paul Parker is standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court after pleading not guilty to a charge of murder. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Pearce asked if Parker's evidence about how he knew Krystal Marshall was dead was "made up", but Parker said it was "all true".

He also asked the alleged murderer why he did not check for a pulse or call an ambulance, and questioned whether it had crossed his mind that she could have died from natural causes.

"The reason that you didn't make any inquiries is because you didn't have to because you are the one that killed her. You knew full well that she was dead, and how she died, because you were responsible," Mr Pearce said.

"That's not correct," Parker responded.

The trial was previously played prison telephone intercepts in which Anastasia Marshall can be heard telling Parker that he had "f***ing murdered my wife for no f***ing reason".

Mr Pearce will continue his cross-examination of Parker on Tuesday.

The trial is expected to conclude next week.

World.title: Israel criticises Labor's draft Palestine policy ahead of party conference
World.content:
Israel's embassy in Australia has strongly criticised Labor's draft national platform, arguing it places too much responsibility for ongoing conflict on Israel and not enough on Palestinian leaders, or Hamas.

The draft platform will be put to delegates at the national conference in Adelaide this week, and significantly expands Labor's position on the status of Israel and Palestine.

The existing 2023 national platform primarily called on Labor to recognise a Palestinian state, which the Albanese government did in September last year alongside countries like Canada and the United Kingdom.

The new draft introduces a more detailed position on Israel and Palestine, including opposition to Israeli "illegal settlement activity" and settler violence, and condemnation of recent Israeli laws approving the death penalty for Palestinians who murder Israelis.

It also includes support for the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and International Criminal Court (ICC), which has issued an arrest warrant for Israel's prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

International condemnation over Israel's plans for West Bank The United Nations says it is "gravely concerned" over Israeli plans to expand control over the occupied West Bank.

The draft includes a line "unreservedly condemn[ing] terrorism and violent extremism, including as perpetrated by Hamas".

But unlike previous platforms, it contains little that calls Labor governments to concrete actions like recognition, other than suggesting sanctions "as necessary" on illegal settlements.

In a four-page statement to the media, Israel's embassy has taken issue with multiple elements of the draft platform.

It contends that Israeli settlements are not violating international law, as borders between Israel and a Palestinian state are "final-status issues to be resolved through direct negotiations".

It describes settler violence as illegal behaviour but also a "marginal phenomenon".

"In contrast to Palestinian attacks on Israelis, which continue frequently and are not even condemned by the PA, Israel condemns any vigilante attacks and acts to bring them to justice," it said.

"In most cases, settler violence targets possessions while Palestinian violence aspires to murder or injure Israelis."

In a four-page statement to the media, Israel's embassy in Australia has taken issue with multiple elements of the draft platform. (ABC: Callum Flinn)

And it continues Israel's criticism of Australia's recognition of a Palestinian state.

"Such recognition does not bring the sides closer but only distances them from one another," it said.

"Recognition in the absence of genuine reform strengthens the radicals, is perceived as a reward for terrorism, and sends a message that terrorism and intransigence pay off."

The statement takes significant issue with the draft platform's stance on the ICC and ICJ, arguing "both bodies are politicised and maintain a disproportionate focus on the Jewish state".

It broadly argues Labor's draft stance is one-sided.

"[Israel] remains committed to a future in which Israelis and Palestinians live alongside one another in peace and security," the statement reads.

"That future, however, cannot be built through unilateral political declarations or international pressure directed at only one side."

Palestine advocates call for stronger stance

The Australian Palestinian Advocacy Network (APAN) has made its own suggestions for Labor's national platform, calling on the party to take a much stronger stance on the issue.

It wants to see stronger commitments around Australia's defence exports to Israel and further action on illegal settlements, among other suggestions.

"This conference is the moment Labor can choose to draw a clear red line on Australian complicity," said APAN executive officer Katie Shammas.

"That means ending defence exports that risk contributing to atrocities, confronting the illegal settlement enterprise, and ensuring Australia meets its obligations under international law."

Palestinian rights groups file legal action over Israel arms exports Palestinian human rights groups hope the Federal Court provide transparency over Australia's weapons exports to Israel.

The federal government has repeatedly insisted it is not manufacturing any ammunition or weapons and exporting it to Israel, and has not done so for more than five years.

The office of Foreign Minister Penny Wong was contacted for comment on Israel's concerns.

Asked about Israel's complaints, Minister for International Development and Multicultural Affairs Anne Aly said she had yet to see them in full.

But she said the conference would see the proposal fully debated.

"The Israeli embassy can put out what they want to say," she said.

"But the conference is about the Labor Party coming together and settling on our platform and having those robust discussions during the conference in a very democratic way."

World.title: ‘We need to be better’: Arise, Andy Burnham, Britain’s seventh PM in a decade
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeUK politics ‘We need to be better’: Arise, Andy Burnham, Britain’s seventh PM in a decade David Crowe Updated July 20, 2026 — 10:46pm ,first published 7:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has vowed to “bring back hope” to the country after being elevated to the leadership in a meeting with King Charles, declaring that the public deserves better from a new generation of politicians. Burnham promised to deliver help with the cost of living within his first 24 hours in the job, as he arrived at his official residence at 10 Downing Street to deliver his first remarks as prime minister in front of hundreds of reporters. “We have not been good enough, and we need to be better,” he said. “We will be.” Andy Burnham gives his first speech as prime minister outside 10 Downing Street. Getty Images The formal transfer of power concluded after the previous prime minister, Keir Starmer, visited King Charles at Buckingham Palace for a private meeting in which he officially resigned.



That meeting cleared the way for Burnham to visit the King soon afterwards and be invited to form government, elevating him to the top post. In a brief statement, the King confirmed that Burnham accepted the invitation and “kissed hands upon his appointment” – the traditional language used to describe a prime minister accepting the monarch’s invitation to lead government. King Charles welcomes Burnham to Buckingham Palace, where he was invited to form government. Getty Images Charles and Burnham. Getty Images The formal events were broadcast live on multiple television networks and online, while a helicopter flew overhead to capture the moments on a warm summer day in London.



Speaking outside Downing Street after the palace meeting, without notes or a lectern, Burnham said he was “acutely” conscious he was the seventh prime minister since 2016. “It requires my generation of politicians to raise our game and rise to the new challenge,” he said. Burnham and his wife, Marie-France van Heel, wave as they enter 10 Downing Street. AP Photo/Thomas Krych The couple is greeted inside the official residence by top political staff and other advisers. Getty Images “Britain needs to show the world that we can regain our stability once again, and that is our challenge: to make politics work, to make it work better.”



Burnham spoke directly to the main television camera to give a personal assurance to the British people that he would do better than previous prime ministers. “I know people at home are fed up with politics. I hear you,” he said, promising to deliver a “circuit breaker” for a system he said had taken wrong turns since the 1980s. Loading Burnham vowed to decentralise power from London, reindustrialise the economy, end rough sleeping, ensure stronger public control of key industries, build more homes and improve mental health support. He said he would outline help with the cost of living, in a funded government policy, within his first 24 hours.



“It’s about putting the right values and the right standards at the heart of government,” he said. “I will put the care of people at the heart of everything I do. I will give this my all, and I ask you all to pull with me. Burnham said his generation of politicians needed to “raise our game”. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth “Let’s build a new national sense of unity, of common purpose, and positivity. Let us make this the moment when Britain starts to believe again – the moment we bring back hope.” Upon those words, he entered 10 Downing Street with his wife, Marie-France van Heel, to be greeted by top political staff and other advisers.



Earlier, Starmer had left the official residence to give his final address as prime minister in front of dozens of ministerial colleagues, staff and family members including his wife, Victoria. “My work is done. In 6½ years, I took our party from a historic defeat in 2019, changed it so it was fit to face the country, and won a landslide general election victory in 2024,” he said. Keir Starmer receives applause as he leaves No. 10 Downing Street. AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth Starmer and his wife, Victoria, depart Downing Street. Getty Images “Since then, it has been the privilege of my life to serve you and this great country as prime minister, and I am confident that Britain is now stronger and fairer than it was two years ago.”



Starmer said Burnham had his “full support”. “As I now pass the baton to Andy Burnham, I wish him every success,” he said. “I go with good grace, I go with a smile, and I go proud of everything that we have achieved.” King Charles welcomes Starmer to Buckingham Palace, where he officially resigned as PM. Getty Images After being hugged by his wife and embracing some of his supporters, Starmer walked to a waiting car with Victoria and drove to the palace to see the King.



Buckingham Palace confirmed soon afterwards that Charles was “graciously pleased to accept” Starmer’s resignation – the same wording used for the statements about the departures of previous prime ministers. The meetings at Buckingham Palace formally concluded a long fight within the Labour Party to replace Starmer after growing discontent over his leadership, and a year of planning by Burnham and his allies to take power within the party. Sir Clive Alderton, left, principal private secretary to the King and Queen, and King Charles III’s Equerry, Major Ben Rigby, right, greet Burnham and his wife Marie-France van Heel at Buckingham Palace. Aaron Chown/Pool PA via AP In being named to the top post on Monday, Burnham became the nation’s seventh prime minister since 2016. While he has set out broad ambitions in speeches and interviews, he is yet to name his cabinet ministers and settle disputes among his supporters about who should hold the key Treasury post of chancellor of the exchequer.



Bond market investors are watching the cabinet decision closely, given the country’s net public debt is £2.9 trillion ($5.6 trillion) – equivalent to 95 per cent of annual economic output – and rising. Related Article Updated

UK politics ‘Number 10 North’: PM-in-waiting vows major power shift out of London Burnham, who has spent the past nine years as mayor of Greater Manchester, set out broad themes about his plans in a speech three weeks ago, knowing he had the numbers within the Labour Party to lead the government. “We will create a more streamlined state with a clearer purpose to power up all parts of the country and put a laser-like focus on growth and regeneration – good growth,” he said. Burnham, however, captured attention with a related pledge to shift some of the powers of 10 Downing Street in London – near the major public service departments around Whitehall – so that a new unit of government would be responsible for northern England and other areas outside the capital.



Burnham called his proposed new office “Number 10 North”, and the phrase dominated media coverage of his speech, although he did not outline any details on how it would work. Related Article UK politics Four things to know about Andy Burnham, the man likely to be the UK’s next PM Labour has 403 seats in the House of Commons, giving it a comfortable majority. The Conservative Party has 117 seats, the Liberal Democrats have 71, Reform UK has seven and the Greens have five. Small parties and independents make up the rest. But the divisions within the Labour parliamentary party have weakened the government, while Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has made big gains in local government elections and has soared in the public opinion polls as a potential prime minister. Burnham’s rise began in earnest on May 19 when he overcame resistance from Starmer’s allies and gained party approval to run as the Labour candidate at a byelection for the seat of Makerfield, which he won on June 19.



Starmer announced on June 22 that he would resign. With Labour MPs making it clear they wanted a new leader, Starmer set up an internal party timeline to decide his replacement. When party officials called for nominations, Burnham was the sole candidate – an extraordinary development given he had become a member of the House of Commons only days earlier. While Burnham is the seventh prime minister in roughly a decade, he is also being described as the sixth prime minister in 10 years. Former Conservative prime minister David Cameron stepped down on July 13, 2016 – 10 years and one week ago. He was followed by Theresa May, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak from the Conservative Party. They were followed by Starmer and Burnham. World.title: Budget improves by billions, but petrol pain about to grow
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget Budget improves by billions, but petrol pain about to grow Shane Wright July 20, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Billions of dollars have been wiped from the budget deficit and government debt thanks to the ongoing strength of commodity prices and the nation’s jobs market, but consumers face more pain as the war against Iran risks a fresh spike in petrol prices beyond $2 a litre. Weeks after Treasurer Jim Chalmers delivered the budget in which he forecast the just completed financial year would show a $28.3 billion deficit, Treasury believes it will be closer to $23 billion. Boys play in the shallow waters of the Strait of Hormuz. The return of war in the area is likely to push oil prices back towards $2 a litre. AP It is well short of the $49.6 billion deficit that Chalmers forecast for 2025-26 when he delivered his first budget in October 2022. Despite the improvement, the deficit remains a substantial increase over the $10 billion shortfall recorded in 2024-25 and a modest improvement over the $31.5 billion deficit forecast for the current financial year.



The better deficit has contributed to a smaller-than-expected amount of government debt. Gross debt finished the financial year at $971.4 billion, about $10 billion lower than had been forecast in the budget. Related Article Federal budget The tax bill for working Australians is in the mail – and it’s growing But the budget would have to improve markedly to avoid gross debt going through the $1 trillion mark as expected this financial year. Chalmers took credit for the smaller deficit, saying the government had saved upward revisions to revenue collections. “This improvement in the bottom line is another powerful demonstration of our responsible economic management,” he said.



“We’re finding savings, banking upwards revisions to revenue, restraining spending, and we’re addressing structural pressures in the budget and that’s all making a meaningful difference.” But Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the government had led Australia into an economic crisis with a collapse in living standards that was the largest in the developed world. “That’s the ability of people to pay for what they’re used to buying with their pay packets. The purchasing power of their pay packets has gone backwards faster than any other developed country in the world,” he said. The budget’s improved condition could be undone by the resumption of hostilities between the United States and Iran. The price of Brent crude, which had fallen to $US71.80 ($102.70) a barrel at the start of the month, climbed back over the $US90 a barrel mark on Monday.



Movements through the Strait of Hormuz, which had approached their pre-war level just a fortnight ago, have collapsed and analysts are arguing the key waterway is now effectively closed. The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed on Monday that two oil tankers had exploded in the strait. The lift is starting to feed into petrol prices across the country. The Australian Institute of Petroleum reported on Monday that the average metropolitan price for unleaded petrol reached 171.6¢ a litre last week, a 4¢ increase over the past seven days. Since the start of the month, the price of unleaded has increased by 15.1¢ a litre. That includes the halving of the federal government’s reduction in fuel excise, suggesting petrol prices will continue to climb through the rest of the month. The government’s reduction in excise is due to end on August 2.



NAB senior economist Taylor Nugent said the increase in Brent crude was occurring just as excise was returning to its pre-war levels. He said unless there was a rapid change in the global energy market, retail petrol prices would be back above $2 a litre “within a couple of weeks”. Related Article Australian economy Chalmers gives financial regulators fresh marching orders Unleaded petrol is about $1.70 a litre in both Sydney and Melbourne. The last time it was above $2 a litre was in mid-April, after peaking at about $2.50 a litre at the end of March when the Strait of Hormuz had been closed for almost a month. Nugent said a surge in the oil price would be a complication for the Reserve Bank, which next meets on August 10 and 11. Financial markets put the chance of a rate rise at next month’s meeting at less than one in five.



“We continue to expect the RBA will remain on hold as elevated inflation risks are balanced by an outlook for below-trend growth as higher rates and the slowdown in the housing market flow through to activity,” he said. “But higher oil and refined product prices in the past week or so are a reminder that inflation risks remain elevated.” It’s not just petrol prices. LNG prices have jumped to almost $US21 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) over concerns access to gas out of the Middle East will be restricted due to the increase in hostilities. Before the war, LNG was priced at about $US11.50 MMBtu. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Young mum dies in Sunshine Coast unit fire, another woman escapes
World.content:
NationalQueenslandTragedy Young mum dies in Sunshine Coast unit fire, another woman escapes Courtney Kruk and Julius Dennis Updated July 20, 2026 — 9:53pm ,first published 1:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 21-year-old Moreton Bay woman who died after suffering significant burns in a unit fire on the Sunshine Coast has been described as a vibrant and devoted young mother, as police continue to investigate whether the blaze was deliberately lit. Emergency services were called to reports of a unit on King Street in Buderim fully engulfed in flames at 7.30pm on Sunday. Kallangur woman Isabella Nicholls was inside at the time and was unable to escape before sustaining significant, life-threatening burns. 21-year-old Moreton Bay mother Isabella Nicholls died after suffering severe burns in a house fire on the Sunshine Coast. A 32-year-old woman known to Nicholls was also inside when the fire broke out, but managed to escape before it took hold.



Fire crews extinguished the blaze about an hour later. Police said a neighbour treated Nicholls for her burns, before she was rushed to Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital. She died as a result of her injuries about 4.30am on Monday. Emergency services were called to the fire on King Street in Buderim about 7.30pm Sunday. Damian Smith In a statement on Monday, Nicholls’ family described her as a “devoted and loving mother to her beautiful baby boy” and said they were “absolutely shattered” by her death.



“It is with the heaviest of hearts that we share the devastating loss of our beautiful Isabella Nicholls. “Despite the incredible efforts of the medical team, our precious girl passed away surrounded by her loving family at Brisbane’s Royal Women’s Hospital. Loading “Our family is absolutely shattered by this unimaginable loss, and the heartbreak is beyond words. “Isabella was a vibrant, kind and beautiful soul with her whole life ahead of her. She had a smile that could light up any room and a contagious laugh that none of us will ever forget.”



Robert Lowry, from the Sunshine Coast district’s Criminal Investigation Branch, said a crime scene had been declared at the unit on Monday. “The scene was quite confronting for all of the emergency services that attended,” he said. “I feel for the family of the deceased lady, and I understand that the family is also receiving support.” A statement from the family described Nicholls as a devoted mother to her baby boy. Lowry said the investigation was in its early stages, but police were speaking with people who were assisting with their inquiries.



Residents of neighbouring units were evacuated when the fire broke out but have since returned to their homes. Her family has set up a gofundme page to help cover the costs of her funeral and memorial service. Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: Buckley at a ‘fork in the road’ after Tassie’s AFL coach call on Hinkley
World.content:
In today’s AFL briefing: Carlton have sought clarity from prominent commentator David King after he questioned Harry McKay’s pain threshold on Saturday night.

The Magpies and premiership forward Bobby Hill are set to part ways.

Essendon star Nate Caddy has been discharged from hospital and is expected to play this week. Nathan Buckley has opened up about his extreme disappointment on missing out on the gig as the Tasmania Devils’ first senior coach and says the situation has left him at a “fork in the road”. Buckley, who coached Collingwood to the 2018 grand final, has cast strong doubt that he’ll throw his hat in the ring for two other vacant coaching jobs in the AFL – the next senior coaches at Carlton and Essendon. Nathan Buckley says he will stay focused on immediate priorities at Geelong. via Getty Images “I haven’t really reflected on where those roles sit,” a candid Buckley said on Fox Footy on Monday night – little more than 24 hours after he discovered his Tasmania dream had been dashed.



“And I don’t think I will enter those processes [to coach the Bombers or Blues]. “I’m absolutely focused on the next six to 10 weeks [as an assistant coach] with Geelong and how that plays out. “I was committed to that [the Tasmania job]. And that [ambition] ended a day ago.” Ken Hinkley is unveiled in Tasmania. Getty Images The dramatic events unfolded in Tasmania on the weekend as the Devils’ board met and settled on Ken Hinkley as their biggest appointment ahead of joining the AFL for the 2028 season.



Buckley said he was informed by Devils CEO Brendon Gale that he had been unsuccessful. “I heard from Brendon Gale yesterday afternoon with a missed call and then a text because obviously things were moving pretty quickly,” Buckley said. “I went home, kicked the dog, threw the toys out of the cot, and then woke up this morning and went to my job at Geelong. Related Article Exclusive

AFL 2026 Carlton’s coach search narrows with three assistants among four contenders “I think it’s taken me a little bit of time to reflect because I was really keen on it. I was in on it.”



Buckley said he would seek feedback from the Tasmania hierarchy – but only at the right time. “I texted back [to Gale] that ‘I’m disappointed, but thanks for letting me know’. And I’ll come back around and touch base in time [with Tasmania, for some feedback] because it’s obviously a busy time for the Devils,” he said. “Obviously Kenny is the right fit for Tassie. Good luck to them all, and I hope that that goes really well. “I’m sure that they’ll be a great fit.” Buckley said he had no regrets about returning to clubland as an assistant to Geelong premiership coach Chris Scott.



“The future there [at the Cats] for me will inform my next step in footy. I’ve probably wouldn’t have come back in unless I’d looked at Tassie, so it’s a fork in the road,” he said. “And I’m really grateful for where I’m at, rather than maybe just being on the couch, five years in media, without really knowing what I was doing with footy. “But now that I’m back in a club - I don’t know what’s next.”



Blues seek clarity from prominent commentator over McKay injury Jon Pierik Carlton have sought clarity from prominent commentator David King after he questioned Harry McKay’s pain threshold when the star forward went off injured in Saturday’s loss to Collingwood at the MCG. King, a dual North Melbourne premiership player and Fox Footy analyst, said on his breakfast radio show on SEN on Monday that the Blues had called him on Sunday to discuss his comments. “I took the call from Carlton [on Sunday] … and had a lot of [public] feedback about it [his commentary]. Look, my thoughts are my thoughts. I am not necessarily going to back over it too much,” King said.



Out of the game: Carlton lost Harry McKay to a knee injury in the opening term against Collingwood on Saturday. AFL Photos “I think we have spoken about players that go off a little bit easy in the past. I am not saying that’s Harry on this occasion. Clearly, he has got an issue, and they are telling me he will miss two weeks. I was basically referring to an old Denis Paganism which you will know if you listened to what I said earlier.” Asked to elaborate, King said: “All good. They [Blues] disagree with what the discussion was about, which is fine. That’s footy. I am happy to move on from that.” Carlton were contacted for comment. On Sunday the Blues said McKay would be tested this week and might play against Gold Coast at Marvel Stadium next Saturday.





When it became clear McKay would take no further part in the game, King said: “Looks like he’s put a line through himself, putting the jacket on, that’s it, night over. Incredible disappointment. You wonder whether there’s any structural issue there or is it just a pain tolerance discussion?” In the box: Fox Footy commentator David King. Getty Images “This Harry McKay discussion will rage. There’s nothing worse than when a player of that significance is not there. It changes the whole game.” In reference to his former coaches, including premiership great Denis Pagan, King said: “My old coaches would say: ‘I hope that’s a two or three-week [injury]. If that’s a 15-20 minute [injury], you lose a lot of respect’.” Carlton said on the night that McKay had been ruled out by club doctors.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 The inside story of a coaching coup 17 years in the making King added at half-time: “If that’s just a bit of pain management then you’ve got a lot more to answer for. I hope that’s not the case with Harry and time will tell.” McKay, the 2021 Coleman medallist, has battled mental health problems through his career. In the AFL Players Association’s annual insights and impact report released last week, 34 per cent of players said they felt a level of disrespect by broadcast media. This included concerns about a focus on negativity and hyperbole. After seven-straight wins under caretaker coach Josh Fraser, the Blues have lost their past two games, against Hawthorn and Collingwood, but remain in contention for a wildcard berth. They host the Gold Coast at Marvel Stadium on Saturday.



Magpies and star premiership forward preparing to split Jon Pierik Collingwood are working towards parting ways with premiership star Bobby Hill. The 2023 Norm Smith medallist is contracted until the end of 2030 on a deal reportedly worth about $750,000 a season. Industry sources have confirmed conversations between the Magpies and Hill’s management at Mac’s Sports Promotions are ongoing. The Magpies and Mac’s Sports Management were contacted for comment.



Uncertain future: Bobby Hill and Collingwood are working towards a split. Getty Images Hill has not played a senior game since round 21 last year, largely because of personal issues. He had an extended break over summer but was welcomed back into the fold earlier this season. He had been training at suburban grounds with a trainer before returning to the club. The dynamic small forward has played three VFL games, but has not been a consistent presence at the club. Coach Craig McRae has repeatedly said he was excited about Hill’s potential return, but there was always the caveat of the unknown.



McRae said in June that Hill was still working through his personal issues. “Truthfully, battling,” McRae replied when asked about Hill. Loading “He has a bit going on, let’s be really clear. He has a lot going on. He’s a work in progress, but it’s nice to have him in the building. “He’s a long way away from playing footy ... but again, when he’s in our building, at least we get some opportunities to make him feel that he’s loved and appreciated.”



Hill and his partner Georgia Devlin welcomed their third child in May. Seven reported on Monday that Hill was keen for a move to the Brisbane Lions, Gold Coast or Port Adelaide. Hill was originally drafted by Greater Western Sydney with pick No.24 in 2018. He has played 102 senior games across eight seasons.



Bombers confident Caddy will face Hawks Jon Pierik Essendon are confident Nate Caddy will be available for selection this week after he was hospitalised with an irregular heart rate during Sunday’s three-point win over Greater Western Sydney. Caddy was taken to hospital for assessment, having collapsed to the turf when he got to the interchange bench in the first quarter. He had further tests but was given the all clear and discharged on Sunday night. Ready to go: Essendon star Nate Caddy is expected to be available to face the Hawks on Saturday. AFL Photos via Getty Images



Essendon’s general manager of football Daniel McPherson said he expected Caddy to train this week ahead of a clash against arch-rival Hawthorn on Saturday. “There was some concern in the first quarter when Nate’s heart rate became elevated,” McPherson said on Monday. “He was removed from the game, and our medical team assessed him at the ground before sending him to hospital for further assessment. He was discharged last night and is back at home. “He is expected to be able to train and play without concern this week.” Caddy recently signed a contract extension until the end of 2031 in a huge boost for the battling Bombers, who no longer sit in last spot on the ladder.



Wingman Xavier Duursma (hamstring) has been ruled out for the rest of the season. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 ‘A bloody good feeling’: Essendon bask in the glow of landing a win, climbing off the bottom The Bombers were able to sing the club song for only the second time in 31 games after edging the shocked Giants. It was their first win since beating Melbourne in Gather Round in Adelaide on April 11, while they had not tasted victory in Victoria since May last year. It was Dean Solomon’s first win as caretaker coach since replacing Brad Scott in May. While only 14,601 fans attended the game, the scenes of joy for the Bombers were palpable.



“It’s a bloody good feeling. Our footy club’s been on its knees for a period of time, and the footy world’s jumped on that, and they enjoy us sitting at the bottom,” Solomon said. “We’ve felt that, and we don’t like that, so to push back a little bit and get one win, albeit one win, I’m just really happy for these players.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Joyce shouts at dog during ABC interview
World.content:
Joyce shouts at dog during ABC interview

One Nation MP and former deputy prime minister Barnaby Joyce was being interviewed by Sarah Ferguson on 7.30 when he roared at a dog off-camera.

World.title: ‘Sit down!’ Barnaby Joyce went on ABC’s flagship current affairs show ... and barked at a dog
World.content:
PoliticsFederalOne Nation ‘Sit down!’ Barnaby Joyce went on ABC’s flagship current affairs show ... and barked at a dog Alexander Darling July 20, 2026 — 9:08pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

“I, I think … SIT DOWN! … Sorry, it’s a dog.” Barnaby Joyce was about to answer a question on the ABC about whether he was comfortable with where his party leader, Pauline Hanson, was taking him, when he roared at a dog off-camera. Loading It wasn’t clear how close the dog was or what it was doing to raise his ire, but the strange outburst proved the climax of a live nine-minute interview during which he claimed Channel Seven had suggested Hanson meet with British right-wing agitator Tommy Robinson, and appeared to suggest that One Nation could try to identify illegal immigrants using the medical system and parking fine data. When he composed himself, Joyce said he had changed his views the way that many other Australians had.



When journalist Sarah Ferguson asked if he had set a limit on how far he was willing to go in defence of Hanson, Joyce didn’t answer directly. “When you say set a limit, you know, I’ve heard other things today, like she supports returning to the White Australia policy. She doesn’t, and she said that quite clearly on the stage,” he said. Joyce roars at the offending dog. ABC Joyce appeared on the public broadcaster’s 7.30 program following Hanson’s highly publicised trip to Europe, in which she was seen relaxing in Italy with billionaire friend Gina Rinehart, told the Conservative Political Action Conference in London not to apologise for being white, and appeared on a podcast and Channel Seven segment with Robinson. Ferguson then asked whether he endorsed Hanson’s call to bring Robinson to Australia, and Joyce immediately claimed Seven’s program, Spotlight, had suggested Hanson and Robinson meet.



When pushed on the fact Seven denied this, Joyce said he’d read emails and had “a different opinion”. When asked if he agreed with Hanson’s remarks in the Spotlight program that Muslims bred at cost to Australian taxpayers, Joyce again defended his leader: “She also said that obviously it’s not a case of every person of the Islamic faith. There is an issue in Australia that if people go and into a form of balkanisation where you … where there’s not an assimilation, where you go into a form of an alternate culture which is at odds with the egalitarian ethos of Australia, then that creates massive problems. And we saw that in Bondi.” One Nation leader Pauline Hanson talking to Tommy Robinson. X/@TRobinsonNewEra Earlier on Monday, Joyce had backed Hanson’s call for mass deportations – which she later clarified to add that this applied only to people in Australia illegally – and he was pressed on this by Ferguson. “You said today you could wait until overstayers go to see a doctor or a nurse. So will you require GPs and doctors to report visa overstayers to authorities?” Ferguson asked.



The mysterious dog that had riled Joyce then resurfaced off-screen. Related Article Updated

Political leadership ‘Do not apologise for being white’: Hanson takes aim at privilege and trans rights “I have to apologise for the dog,” Joyce began his answer, though there was no disturbance obvious to viewers. “Don’t worry about the dog, just answer the question,” Ferguson pressed calmly. Joyce bristled at this: “Don’t be rude, otherwise this interview will come to a grinding halt.”



Ferguson asked the question again, with Joyce interrupting before she could finish. Editor's pick FIFA World Cup Oops, he did it again: Trump hogs the stage, crashes World Cup trophy lift “Oh no, Sarah that’s ridiculous, unless you want to keep illegal immigrants here, then there’s no point in calling them illegal ...” Asked a third time how One Nation would detect illegal immigrants to deport, Joyce said: “From time to time, they’re going to come across all range of things, whether it’s health issues, whether it’s parking fines, whatever it is. And when they pop up, they’re going to be sent off because otherwise the whole thing’s a farce.” The interview ended with one more reference to the offending, unseen canine.



“Thank you very much indeed for joining us. The dog was no problem,” closed Ferguson. Joyce replied: “It was for me.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.
